title: AxiosHeaders doesn't handle multiple headers returned via fetch adapter
security_topic: Axios header parsing of fetch response
qa_summary: How AxiosHeaders should aggregate multiple Set-Cookie headers without overwriting, answered by citing Node.js HTTP header behavior (Node.js docs: https://nodejs.org/api/http.html#messageheaders).

comments.author: panta82
comments.body:
### Describe the bug

When using fetch adapter in node.js, axios iterates over headers by using `header.entries()` (https://github.com/axios/axios/blob/c96aa6257f5a060fedac27ae424486acd3ee705f/lib/core/AxiosHeaders.js#L104).

Headers from fetch will be in this format:
```
[
  [
    "access-control-allow-credentials",
    "true"
  ],
  [
    "access-control-allow-origin",
    ""
  ],
  [
    "connection",
    "keep-alive"
  ],
  [
    "content-length",
    "1991"
  ],
  [
    "content-type",
    "application/json; charset=utf-8"
  ],
  [
    "date",
    "Tue, 01 Oct 2024 15:49:38 GMT"
  ],
  [
    "keep-alive",
    "timeout=5"
  ],
  [
    "set-cookie",
    "test-name1=test-token1; path=/; httponly"
  ],
  [
    "set-cookie",
    "test-name2=test-token2; path=/; httponly"
  ],
  [
    "vary",
    "Origin, Accept-Encoding"
  ]
]
```

Note that there are 2 cookies set. However, axios will overwrite the first cookie with the second one.

I presume it's expecting to get cookies in an array form. But fetch adapter returns a raw list.

### To Reproduce

https://codesandbox.io/p/devbox/optimistic-worker-mx8tcx?file=%2Findex.js

My output:
```
with http adapter [ 'a=x; Path=/', 'b=y; Path=/' ]
with fetch adapter b=y; Path=/
```

### Code snippet

```js
import axiosLib from "axios";

const axios1 = axiosLib.create({adapter: 'http', maxRedirects: 0, validateStatus: () => true}); 
const resp1 = await axios1.get("http://httpbin.org/cookies/set?a=x&b=y");
console.log('with http adapter', resp1.headers['set-cookie']);

const axios2 = axiosLib.create({adapter: 'fetch', maxRedirects: 0, validateStatus: () => true}); 
const resp2 = await axios2.get("http://httpbin.org/cookies/set?a=x&b=y", {
    fetchOptions: {
        redirect: 'manual'
    }
});
console.log('with fetch adapter', resp2.headers['set-cookie']);
```


### Expected behavior

Fetch adapter should reorganize headers so they are in node.js format, where repeated headers are collected.

### Axios Version

1.7.7

### Adapter Version

bundled fetch

comments.author: panta82
comments.body:
In node.js, I think the rule is:

for all headers:
- for the first occurance -> set as `'h1=v1'`
- for the second occurrence -> convert to `['h1=v1', 'h2=v2']`

for `set-cookie`:
- for the first occurrence -> set as `['h1=v1']`
- for the second occurrence -> append to existing list `['h1=v1', 'h2=v2']`

More info: https://nodejs.org/api/http.html#messageheaders

comments.author: mkhani01
comments.body:
After literally light‑years of debugging I finally discovered that Android’s OkHttp **will not** fetch missing intermediates the way iOS or desktop browsers do. My server was only ever serving the leaf certificate, so every HTTPS call on Android instantly failed with `ERR_NETWORK`.

**The fix is 100% Nginx‑side**—no application‑level hacks needed:

1. **Build a true full‑chain bundle**  
   Concatenate your leaf cert plus all intermediate certs into one file:
 
```bash
   cat /etc/nginx/ssl/<YOUR_DOMAIN>.crt \
       /etc/nginx/ssl/<YOUR_DOMAIN>.ca-bundle \
     > /etc/nginx/ssl/<YOUR_DOMAIN>_fullchain.crt
```


Verify you now have two or more certificates in it:

```bash
grep -c "BEGIN CERTIFICATE" /etc/nginx/ssl/<YOUR_DOMAIN>_fullchain.crt
# → should print 2+
```

2. **Point Nginx at the full‑chain**
   In your SSL server block, reference the new bundle:

   ```nginx
   server {
     listen 443 ssl;
     server_name <YOUR_DOMAIN> www.<YOUR_DOMAIN>;

     ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/ssl/<YOUR_DOMAIN>_fullchain.crt;
     ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/ssl/<YOUR_DOMAIN>.key;

     # …your proxy_pass and other config…
   }
   ```

3. **Test & reload Nginx**

   ```bash
   nginx -t && nginx -s reload
   ```

4. **Confirm the chain**

   ```bash
   openssl s_client -connect <YOUR_DOMAIN>:443 -showcerts
   ```

   You should see both your leaf **and** intermediate(s) listed, ending with:

   ```
   Verify return code: 0 (ok)
   ```

Once Android sees the complete chain, OkHttp will happily complete the TLS handshake and your HTTPS requests will succeed on **both** iOS and Android.

```
::contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
```

title: Server-Side Request Forgery Vulnerability (CVE-2024-39338)
security_topic: availability of fix for SSRF vulnerability in axios
qa_summary: The developer asked if a fix exists for the SSRF vulnerability (CVE-2024-39338), and the answer cites PR #6539 merged and the vulnerability being fixed in axios 1.7.4 (see GHSA-8hc4-vh64-cxmj).

comments.author: jeffhacks
comments.body:
### Describe the bug

Axios is vulnerable to a Server-Side Request Forgery attack caused by unexpected behaviour where requests for path relative URLS gets processed as protocol relative URLs.

This could be leveraged by an attacker to perform arbitrary requests from the server, potentially accessing internal systems or exfiltrating sensitive data.

### To Reproduce

In this vulnerable code snippet, the developer intended to invoke a path relative to the base URL, however it allows an attacker to craft a malicious protocol-relative URL which is then requested by the server. Given protocol-relative URLs are not relevant server-side as there is no protocol to be relative to, the expected result would be an error. Instead, a valid URL is produced and requested.

Example Vulnerable Code
```typescript
const axios = require('axios');

this.axios = axios.create({
  baseURL: 'https://userapi.example.com',
});

//userId = '12345';
userId = '/google.com'

this.axios.get(`/${userId}`).then(function (response) {
  console.log(`config.baseURL:  ${response.config.baseURL}`);
  console.log(`config.method:   ${response.config.method}`);
  console.log(`config.url:      ${response.config.url}`);
  console.log(`res.responseUrl: ${response.request.res.responseUrl}`);
});
```

Expected Output (Prior to axios 1.3.2):
```typescript
(node:10243) UnhandledPromiseRejectionWarning: TypeError [ERR_INVALID_URL]: Invalid URL: //example.org
```

Developer might also have expected:
```yaml
config.baseURL:  https://userapi.example.com
config.method:   get
config.url:      https://userapi.example.com//www.google.com/
res.responseUrl: https://userapi.example.com//www.google.com/
```

Observed Output:
```yaml
config.baseURL:  https://userapi.example.com
config.method:   get
config.url:      //google.com
res.responseUrl: http://www.google.com/
```

This behaviour is potentially unexpected and introduces the potential for attackers to request URLs on arbitrary hosts other than the host in the base URL.

The code related to parsing and preparing the URL for server-side requests, prior to version 1.3.2, only passed one argument to the Node.js URL class.
```typescript
    const fullPath = buildFullPath(config.baseURL, config.url);
    const parsed = new URL(fullPath);
    const protocol = parsed.protocol || supportedProtocols[0];
```

Version 1.3.2 introduced `http://localhost` as a base URL for relative paths (https://github.com/axios/axios/issues/5458)
```typescript
    const fullPath = buildFullPath(config.baseURL, config.url);
    const parsed = new URL(fullPath, 'http://localhost');
    const protocol = parsed.protocol || supportedProtocols[0];
```

As protocol-relative URLs are considered to be absolute, the config.baseURL value is ignored so protocol-relative URLs are passed to the URL class without a protocol. The node.js URL class will then prepend the protocol from `'http://localhost'` to the protocol-relative URL.

For example
```typescript
> new URL('//google.com', 'https://example.org');
URL {
  href: 'https://google.com/',
  ...
}

> new URL('//google.com', 'file://example.org');
URL {
  href: 'file://google.com/',
  ...
}
```

### Expected behavior

An error could be raised when attempting to request protocol-relative URLs server-side as unlike in a client-side browser session, there is no established protocol to be relative to.

comments.author: SilverSting
comments.body:
Hi. Trying to understand this vulnerability better.

**Mixed use of relative and absolute (including, protocol-relative) URLs**

Axios will see `//google.com` as an argument to `get` call, since the text substitution will occur outside of the function call and that's an acceptable value, isn't it? It's quite possible that the same client instance could be used for fetching both relative URL and absolute URL based resources.
```
userId = '/google.com'
this.axios.get(`/${userId}`);
```

Of course this may not align with application developer's expectation (ie. to be relative path). But it feels like that's not Axios' problem to solve. Axios could potentially warn this use pattern (ie. use of baseUrl with non relative path), but it seems too harsh for axios to dictate this.

**Impact of using protocol-relative URLs**

The following code kinda forces `http` protocol if protocol-relative URLs are used. 
```
const parsed = new URL(fullPath, 'http://localhost');
```

Is this the main concern here? I guess an attacker could potentially move away from non-http protocol (eg. local file location, deemed safe) to http protocol to deliver remotely located malicious files into the target system.

**Expected behavior**

>An error could be raised when attempting to request protocol-relative URLs server-side as unlike in a client-side browser session, there is no established protocol to be relative to.

If this is indeed a good solution, then `isAbsoluteURL` could be updated to ignore protocol-relative URLs to produce this output. Please note `config.url` is set by the `_request` [implementation,](https://github.com/axios/axios/blob/c6cce43cd94489f655f4488c5a50ecaf781c94f2/lib/core/Axios.js#L65), so it will be still `//google.com`. But requested url will be **combined** url.

```
config.baseURL:  https://userapi.example.com
config.method:   get
config.url:      //google.com
res.responseUrl: https://userapi.example.com//google.com
```

comments.author: gabrieel1007
UlisesGascon
comments.body:
In this case, the reported vulnerability in `qs` (CVE-2025-15284) is already addressed by default in Express. Current Express releases depend on patched versions of `qs`:

- **Express 4** specifies `"qs": "~6.14.0"`, which resolves to `>=6.14.0 <6.15.0` and therefore pulls in the patched `6.14.1` release by default. Reference: https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/f62378e1bc776259c0a471476c2dc043a02ac762/package.json#L56

- **Express 5** specifies `"qs": "^6.14.0"`, which also pulls in the patched versions automatically. Reference: https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/c2fb76e99f7379b706a5510b4b2dd08a1b710b7b/package.json#L55

As a result, users installing Express without overriding dependency resolutions already receive a version of `qs` that includes the fix, and the reported issue does not represent an unpatched vulnerability in Express itself.

title: location function does not validate potentially malicious URLs
security_topic: validation of Location header schemes
qa_summary: The developer asked whether res.location should validate and reject malicious URL schemes such as javascript: to prevent XSS, and the maintainer replied that per the Express Threat Model (see ThreatModel.md) it is the application's responsibility and non‑HTTP schemes are permitted.

comments.author: xzyingxiashubro
SantiagoCecena
comments.body:
Hi,

I'm interested in working on this issue.

The current behavior of `res.location()` allowing `javascript:` or `data:` schemes in the `Location` header poses a significant **XSS vulnerability**, as browsers might execute such malicious URLs. While `encodeUrl` handles URL encoding, it doesn't validate the safety of the URL scheme itself.

I'd like to propose adding a **scheme validation** step within the `res.location` function. This would involve checking if the provided URL starts with safe schemes like `http://`, `https://`, or is a relative path (`/`). Any other schemes (e.g., `javascript:`, `data:`) would be rejected or handled safely to prevent this type of attack.

I believe this enhancement would significantly improve the **default security of Express** for all users.

Would it be possible for me to pick this up and submit a pull request? I'm happy to discuss the implementation details further.

Thanks,
Santiago

Furthermore, there are perfectly valid use cases for non http schemes in location headers.

qa_summary: Whether CVE-2024-10491 affects Express versions beyond 3.x, with the answer that it is fixed after 3.21.2 and patched in v4 (see CVE-2024-10491 report and maintainer comment).

<!-- The process for bug fixing is:

A vulnerability has been identified in the Express response.links function, allowing for arbitrary resource injection in the Link header when unsanitized data is used.

The issue arises from improper sanitization in Link header values, which can allow a combination of characters like ,, ;, and <> to preload malicious resources.

This vulnerability is especially relevant for dynamic parameters.

comments.author: wesleytodd
ex1st
wesleytodd
comments.body:
We will be recommending folks use a more robust input validation approach for this. If you want, here is the open api library I maintain: https://github.com/wesleytodd/express-openapi/

The reason for this is mainly security around DOS protection. There is no way to support path segment regular expression matching while also avoiding major performance regressions. See more here: https://blakeembrey.com/posts/2024-09-web-redos/

This is a 100% big win for the ecosystem longer term, as regular expression route matching was one of the worst decisions from the early days which has stuck around. So while we understand the pain this change will cause, we stand by this decision as the right thing for the ecosystem and all express users (even if you need to change your approach to this sort of routing).

title: Can express req.headers[x] be an array?
security_topic: array values in request headers for Express/Node.js
qa_summary: The developer needed to know whether Express can include array‑valued headers such as set‑cookie and how to safely combine them, and the answer cites the Node.js HTTP documentation (https://nodejs.org/dist/latest-v21.x/docs/api/http.html#messageheaders) which states that only the set‑cookie header is an array and should not be merged into a string.

comments.author: RobertSandiford
dougwilson
comments.body:
Hello, so the `req.headers` object is just from Node.js HTTP itself; Express.js doesn't set anything there. This means the rules are types are that of the version of Node.js you are running on. Here is their documentation:

https://nodejs.org/dist/latest-v21.x/docs/api/http.html#messageheaders

And notably I see this about array values:

> set-cookie is always an array. Duplicates are added to the array.

I don't think `set-cookie` can be safely combined into a string, which is why it seems the only one that Node.js will put as an array.

I hope that helps.

Edit: also, it is pretty much non-existent that `set-cookie` header would even be in a request to a server like express, as that is a response header, not a request header.

human_note: Accepted because the question is about header typing and runtime behavior in Express/Node, which is valid framework-level behavior. The answer is valid since it correctly states that Express does not transform headers (they come from Node.js), and accurately identifies that set-cookie is the only header that Node may represent as an array in req.headers, while also correctly noting it is primarily a response header rather than a request header.

Instead of using ` res.cookie() ` I've resorted to using the native ` res.setHeader() ` coupled with the [jshttp cookie](https://www.npmjs.com/package/cookie).

```js
        maxAge: 86400,
        secure: true,
        sameSite: 'none',
```

comments.author: sehraramiz
comments.body:
[Dependant](https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/63a5ffcf577abc6015d021f65857b3826d8db74e/fastapi/dependencies/models.py#L15) object has a cache_key attribute which the dependency resolver of fastapi uses it to cache dependencies and use the already resolved dependencies (get_session in this case).
according to [this line](https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/63a5ffcf577abc6015d021f65857b3826d8db74e/fastapi/dependencies/models.py#L58) of Dependant class the cache_key is generated using the **dependency function reference** and **security scopes**.
when you use get_authenticated_user as a security dependency every param in get_authenticated_user gets the security scopes of the parent api (user_activate).
so when resloving dependencies from user_activate with scopes, the param ```session: Session = Depends(get_session)``` gets saved in dependency_cache with a key like ```(<function get_session at 0x7fb87827c9d0>, ('activate'))```
when resloving dependencies from user_activate with no scopes, the param ```session: Session = Depends(get_session)``` gets saved in dependency_cache with a key like ```(<function get_session at 0x7fb87827c9d0>, ())```

i think this behavior might be a security feature.

it might help you to read [this part of the doc](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/sub-dependencies/?h=dependenc#using-the-same-dependency-multiple-times) on dependency cache
and [this part](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/security/oauth2-scopes/?h=dependency#dependency-tree-and-scopes) about dependency tree and scopes.

human_note: Security-relevant dependency injection caching behavior where OAuth2 scopes affect FastAPI dependency resolution keys.

@araujo88 you can ref this issue: https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/issues/394

in summary it is a bug or design issue from starlette, and there is work around:

```python
from typing import Mapping

from starlette.requests import Request

from fastapi import FastAPI, APIRouter, Depends

app = FastAPI()
api_router = APIRouter()

@api_router.post("/")
def read_root(arg: Mapping[str, str]):
    return {"Hello": "World"}

async def auth_middleware(request: Request):
    # you can implement your auth here
    print(await request.json())

# the trick here is including auth_middleware in the dependencies:
app.include_router(api_router, dependencies=[Depends(auth_middleware)])
```
thus this middleware logic will work on every requests, we use it same way in our production env, works fine.

note: `Dependencies` will inject your auth logic into each request, for more detail ref: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/

comments.author: xingdongzhe
comments.body:
@araujo88 It can't be using `self.stream()`, for per request, only one time can use `self.stream()`.  
Or you will hang forever because of `await self.event_message.wait()`  
[You can see here: uvicorn/protocols/http/h11_impl.py#L543](https://github.com/encode/uvicorn/blob/fedf67e68d3f81c846bf3740c8ae21fa133000a4/uvicorn/protocols/http/h11_impl.py#L543)  
This is because that when `self.stream()` done, there are no action to notify `self.event_message`
This `asyncio.Event` will be notified of four actions:
- when Connection Lost
- when body_data received
- when body_data readed done
- when write reponse data done

And you can try this:
```
async for chunk in request.stream():
    print(chunk)
await request.json()
```

I guess that he meant that yellow warning sign.
If you use `SameSite=none`, it is required to set `secure` attribute aswell as described [here](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Set-Cookie/SameSite).

title: jsonable_encoder alters json_encoders of Pydantic objects
security_topic: global encoder mutation causing secret value leakage
qa_summary: The developer needed to know why jsonable_encoder mutates the Pydantic model’s json_encoders causing secret values to be exposed, and the answer provides a concrete fix by merging encoders with `{**encoder, **custom_encoder}` anchored in commit 39cc2925 (see the diff).

comments.author: slackner
comments.body:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar issue and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/samuelcolvin/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, SecretStr
from fastapi.encoders import jsonable_encoder


class Credentials(BaseModel):
    password: SecretStr


ENCODERS = {SecretStr: lambda v: v.get_secret_value() if v is not None else None}

creds = Credentials(password="helloworld")

a = jsonable_encoder(creds)
print(a)  # {'password': '**********'}, as expected
b = jsonable_encoder(creds, custom_encoder=ENCODERS)
print(b)  # {'password': 'helloworld'}, as expected
c = jsonable_encoder(creds)
print(c)  # gives {'password': 'helloworld'}, but should be {'password': '**********'}?


creds = Credentials(password="123456789")

d = jsonable_encoder(creds)
print(d)  # gives {'password': '123456789'}, but should be {'password': '**********'}?
```


### Description

* I'm using `jsonable_encoder` at multiple locations in the code, sometimes with `custom_encoder` and sometimes without.
* My understanding is that passing `custom_encoder` should only affect the current call and not modify any global state.
* What actually happens is that it modifies `__config__.json_encoders`, and as a result, public API endpoints might suddenly start returning secret values that should be filtered.


### Operating System

Linux

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.78.0

### Python Version

Python 3.9.2

### Additional Context

Using Pydantic version 1.9.1.

comments.author: xingdongzhe
comments.body: I see that it use `__config__.json_encoders` and also pass to next call with `encoder`, so could we use `encoder = encoder.copy()` to avoid  modifies `__config__.json_encoders`?

comments.author: slackner
comments.body:
Yes, copying `encoder` before modifying it fixes the issue. Since FastAPI requires at least Python 3.6 merging the dictionaries could also be done with `{**a, **b}`, so an alternative fix would look like this:

```diff
diff --git a/fastapi/encoders.py b/fastapi/encoders.py
index 4b7ffe31..39cc2925 100644
--- a/fastapi/encoders.py
+++ b/fastapi/encoders.py
@@ -52,7 +52,7 @@ def jsonable_encoder(
     if isinstance(obj, BaseModel):
         encoder = getattr(obj.__config__, "json_encoders", {})
         if custom_encoder:
-            encoder.update(custom_encoder)
+            encoder = {**encoder, **custom_encoder}
         obj_dict = obj.dict(
             include=include,  # type: ignore # in Pydantic
             exclude=exclude,  # type: ignore # in Pydantic
```

Note that I'm not sure yet if the change has any negative side effects. Would be good to know to know if there was a reason why `.update()` was used in the first place. :thinking:

comments.author: slackner
comments.body: For reference, the code in question was initially added in https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/pull/715. There is no explanation why the pydantic config itself is updated, so it probably was meant to be a copy in the first place.

https://github.com/zclconf/go-cty/blob/v1.18.0/cty/value_ops.go#L1460-L1462

The https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/pull/38628 fix does not account for the case where the value after evaluation is null.

Just to be clear, this issue did not occur in actual production code. It was discovered during white-box testing when [supporting dynamic module sources in TFLint](https://github.com/terraform-linters/tflint/pull/2521), and such cases are likely to be rare in practice.

title: HTTP backend: TLS config defaults to TLS 1.0, allows protocol downgrade
security_topic: TLS minimum version default and downgrade risk
qa_summary: Whether the HTTP backend really permits a TLS downgrade is answered by Go's crypto/tls documentation showing Config.MinVersion defaults to TLS 1.2, not TLS 1.0.

comments.author: SebTardif
comments.body:
### Terraform Version

```
Terraform v1.16.0-dev (main branch, HEAD)
```

### Terraform Configuration Files

This is an internal code issue in the HTTP backend TLS configuration, not triggered by a specific user config. Any configuration using the HTTP backend with TLS client certificates is affected:

```terraform
terraform {
  backend "http" {
    address        = "https://example.com/state"
    client_cert_file = "/path/to/cert.pem"
    client_key_file  = "/path/to/key.pem"
  }
}
```

### Debug Output

No debug output needed. The issue is visible in the source code at `internal/backend/remote-state/http/backend.go` in the `configureTLS` function: the `tls.Config` is created without setting `MinVersion`, which defaults to TLS 1.0.

### Expected Behavior

The HTTP backend should enforce TLS 1.2 as the minimum protocol version, consistent with the OCI backend (`internal/backend/remote-state/oci/auth.go:323`) and the deprecation of TLS 1.0/1.1 per [RFC 8996](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8996) (March 2021).

### Actual Behavior

The `tls.Config` created by `configureTLS` uses Go's default `MinVersion` of 0, which permits TLS 1.0 and 1.1 connections. This allows protocol downgrade attacks against state data in transit.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Review `internal/backend/remote-state/http/backend.go`, function `configureTLS`
2. Note that `tls.Config{}` is created without `MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12`
3. Compare with OCI backend at `internal/backend/remote-state/oci/auth.go:323` which correctly sets `MinVersion`

### Additional Context

The omission was introduced in #34806 (2024-03-05) during the `helper/schema` refactoring. I intend to submit a fix for this issue and have a working implementation on my fork.

### References

- #34806 (introduced the omission)
- [moby/moby#32056](https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/32056) (Docker/Moby added TLS minimum version enforcement for the same class of downgrade risk)
- Previously submitted as #38546 (closed; resubmitting with issue-first workflow per Contributing.md)
- Fork branch with fix: [`SebTardif/terraform@fix/http-backend-tls-minversion`](https://github.com/SebTardif/terraform/tree/fix/http-backend-tls-minversion)

Thanks for the report! We are actively looking into the issue.

comments.author: liamcervante
comments.body:
Hi @fancybear-dev, Terraform is behaving as documented in this instance: https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/internals/provider-network-mirror-protocol#authentication

Specifically:

> Terraform does not send credentials when retrieving the archives whose URLs are given in the "List Available Installation Packages" response below. If a particular mirror considers the distribution packages themselves to be sensitive then it must use cryptographically-secure, user-specific, and time-limited URLs in the metadata response. Strategies for doing so are out of scope of this protocol documentation.

The next version of Terraform (v1.11) will support using a `.netrc` file to support adding credentials to the follow up requests, which may work for you in the short term: https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.11.x/providers#private-providers

In the longer term, please follow this enhancement requests for updates on this issue more generally: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/29349

Thanks!

Hey @BroMattMiller,

Thank you for reporting this! The S3 backend is managed by the AWS Provider team at HashiCorp, and this issue has been added to their triage queue. Thanks again!

comments.author: bschaatsbergen
comments.body:
Based on your debug logs, I noticed references to object locking. Could you confirm if S3 Object Lock is enabled on your bucket, and if default retention is enabled, as this is often used to prevent deletion and overwriting of files? AFAIK, the `Content-MD5` or `x-amz-sdk-checksum-algorithm` header is required for any request to upload an object with a retention period configured using Object Lock.

Please note that the lock file is expected to be written to the S3 bucket and deleted when the lock is cleaned up, which could potentially conflict with how Object Lock is configured on the S3 bucket.

I haven’t been able to replicate this issue with an S3 bucket that has Object Lock enabled but default retention disabled. I’ll take some time to set up an S3 bucket with both Object Lock and default retention enabled to investigate further and get back to you as soon as I have an update.

**Update**: I can replicate the issue with an S3 bucket configured with Object Lock and default retention set to Governance for X days.

comments.author: BroMattMiller
comments.body: Yes, I have enabled Object Lock, per AWS Security Hub control S3.15, "S3 general purpose buckets should have Object Lock enabled." The retention mode is Governance and the retention date is 30 days. The credentials used by Terraform do have the necessary privileges to override this.

comments.author: bschaatsbergen
comments.body:
For some additional context, when S3 Object Lock is enabled on a bucket with a retention period, Amazon S3 requires the `Content-MD5` or` x-amz-sdk-checksum-algorithm` header for object uploads via PutObject to ensure data integrity during the upload process. For more details, see [Uploading objects to an Object Lock enabled bucket](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock-managing.html#object-lock-managing-events).

It appears that the default behavior of the `skip_checksum` flag for the lock file was not maintained when writing the lock file to S3 Object Lock-enabled buckets.

To clarify the default behavior of `skip_checksum`: by default, if this argument is not set in the backend, we set the S3 checksum algorithm behavior to SHA256. This causes the underlying S3 AWS SDK V2 serializers to automatically append the that required `x-amz-sdk-checksum-algorithm` header. For more details, see the relevant code in the [AWS SDK v2 serializers](https://github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/blob/8939ed049c8b3490f9a3dbd4e4d3d56cf22a27f2/service/s3/serializers.go#L7494-L7497).

I think it should be possible to swap out the current base S3 client with the [s3manager](https://github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/tree/8939ed049c8b3490f9a3dbd4e4d3d56cf22a27f2/feature/s3/manager) to handle writing lock files to S3 Object Lock-enabled buckets the same way as we write state, and perserve the default behavior of `skip_checksum` when writing a lock file too.

A vulnerability was identified in Consul and Consul Enterprise (“Consul”) such that using Headers in L7 traffic intentions could bypass HTTP header based access rules.

Installed version: v1.13.0 

Fixed version: 1.20.1

CVE-2024-51744 - github.com/golang-jwt/jwt/v4

golang-jwt is a Go implementation of JSON Web Tokens. Unclear documentation of the error behavior in `ParseWithClaims` can lead to situation where users are potentially not checking errors in the way they should be. Especially, if a token is both expired and invalid, the errors returned by `ParseWithClaims` return both error codes. If users only check for the `jwt.ErrTokenExpired ` using `error.Is`, they will ignore the embedded `jwt.ErrTokenSignatureInvalid` and thus potentially accept invalid tokens. A fix has been back-ported with the error handling logic from the `v5` branch to the `v4` branch. In this logic, the `ParseWithClaims` function will immediately return in "dangerous" situations (e.g., an invalid signature), limiting the combined errors only to situations where the signature is valid, but further validation failed (e.g., if the signature is valid, but is expired AND has the wrong audience). This fix is part of the 4.5.1 release. We are aware that this changes the behaviour of an established func

Installed version: v4.4.2

Fixed version: v4.5.1

comments.author: liamcervante
comments.body:
Hi @yolocs, thanks for filing this.

I can confirm that Terraform isn't attaching authentication to the follow up requests when retrieving the `downloadUrl` and the `shasumUrl`. This is because both the public and private registries return publicly available URLs for these attributes. This means that it is difficult for us to change this without breaking our primary points of integration.

I do agree that this behaviour isn't documented, I've tagged this issue as a documentation improvement and raised with the internal docs team.

Could you attach temporary credentials to the returned URLs? Or copy the behaviour of the private registry which returns temporary unauthenticated endpoints?

Thanks!

title: Using hashes for sensitive variables in terraform.tfstate
security_topic: hashing sensitive variables in state files
qa_summary: Whether Terraform should protect sensitive values in tfstate by hashing them, with the maintainer pointing to issue #516 and the in-progress ephemeral values concept as the relevant source.

comments.author: wieso-itzi
comments.body:
### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.9.7
on linux_amd64
```


### Use Cases

Terraform stores the values of variables inside the terraform.tfstate file in plain-text, no matter if they are sensitive or not. The reasoning behing this is that Terraform needs to be aware of changes to these variables in order to properly handle e. g. a terraform apply after changing a variable.

However I believe that if for sensitive variable the text in the tfstate file wasn't the plain-text variable but something like a hash digest of the actual value, it would increase security drastically and this would still allow Terraform to check for changes since different input variables lead to different digests.

### Attempted Solutions

I haven't yet tried or looked into how this could be implemented, but I would be glad to work on the proposed solution.

### Proposal

_No response_

_No response_

Any link to the original bug fix around this?

comments.author: liamcervante
comments.body:
Hi @seblatre, we don't have a specific issue for this as it seems to have been fixed by a change made to add additional support for an unrelated feature.

The PR that fixed it is #34414, with this being the more specific commit: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/commit/fc756571130af35fc33e4f5651c9db487df6d861

In the current code the line that removes the marks you can see are being complained about in the error is here: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/terraform/context_plan.go#L287.

comments.author: liamcervante
comments.body:
Actually, I will reopen this. Within the test framework specifically we are checking for sensitive marks as a way to warn if they are being lost: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/backend/local/test.go#L1249-L1269

However, we are not checking the embedded values within complex types so that is probably the actual root cause of this issue originally. The fact the plan functionality now handles marked values does not address the bug in the test framework.

As it is I think we don't need to print that warning anymore, as the plan can now handle sensitive marks on inputs properly. I'll leave this open as a bug, and we can stop stripping the sensitive marks from inputs within the test framework.

### What feature do you want to see added?

I would like to see the ability to grant Admin rights to a user, but fence them into specific categories of configuration. For example, on a shared Jenkins site you don't want to grant Admin rights to users and risk exposing projects others should not see. But that also prevents users from creating Cloud Nodes that use Docker images as slaves.

_No response_

comments.author: daniel-beck
comments.body:
This is what Overall/Manage permission is for: https://www.jenkins.io/jep/223

Anything that cannot be used to elevate one's own permission to Administer should ultimately use Manage. The problem is that many features can be used in that way. If a feature you want them "fenced in" like that can be used to elevate permissions, it's not suitable.

### What Operating System are you using (both controller, and any agents involved in the problem)?

Fedora 43

### Reproduction steps

   1. Initialize a clean Jenkins installation using `HudsonPrivateSecurityRealm` as the security realm.
   2. Ensure no user accounts have been created yet (initial setup state).
   3. Simultaneously send multiple concurrent POST requests to the `/securityRealm/createFirstAccount` endpoint with different usernames and valid account details.
   4. Verify the number of users created and their permissions.


### Expected Results

Only the very first request should succeed in creating an account. All subsequent concurrent requests should fail with a 401 Unauthorized error (or similar) because a user already exists or is being created, preventing the creation of multiple initial administrator accounts.

### Actual Results

A race condition exists in `HudsonPrivateSecurityRealm.doCreateFirstAccount`. The `hasSomeUser()` check is non-atomic and unsynchronized. In testing with 20 concurrent threads, 20 different user accounts were created, and all 20 were granted administrative privileges via `tryToMakeAdmin(u)`.

### Anything else?

The vulnerability is a classic Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use race condition in `core/src/main/java/hudson/security/HudsonPrivateSecurityRealm.java` between lines 366-376. While impact is limited to the initial setup phase, it allows an attacker to gain admin access if they can time requests during the window before the first user is fully persisted.

### Are you interested in contributing a fix?

Yes, the fix involves adding a static lock object to synchronize the `doCreateFirstAccount` method. This ensures the `hasSomeUser()` check and subsequent user creation are atomic.

title: kube-proxy nftables: entire sync fails when any single Service generates a comment exceeding 128 characters
security_topic: nftables comment length limit causing kube-proxy sync failure
qa_summary: Whether kube-proxy’s nftables sync can fail cluster-wide from an overlong comment, based on the nft error confirming the 128-character limit.

comments.author: RomanPavelko
comments.body:
__What happened?__

When running kube-proxy in `mode: nftables`, if any Service causes kube-proxy to generate an nftables comment exceeding the Linux kernel's 128-character limit, __the entire nftables transaction is rejected and no service routing rules are applied on that sync cycle__. kube-proxy retries every 30 seconds and fails every time until the offending Service is removed. During this time, __all ClusterIP routing is broken cluster-wide__, including kube-dns.

__How to reproduce__

1. Run a cluster with kube-proxy in `mode: nftables` (recommended default since Kubernetes 1.35)
2. Create a Service where the combined kube-proxy comment string `<namespace>/<service-name>:<port-name>` exceeds 128 characters

A realistic example:

- Namespace: `loft-acme-platform-services-team-dev-v-shared-workloads-ns-001` __(62 chars ✅ valid k8s namespace)__
- Service name: `my-api-svc-x-my-api-namespace-x-acme-shared-vcluster--a1b2c3d4e` __(63 chars ✅ valid k8s service name)__
- kube-proxy comment: `loft-acme-platform-services-team-dev-v-shared-workloads-ns-001/my-api-svc-x-my-api-namespace-x-acme-shared-vcluster--a1b2c3d4e:http` → __131 characters ❌ kernel rejects__

Both the namespace (62 chars) and the service name (63 chars) are individually valid Kubernetes DNS labels (≤63 chars each) and are accepted by the Kubernetes API. It is only the __combined string that kube-proxy constructs for the nftables comment__ — `<namespace>/<name>:<port>` — that exceeds the 128-char kernel limit.

This scenario occurs naturally with tools like __vCluster__, which syncs virtual-cluster Services to the host namespace using the pattern `<svc>-x-<ns>-x-<vcluster>--<hash>`. vCluster correctly truncates the service name to ≤63 chars per Kubernetes spec. However, when combined with a long management namespace name (e.g. `loft-<team>-<env>-v-<vcluster>`), the resulting nftables comment string can exceed 128 characters.

__What you expected to happen__

kube-proxy should either:

- Truncate the nftables comment to ≤128 characters (or omit it entirely) and continue syncing all other service rules successfully, OR
- Skip only the offending Service and continue applying rules for all others

__What actually happened__

kube-proxy logs show the following error on every sync attempt (every 30 seconds):

```javascript
E proxier.go:1788] "nftables sync failed" err=<
    /dev/stdin:1473:84-216: Error: comment too long, 128 characters maximum allowed
    add element ip kube-proxy no-endpoint-services { 10.96.1.100 . tcp . 80 comment "loft-acme-platform-services-team-dev-v-shared-workloads-ns-001/my-api-svc-x-my-api-namespace-x-acme-shared-vcluster--a1b2c3d4e:http" : goto reject-chain }
                                                                                     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
 > ipFamily="IPv4"
I proxier.go:1143] "Sync failed" ipFamily="IPv4" retryingTime="30s"
```

The sync fails __atomically__ — nftables applies rules in a single transaction, so one bad comment causes the __entire ruleset to be rejected__. This means zero ClusterIP routing rules exist on any node during the failure window.

__Impact__

- All Kubernetes Services become unreachable via ClusterIP on all nodes simultaneously
- `kube-dns` ClusterIP is unreachable → DNS stops working for all pods cluster-wide
- Workloads that depend on DNS (e.g. StatefulSets using headless service DNS for peer discovery such as etcd HA clusters) cannot initialize
- The failure is silent from a pod perspective — packets are dropped, not refused with an error
- Only removing the offending Service restores normal operation

__Kubernetes version__

```javascript
Server Version: v1.35.0
```

__kube-proxy mode__

```yaml
mode: nftables
```

__OS / kernel__

Talos Linux, kernel 6.x (nftables native mode)

__Suggested fix__

The nftables comment is purely for human readability — it has no functional effect on routing. The fix should be straightforward: __truncate comment strings to ≤128 characters__ before including them in nftables statements. The iptables proxier does not have this issue.

Only observed so far in `pull-kubernetes-kind-dra-all`, not yet in `ci-kind-dra-all`.

This definitely isn't related to any particular PR. The same failure can be seen in at least 5 different PRs, including https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137664 which makes no changes.

security_topic: whether kubelet serving-certificate rotation is actually broken or just delayed by rotation jitter relative to EKS certificate lifetime

comments.author: mlushpenko
comments.body:
### What happened?

On EKS clusters running kubelet `v1.34.4-eks-f69f56f` on Bottlerocket 1.57.0 (`aws-k8s-1.34`), a subset of nodes appear to silently skip serving-certificate rotation entirely.

The initial bootstrap CSR is issued at node boot and approved normally by EKS's built-in CSR approver. After that, for the full life of the affected node (38+ days observed):

- `kubelet_certificate_manager_server_rotation_seconds_count` stays at `0`.
- `kubelet_server_expiration_renew_errors == 0`.
- No CSR is ever submitted from the node (`kubectl get csr` shows none from the affected node while sibling nodes' CSRs exist and are approved).
- `journalctl -u kubelet --since -40d | grep -iE "certificate_manager|csr|rotat|serving cert"` returns only the initial-bootstrap `"no serving certificate available for the kubelet"` TLS handshake errors from the first minute of boot. Nothing afterward.
- The serving cert's `NotAfter` passes through the usual rotation threshold (~day 30 of its ~45-day lifetime) without any attempt, and eventually triggers the `KubeletServerCertificateExpiration` alert.

Only one cert file exists on disk:

```
-rw-------.  1 root root 1256 Mar 27 15:34 kubelet-server-2026-03-27-15-34-40.pem
lrwxrwxrwx.  1 root root   59 Mar 27 15:34 kubelet-server-current.pem -> .../kubelet-server-2026-03-27-15-34-40.pem
```

Kubelet PID is unchanged for the full 38 days (process never restarted/crashed). Node is `Ready`, heartbeats OK, `node.status.addresses` populated on the API server.

I'm not 100% sure this is a kubelet bug rather than something I've missed in our setup — posting cautiously in case someone more familiar with the cert-manager code can sanity-check. I believe I've ruled out the usual config/infra suspects (see "Anything else" below).

**Related, already-closed issues/PRs I reviewed:**

- #130001 (Kubelet serving CSR never created)
- #130415 (node reports Ready before server CSR created → templates never populate)
- #130409 (link-local IPv6 → no addresses → no CSR)
- Fix PR #130362 "Use node addresses from informer in kubelet certificate manager" (merged 2025-04-25, confirmed present in v1.34.4 via `git log --contains`)

The symptom here is in the same family as #130415 but on the *rotation* path rather than initial bootstrap (the initial bootstrap CSR *does* succeed). So I suspect the 2025-04 fix may not fully cover the rotation-deadline path.

**Speculative root-cause trace (please sanity-check):**

Tracing v1.34.4:

- `pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go:900` constructs the server cert manager with `klet.getLastObservedNodeAddresses` as the `getAddresses` callback.
- `pkg/kubelet/kubelet_getters.go:472` implements it as `kl.GetNode()` → `kl.nodeLister.Get(nodeName)` on a per-node field-selector-filtered SharedInformer (`pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go:465-475`).
- `pkg/kubelet/certificate/kubelet.go:47` `newGetTemplateFn` returns `nil` when `len(ips) == 0`.
- `staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/certificate/certificate_manager.go:449-452`:

  ```go
  // Don't enter rotateCerts and trigger backoff if we don't even have a template to request yet
  if m.getTemplate() == nil {
      return
  }
  ```

If at the moment the rotation deadline fires the per-node informer transiently returns an empty `status.addresses` (or the goroutine evaluating `getTemplate()` races with informer re-list/resync), the rotation function `return`s **without rescheduling**. The only way it re-enters is via a template-changed watch event — so if no subsequent event makes the template transition (informer already settled at the same state), the rotation loop never re-fires for the lifetime of the kubelet.

That code shape — a silent early return with no retry timer — would explain the exact pattern we see (zero attempts, zero errors, zero logs, across 38 days of uptime). PR #130362 moved the *initial* template sourcing off a field that depended on the node-status-update loop, but the rotation-deadline path still depends on `nodeLister.Get()` returning a populated `status.addresses`.

I may be wrong about the root cause — if someone who knows this code can confirm/deny the race, I'd be happy to add `klog.V(2)` around the `return` at `:449` to distinguish "template nil" from "template matches last" on long-running nodes.

### What did you expect to happen?

Either:

- The cert-manager wakes at `nextRotationDeadline` (~day 30 of a 45-day cert), submits a CSR, and logs `"Certificate rotation deadline determined"` / `"Certificate template changed, rotating"` from `staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/certificate/certificate_manager.go`;

- OR a failure increments `kubelet_server_expiration_renew_errors` with a descriptive log line.

On the affected nodes, neither happens — the rotation loop appears to either never start or to exit early before reaching `rotateCerts`, and stays silent for the rest of the node's life.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I don't have a deterministic reproducer — it looks probabilistic at boot.

Environment where it reliably reproduces at roughly 15–20% per-node rate:

1. EKS 1.34 control plane (tested with `v1.34.6-eks-bbe087e`).
2. Bottlerocket `aws-k8s-1.34` v1.57.0 nodes, kubelet `v1.34.4-eks-f69f56f`.
3. Kubelet config: `serverTLSBootstrap: true`, default `RotateKubeletServerCertificate` (enabled), no flag overrides.
4. EKS built-in kube-controller-manager CSR auto-approver (no external approver needed — sibling nodes' CSRs approve with message `"Auto approving self kubelet server certificate after SubjectAccessReview"` which matches upstream `pkg/controller/certificates/approver/sarapprove.go`).
5. Karpenter-managed on-demand nodes.

Observation procedure on any long-lived node:

```
# On apiserver
kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/metrics" \
  | grep -E 'kubelet_certificate_manager_server_(ttl_seconds|rotation_seconds_count)|kubelet_server_expiration_renew_errors'

# On node (via Bottlerocket admin container):
sheltie ls -la /var/lib/kubelet/pki/
sheltie journalctl -u kubelet --since $(boot-time) | grep -iE "certificate_manager|csr|rotat|serving cert"
```

Across a prod cluster of ~115 non-Fargate nodes, 6 system-nodes booted within the same minute from the same AMI / same NodePool / same IAM role / same kubelet config:

- 5 rotated cleanly at ~day 35 (`rotation_seconds_count == 1`, matching CSR present and approved).
- 1 did not (`rotation_seconds_count == 0` at day 38, no CSR ever requested).

Fleet-wide across four EKS 1.34 clusters: ~15–20% of nodes that survive past the rotation window silently fail to rotate. Most of our churn replaces nodes before the rotation window fires, which is why the bug is easy to miss on faster-churning clusters.

Happy to capture additional diagnostics on a confirmed-affected node if it would help — goroutine dump, `klog -v=4` after kubelet restart (though restart may mask the bug), captured CSR history from siblings, etc.

### Anything else we need to know?

**Config I was able to rule out before posting:**

- `serverTLSBootstrap: true` in kubelet config (Bottlerocket ships this default in `sources/shared-defaults/kubernetes-aws.toml`), confirmed via `apiclient get settings.kubernetes.server-tls-bootstrap`.
- `RotateKubeletServerCertificate` feature gate — GA since 1.12, enabled by default, no flag overrides on our end.
- `rotateCertificates` — default `true` in `KubeletConfiguration`.
- EKS CSR auto-approver is working (same cluster, same approver, approves 5/6 sibling CSRs cleanly).
- RBAC / IAM — identical to siblings that rotate fine.
- Node clock — node posts heartbeats correctly.

Six sibling nodes booted **within the same minute** from the same Karpenter NodeClass (identical AMI, kubelet flags, NodePool, IAM role, subnet, VPC). Five rotated; one didn't. That isolates the fault to kubelet-internal rotation logic, not our config / approver / infra.

**Fleet-wide impact** (for sense of scope, not for dramatic effect):

- Prod `application` cluster: 101/115 non-Fargate nodes currently have `rotation_seconds_count=0`. Most are too young to have entered the rotation window — the bug is latent, only materializing on nodes that survive past ~day 30–35.
- Our workaround: reducing Karpenter `expireAfter` from 100d to 35d to guarantee nodes are replaced before the rotation window is ever reached. This avoids the alert but doesn't surface the underlying bug.

**Why I chose "probably a bug" rather than user error:** given identical config across 6 nodes with 5 rotating cleanly, I don't see a config-level explanation. Happy to be told otherwise.

```console

Client Version: v1.35.4
Kustomize Version: v5.7.1
Server Version: v1.34.6-eks-bbe087e

# Affected node kubelet version:
Kubernetes v1.34.4-eks-f69f56f
```

comments.author: lumaks-redox
comments.body:
Retracting this report. I grabbed a goroutine dump from an affected node and my theory turned out to be wrong.

```
goroutine 211 [select, 54886 minutes]:
k8s.io/client-go/util/certificate.(*manager).run.func1(...)
    certificate_manager.go:436 +0x229
```

The rotation goroutine is **not** stuck or missing — it is legitimately asleep inside the `select { case <-timer.C: case <-templateChanged: }`, waiting for a timer set by `sleepInterval := deadline.Sub(m.now())`. The sleep age (54886 min ≈ 38.11 d) matches kubelet uptime, so `rotate` was called once at boot, computed its deadline, entered the select, and has been waiting ever since. My "silent early return with no retry" analysis was incorrect; I missed that the outer `wait.UntilWithContext(..., rotate, time.Second)` (line 496) is a retry loop anyway, and more importantly that the goroutine simply hadn't woken up yet — it hasn't missed any wakeup.

The actual situation on the affected node:

- Cert `NotAfter` ≈ `now + 6.97d`, lifetime = 45d → `NotBefore ≈ now − 38.03d`.
- `nextRotationDeadline` returns `NotBefore + jitteryDuration(45d)`, where `jitteryDuration ∈ [0.7, 0.9) × 45d = [31.5d, 40.5d)`.
- The timer hasn't fired, so the jitter value must be ≥ 38.03/45 = **0.845**. Deadline is somewhere in the next ≤ 2.47 days, still comfortably before expiry.
- Rotation will happen on its own before the cert actually expires.

The alert I was chasing (\`KubeletServerCertificateExpiration\`, threshold < 7d) fires naturally when jitter lands in \`[0.844, 0.9)\` of the cert lifetime, because:

- EKS hard-caps \`kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving\` certs at **45 days** (per [AWS EKS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/cert-signing.html)).
- Kubelet's rotation jitter ends at \`0.9 × lifetime = 40.5d\`, i.e. a rotation wake-up as late as **4.5 days before expiry**.
- The Prometheus-operator alert threshold is **7 days**.

On a cert lifetime of ~45d, about 28% of nodes will mathematically land in \`[0.844, 0.9)\` and trip the 7-day alert even though rotation is perfectly healthy and will fire before expiry. On longer cert lifetimes (kube-controller-manager default 1 year), 0.9 × 365 = 328.5d leaves 36.5d of headroom above the 7-day threshold — not a problem. The interaction is specifically with EKS's unusually short 45-day signer lifetime.

None of this is a kubelet bug. Sorry for the noise. Closing as not planned. If someone wants to argue the jitter range should scale down for shorter cert lifetimes, or that the upstream alert threshold should be a fraction of lifetime rather than a fixed 7d, those are defensible discussions but belong in the respective component repos (kubelet / kube-prometheus-stack).

Workarounds for anyone hitting this on EKS:

1. Replace nodes before \`0.844 × lifetime\` (e.g. Karpenter \`expireAfter: 840h\` for a 45-day cert) — avoids the jitter window entirely.
2. Lower the alert threshold below \`0.1 × lifetime\` (<4.5d for EKS), or express it as a fraction of the cert lifetime.

Thanks for the patience.

title: Kubelet can leave projected service account token expired after transient TokenRequest/NodeAuthorizer failures during control-plane restart
security_topic: projected service account token refresh after transient kubelet/apiserver failures
qa_summary: Whether projected service account token refresh can get stuck after transient kubelet TokenRequest failures, with the concrete anchor being the linked kubelet token manager code in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3cf3d54eaa58738efa283b2273a4dd24c8fd6766/pkg/kubelet/token/token_manager.go#L96-L103 and the maintainer’s explanation of its retry behavior.

comments.author: Zariel
comments.body:
### What happened?

After upgrading a Talos Kubernetes cluster from v1.35 to v1.36, some running pods stopped receiving projected service account token rotations. The affected pods were not terminating.

During the control-plane restart window, kubelet logged transient TokenRequest / NodeAuthorizer failures like:

`Error preparing data for projected volume sa-token for pod network/external-5f8b6fdd5c-g4vzm: failed to fetch token: serviceaccounts "external" is forbidden: User "system:node:k8s-1" cannot create resource "serviceaccounts/token" in API group "" in the namespace "network": no relationship found between node 'k8s-1' and this object`

There were also kubelet TokenRequest EOFs against the local API endpoint:

`Couldn't update token: Post "https://127.0.0.1:7445/api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/serviceaccounts/default/token": EOF`

After the API server became healthy again, the projected token files stayed stale for hours. Example affected pod:

pod: network/external-5f8b6fdd5c-g4vzm
node: k8s-1
token iat: 2026-04-28T20:46:41Z
token exp: 2026-04-28T21:46:41Z
projected volume symlink stayed at: ..2026_04_28_20_46_41...

A second pod on another node had a token issued at 2026-04-28T20:52:02Z, expiring at 2026-04-28T21:52:02Z, and also remained frozen at that timestamp.

The application impact was Envoy Gateway data-plane pods failing xDS authentication after token expiry:

`failed to validate token {"error": "token review found error: [invalid bearer token, service account token has expired]"}`

Because the Envoy data-plane could not reconnect to xDS, it kept stale endpoint config until the pods were restarted.


### What did you expect to happen?

For running pods, kubelet should keep retrying projected service account token refresh after transient TokenRequest/API server/NodeAuthorizer failures.

A temporary failure during apiserver restart should not leave the projected token file permanently stale or expired. Once the apiserver/NodeAuthorizer state is healthy again, kubelet should recover token rotation without
requiring the pod to be restarted.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I do not yet have a minimal deterministic reproducer, but the observed incident was:

1. Run a pod with a projected service account token, for example expirationSeconds: 3600.
2. Restart or upgrade the control plane while kubelet is refreshing projected tokens.
3. During the restart, kubelet receives TokenRequest failures such as:
   serviceaccounts "<name>" is forbidden ... no relationship found between node '<node>' and this object
   or EOFs from the API endpoint.
4. Wait past the projected token expiration.
5. Inspect the projected token file/symlink inside the pod or from the host.
6. Observe that the token remains expired and the projected volume timestamp does not advance, even after the API server is healthy again.
7. Restarting the pod causes a fresh token to be mounted and resolves the issue.


### Anything else we need to know?

This does not appear to be an application-level token caching issue. In the observed case, Envoy’s SDS secret last-updated timestamp matched the projected token file timestamp. The file itself stopped changing.

This also seems different from:

- #116481, which involves terminating pods/preStop hooks.
- #130442, which involved PVCs in terminating state.

The affected pods here were ordinary running pods.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version -o yaml
serverVersion:
  gitVersion: v1.36.0
  gitCommit: ecf6decece6a6de25a57aad9ba90b6ce580f6f78
  platform: linux/amd64
clientVersion:
  gitVersion: v1.34.3
  platform: darwin/arm64
```

</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
Bare metal / home lab. No external cloud provider.
</details>


### OS version

<details>

```console
Talos v1.13.0
Kernel: 6.18.24-talos
Architecture: amd64
Nodes: k8s-0, k8s-1, k8s-2
```

</details>


### Install tools

<details>

</details>


### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

<details>
containerd://2.2.3
</details>


### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

<details>

Multus: v4.2.4
CSI/storage: Rook Ceph v1.19.5

comments.body:
I'd like to work on this.

The flake is a race condition in the `wait.PollUntilContextTimeout` callbacks. When the node authorizer can't find the pod yet (informer lag), the callback returns `(false, err)` which terminates the poll immediately instead of retrying. The fix is to return `(false, nil)` on transient errors so the poll keeps retrying as intended.

The same pattern exists in several other poll callbacks in the file -- I'll fix those too.

title: kubelet: QoS-level memory.min / memory.low is not cleared after MemoryQoS feature gate is disabled (regression from #138430)
security_topic: feature-gate rollback behavior for memory QoS cleanup
qa_summary: Whether disabling Kubernetes MemoryQoS should reset QoS-level memory.min/memory.low to default values, anchored on the KEP 2570 MemoryQoS rollback promise and the referenced fix PRs #137719 and #138430.

comments.author: shaun0927
comments.body:
### What happened?

After #138430 re-gated the call to `setMemoryQoS` behind `utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.Enabled(kubefeatures.MemoryQoS)`, disabling the `MemoryQoS` alpha feature gate no longer clears stale `memory.min` / `memory.low` values from QoS-level cgroups (`kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice`, `kubepods.slice/kubepods-guaranteed.slice`, etc.) on cgroup v2 unified systems.

Before #138430, `setMemoryQoS` was invoked unconditionally from `UpdateCgroups` on cgroup v2 unified mode. Its zero-out branch at [`pkg/kubelet/cm/qos_container_manager_linux.go#L303-L308`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/qos_container_manager_linux.go#L303-L308) resets `memory.min` / `memory.low` to 0 whenever `memoryReservationPolicy != TieredReservation`, which covers the "feature disabled or policy = None" case. With the gate check added at [L358](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/qos_container_manager_linux.go#L358), that zero-out branch is unreachable whenever the gate is off.

This is the QoS-level analogue of the pod-level regression that #137674 / #137726 already address. #137726 added `ReconcilePodMemoryMin` on `podContainerManagerImpl` but does not touch QoS-level cgroups, so the stale values at the QoS level remain indefinitely on any node that previously ran with the alpha gate enabled and was later rolled back.

### What did you expect to happen?

When MemoryQoS is disabled (feature gate off, or `memoryReservationPolicy = None`), QoS-level `memory.min` / `memory.low` should be reset to 0 on the next `UpdateCgroups` cycle. This matches the explicit assumption in #137674 that "QoS-level cgroups are correctly reset via the periodic `setMemoryQoS()` loop."

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Cgroup v2 unified node.
2. Start kubelet with `--feature-gates=MemoryQoS=true` and `memoryReservationPolicy: HardReservation`.
3. Create a few Burstable pods so that QoS-level values are populated. Verify:
   `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/memory.low` → non-zero.
4. Disable the gate by restarting kubelet with `--feature-gates=MemoryQoS=false` (or set `memoryReservationPolicy: None`).
5. After the next `UpdateCgroups` cycle, observe that `memory.low` still carries the previous non-zero value. Restart kubelet and repeat — the value persists.

### Anything else we need to know?

- Closely related: #137674 (pod-level tracking issue), #137726 (pod-level fix), #137889 (earlier removal of `reconcilePodMemoryProtection`), #138431 (motivated #138430).
- The pod-level fix in #137726 does not cover QoS-level cgroups; there is no existing analogue on `qosContainerManagerImpl`.

### Proposed fix options

There are two viable approaches; I would appreciate guidance from sig-node on which shape is preferred:

1. **Keep `setMemoryQoS` unconditional** on cgroup v2 unified mode inside `UpdateCgroups`, and move the feature-gate check *inside* `setMemoryQoS` so it still runs the zero-out branch (L303–L308) but skips the populate branch. Minimal diff; preserves the original cleanup contract.
2. **Add a QoS-level reconcile method** analogous to `ReconcilePodMemoryMin` (#137726) that walks QoS cgroups and zeroes `memory.min` / `memory.low` when the gate is off. Larger diff but symmetric with the pod-level structure.

### Kubernetes version

master at `03779bbd0042` and any release branch that carries the #138430 backports.

/sig node
/area kubelet
/kind bug
/kind regression

comments.author: liggitt
comments.body: I'm not sure I agree this is a regression, the current behavior in master matches 1.35 behavior, right?

comments.author: liggitt
comments.body: In any case, we should not be adding new ungated behavior into 1.36 related to Alpha features that impacts clusters that never opted into the alpha.

comments.author: liggitt
comments.body:
> Before https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138430, setMemoryQoS was invoked unconditionally from UpdateCgroups on cgroup v2 unified mode. 

Yes. That was a regression from 1.35 behavior with undesirable side effects on cpu cgroups and modifying cluster behavior for node which hadn't opted into the alpha feature.

title: [sig-node] Summary API should report resource usage through the stats api failing on ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-alpha-features
security_topic: kubelet/containerd CPU stats reporting bypass due to zero UsageNanoCores
qa_summary: Whether containerd’s 1-second CPU stats returning UsageNanoCores=0 can make kubelet bypass its fallback and fail the summary API test, anchored on containerd/containerd#13138, containerd/containerd#12629, and the referenced kubernetes/kubernetes#138423 PR.

comments.author: kannon92
comments.body:
### Which jobs are failing?

`ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-alpha-features`

Example run: https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-alpha-features/2044318744003481600

### Which tests are failing?

`[sig-node] Summary API [NodeConformance] when querying /stats/summary should report resource usage through the stats api`

Fails on both COS and Ubuntu nodes with:
```
.Pods[...::stats-busybox-{0,1}].Containers[busybox-container].CPU.UsageNanoCores:
    Expected <uint64>: 0 to be >= <int>: 10000
.Pods[...::stats-busybox-{0,1}].CPU.UsageNanoCores:
    Expected <uint64>: 0 to be >= <int>: 10000
```

### Since when has it been failing?

All available runs (90+) are failing, going back to at least `v1.36.0-alpha.0.647` (build 2011700799951867904).

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#cos-cgroupv2-containerd-node-e2e-alpha-features

### Reason for failure (if possible)

The job runs with `AllAlpha=true`, which enables `PodAndContainerStatsFromCRI=true`. This causes the kubelet to fetch stats via `ListPodSandboxStats` from containerd (built from main branch).

Containerd returns `UsageNanoCores` as a non-nil `UInt64Value{Value: 0}` rather than computing the actual value or leaving the field nil. Because the kubelet sees a non-nil value, it trusts it and bypasses its own cache-based delta computation (`cri_stats_provider.go:1002-1003`, `1026-1027`) that would correctly calculate nanocores from `UsageCoreNanoSeconds`.

The fix could be:
1. **containerd**: compute `UsageNanoCores` from the cgroup CPU delta, or leave the field nil so the kubelet's fallback kicks in.
2. **kubelet**: treat `UsageNanoCores.Value == 0` as "not provided" and fall through to the cache-based computation.
3. **test**: relax pod/container CPU expectations to allow 0 when `PodAndContainerStatsFromCRI` is enabled, similar to what was already done for system containers at `summary_test.go:105`.

### Anything else we need to know?

The system container CPU expectation already allows zero at `summary_test.go:105`:
```go
"UsageNanoCores": gomega.SatisfyAny(gstruct.PointTo(gomega.BeZero()), bounded(10000, 2e9)),
```
But pod container (`summary_test.go:184`) and pod-level (`summary_test.go:235`) expectations strictly require `bounded(10000, 1e9)`.

### Relevant SIG(s)

/sig node

comments.author: natasha41575
comments.body:
Discussed in the sig node CI meeting that we might just want to skip this test for versions of containerd that does not have the support

to dive deeper into it

comments.author: kannon92
comments.body:
### Additional analysis: containerd stats collector returning 0

The containerd fix in containerd/containerd#13138 (merged 2026-03-30) is included in the containerd build used by this job (`2.3.0-beta.1-23-g95cc75cc6`), but it doesn't fully resolve the issue.

That fix only addresses the case where there aren't enough samples yet (< 2) — it now returns `nil` instead of `{Value: 0}`. However, the background `StatsCollector` (added in containerd/containerd#12629) runs every 1 second, and `GetLatestUsageNanoCores()` returns the rate from the **single latest 1-second sample only**:

```go
// timed_store.go
func (s *TimedStore) GetLatestUsageNanoCores() (uint64, bool) {
    if len(s.buffer) < 2 {
        return 0, false  // fixed by #13138
    }
    sample := s.buffer[len(s.buffer)-1]
    return sample.UsageNanoCores, true  // can return 0, true for idle containers
}
```

When the computed rate is `0` (container idle during that 1-second window), it returns `(0, true)`. The caller in `getUsageNanoCores` treats that as a valid authoritative value and sends `UsageNanoCores: {Value: 0}` to the kubelet, which bypasses its own cache-based fallback computation.

The test pods run `ping -c 1 google.com; echo ...; sleep 1` in a loop. With cgroupv2 reporting CPU in microseconds, a container in `sleep` can show zero CPU delta between two consecutive 1-second samples. Unlike cAdvisor (which computes instantaneous CPU over a longer housekeeping interval), containerd's collector uses only the latest 1-second rate, making it much more susceptible to reporting 0 for low-CPU workloads.

Prior discussion on the same underlying problem:
- containerd/containerd#9531 (closed as not-planned)
- kubernetes/kubernetes#122092
- containerd/containerd#10010 (closed, superseded by #12629)

security_topic: applicability of a dependency PATH-hijacking advisory to unsupported platforms
qa_summary: Whether the OpenTelemetry SDK PATH hijacking vulnerability GHSA-hfvc-g4fc-pqhx / CVE-2026-39883 affects Kubernetes, with the answer resting on the opentelemetry-go host_id_bsd.go source and the Kubernetes changelog link noting unsupported BSD/Solaris platforms.

comments.author: Sheikh-Abubaker
comments.body:
### What happened?

### Summary
A high-severity (7.3/10) vulnerability (GHSA-hfvc-g4fc-pqhx / CVE-2026-39883) has been identified in the `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk` dependency used by Kubernetes. The issue arises from an incomplete fix for a prior advisory, where the BSD `kenv` command is executed without an absolute path, enabling a potential PATH hijacking attack.

This vulnerability was discovered using **[Vulnerabilis](https://vulnerabilis.com/ )**, an AI-powered vulnerability analysis agent for Open Source that generates SBOMs, scans them using Grype, and provides AI-driven risk analysis and remediation steps.

### Vulnerability Details
- **CVE:** CVE-2026-39883
- **GHSA:** GHSA-hfvc-g4fc-pqhx
- **Package:** go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk
- **Affected Versions:** >= v1.15.0, <= v1.42.0
- **Patched Version:** v1.43.0
- **Severity:** High (7.3)

### Discovery Methodology
This vulnerability was identified through **[Vulnerabilis](https://vulnerabilis.com/)** with the following automated pipeline:

1. **SBOM Generation:** Created for the Kubernetes repository using Syft.
2. **Vulnerability Scanning:** The SBOM is analyzed using Grype.
3. **AI-Powered Analysis:** Vulnerabilis evaluated risk, impact, and remediation steps.

title: edit ClusterRole grants namespace-scoped ServiceAccount impersonation — documentation + hardening request
security_topic: applicability of ServiceAccount impersonation in the edit ClusterRole
qa_summary: Whether the default `edit` ClusterRole’s ServiceAccount impersonation is a real namespace privilege-escalation risk, with the answer resting on the referenced `bootstrappolicy/policy.go:157-159` comment and the cited impersonation filter code plus KEP 5284 constrained impersonation.

comments.author: travis-burmaster
comments.body:
## Summary

A source-code audit of the kube-apiserver RBAC, admission, and authentication subsystems found that the default `edit` ClusterRole grants the `impersonate` verb on `serviceaccounts`, enabling namespace-scoped privilege escalation when privileged ServiceAccounts exist in the same namespace.

This behavior is acknowledged in code comments (`bootstrappolicy/policy.go:157` labels it an "escalating resource") and KEP 5284 introduces constrained impersonation as a replacement, but the risk is not prominently documented in the ClusterRole reference pages and most cluster operators are unaware.

## Impact

Any user with `edit` (via RoleBinding) in namespace X can:
1. Impersonate **any** ServiceAccount in namespace X via `Impersonate-User: system:serviceaccount:X:<name>`
2. Inherit all permissions of that ServiceAccount, including ClusterRoleBindings
3. If any SA in the namespace has `admin` or `cluster-admin` privileges (common for CI/CD, GitOps, and monitoring SAs), this is a direct privilege escalation path

The `admin` ClusterRole also inherits this rule via aggregation.

## Reproduction

```bash
# User has "edit" RoleBinding in namespace "production"
# "deploy-bot" SA in the same namespace has admin ClusterRoleBinding

kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:production:deploy-bot
kubectl get secrets -n production --as=system:serviceaccount:production:deploy-bot
kubectl create rolebinding escalate --clusterrole=admin \
  --user=attacker -n production \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:production:deploy-bot
```

## Scope Limitations

- Namespace-scoped only (RoleBinding in X does not grant impersonation in Y)
- SA-only (edit does not grant impersonate on users, groups, UIDs, or extras)
- Impersonation chaining is blocked (headers stripped before forwarding)

## Requests

1. **Documentation:** Add a prominent security note to the `edit` and `admin` ClusterRole reference documentation warning that these roles include ServiceAccount impersonation
2. **Hardening guidance:** Recommend operators audit SA bindings in namespaces where `edit`/`admin` is granted
3. **Consider removing `impersonate` from `editRules()`** in `bootstrappolicy/policy.go:159`, gated behind a feature flag if needed for backward compatibility
4. **Accelerate KEP 5284** constrained impersonation as the long-term replacement

## Code References

- Bootstrap policy rule: `plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/policy.go:159`
- Impersonation filter: `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/filters/impersonation/impersonation.go:74-118`
- "Escalating resource" comment: `bootstrappolicy/policy.go:157`
- KEP 5284: constrained impersonation (`staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/filters/impersonation/constrained_impersonation.go:41`)

## Full Audit Report

The complete audit (9 findings across RBAC, admission, and authn — 420 Go files reviewed) is published in the OSS Security Knowledge Base:

https://github.com/travis-burmaster/oss-security-kb/blob/main/wiki/kubernetes/kube-apiserver.md

## Additional Findings

The same audit identified three additional medium-severity issues in the admission control subsystem:
- Admission reinvocation skips newly-matching webhooks after label mutation
- Dry-run requests silently skip webhooks with `failurePolicy: Ignore` + `sideEffects: nil`
- Fail-open webhook bypass via induced timeout/network disruption

Details in the full audit report linked above.

title: `iptables.minSyncPeriod` working on iptables-restore start, rather than completion
security_topic: minSyncPeriod timing semantics in kube-proxy bounded frequency runner
qa_summary: Whether kube-proxy’s minSyncPeriod behavior is intentionally burst-based in older BoundedFrequencyRunner code and how the updated 1.34 implementation changes that, anchored by the linked runner source and the 6c1cd99aef09161ddb07b8ade6c9564e9b9bfe27 commit.

comments.author: cdirubbio
comments.body:
### What happened?

Was looking into the use/adjustment of minSyncPeriod of `kube-proxy` in my clusters and have seen that `minSyncPeriod` is measured based off of sync-start to sync-start, rather than completion of last sync to the start of the next sync.

See an example below, where my `minSyncPeriod` is set to 14s, and the time between completion of last sync, and start of next sync, is only 12 seconds. BUT, the time between sync-start to sync-start, is the actual 14s minSyncPeriod time.
```
I0327 21:36:58.067431       1 proxier.go:815] "Syncing iptables rules" ipFamily="IPv4" fullSync=false
I0327 21:36:59.360840       1 proxier.go:1536] "Reloading service iptables data" ipFamily="IPv4" numServices=3595 numEndpoints=138792 numFilterChains=6 numFilterRules=46 numNATChains=12044 numNATRules=38841
I0327 21:37:00.882055       1 proxier.go:809] "SyncProxyRules complete" ipFamily="IPv4" elapsed="2.837692607s"
I0327 21:37:12.067991       1 proxier.go:815] "Syncing iptables rules" ipFamily="IPv4" fullSync=false
```



### What did you expect to happen?

Doing some checking of the KP code, I came across the [boundedFrequencyRunner](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/16c5a6be07bb2eab06b6e7732eb1cb759a7fe61c/pkg/proxy/runner/bounded_frequency_runner.go#L44-L62) code comments which mention the below, **seemingly contradicting what sounds like is supposed to happen.**
```
// The runner guarantees two properties:
//  1. Minimum Interval (`minInterval`): At least `minInterval` must pass between
//     the *completion* of one execution and the *start* of the next. Calls to
//     `Run()` during this cooldown period are coalesced and deferred until the
//     interval expires. This prevents burst executions.
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
~ on ☁️  (us-east-1) ➜  kgd nginx -oyaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  labels:
    app: nginx
    role: backend
  name: nginx
  namespace: default
spec:
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 600
  replicas: 50
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
      role: backend
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
    type: RollingUpdate
  template:
    metadata:
      creationTimestamp: null
      labels:
        app: nginx
        role: backend
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: nginx:stable
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        name: nginx
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
```

```

DEPLOYMENT="nginx"
NAMESPACE="default"
MIN=50
MAX=100
INTERVAL=10  # seconds between scale operations

while true; do
  echo "$(date) - Scaling up to $MAX"
  kubectl scale deployment "$DEPLOYMENT" --replicas="$MAX" -n "$NAMESPACE"
  sleep "$INTERVAL"

  echo "$(date) - Scaling down to $MIN"
  kubectl scale deployment "$DEPLOYMENT" --replicas="$MIN" -n "$NAMESPACE"

done
```
