comments.author: deivse
comments.body:
For examples on how the ExtensionPolicy API can be used, you can reference the tests, for example this one:
https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/5e899038809a0895f75423524dcb832a580b77de/tests/x509/verification/test_verification.py#L383

### There are two main differences between a ClientVerifier and a ServerVerifier:
1. A ServerVerifier is built with a specific `subject`, and the verification will fail if the certificate doesn't contain a SAN extension which matches the `subject` specified in `build_server_verifier`. So this is intended to be used when you know who the certificate must belong to, which is the case when connecting to a server via https. In many other cases you don't know the subject in advance. Then ClientVerifier can be used, which doesn't require that the SAN extension contains a specific value.
Despite not knowing the exact subject, you may still have eg. a whitelist of possible subjects, and after calling `ClientVerifier.verify`, you can access the subjects from the SAN extension via `VerifiedClient.subjects`.

2. The default EE extension policies check the EKU extension. For ClientVerifier, it is required to have the ClientAuth EKU, and for ServerVerifier, ServerAuth. The EKU is not currently user configurable (although this may be exposed later via a method on PolicyBuilder), however you can create a custom extension validator callback and use a custom extension policy that will constrain the EKU in any way you want.

### Why some properties are on `Policy` but not on `PolicyBuilder` 
The current `Policy` class is basically a direct mapping to python from a rust struct that contains context required for chain building and certificate verification/validation. The main purpose of the `Policy` class is to expose this context to python extension validation callbacks (as set by `ExtensionPolicy.may_be_present` and similar methods) so that the callbacks can express complex constraints based on these parameters. There wasn't really a per-property decision process on whether to include something there or not, but I don't think it hurts to have extra stuff there since we can't envision every use case. Some of these properties, for example, EKU, as you have noted, can not yet be configured by the user. However they can still be useful, for example you might want to write a verification callback for another extension that makes a decision based on what EKU value is required by the policy.

You are right that this might be a bit confusing currently, and there is a slight leakage of implementation details into the public API. However this could not be reasonably avoided currently I would say, and I would err on the side of the `Policy` class providing access to extra properties rather than trying to predict every use case. Maybe there's something to be said about the naming - there is a clear parallel between `PolicyBuilder` and `Policy`, but, as @loewexy said, not all properties configurable via the builder are accessible on `Policy` and vice versa. I don't have any good ideas on how to improve this currently, but maybe we _can_ come up with a better name for `Policy`

comments.author: deivse
comments.body:
Oh yeah, and regarding having the extension policies or the store as properties on `Policy`:
1. For the extension policies, I don't see a strong use case currently, and it would require creating a mapping from rust to python (which currently is only the other way around), which is not something you want to do, trust me 😄
2. The store is not really part of the `Policy`, since it's potentially specific to verifying a single certificate, whereas a policy (conceptually here, not necessarily the `Policy` class) can be used to verify any number of certificates issued by different CAs.

That second point brings me to a renaming idea, which might actually make sense, but it's a breaking change unfortunately - instead of renaming `Policy` it would maybe make more sense to rename `PolicyBuilder` to something like `VerifierBuilder`. It sounds worse, but does make more sense conceptually imo, since what you actually build with it are verifiers, not policies, and you can also set things that are not part of the policy - the certificate store. Any thoughts on this, @alex, @reaperhulk?

DISCLAIMER: I sound pretty confident about some of these things here, but I'm not a core contributor here, so take what I say with a small grain of salt 😄 I just happened to work on this feature.

qa_summary: The developer needed to know that the type signature for `CertificateRevocationList.is_signature_valid` is correct because a certificate can contain a public key not valid for issuing, and they should refer to the Cryptography library’s `CertificateIssuerPrivateKeyTypes` documentation (https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/asymmetric/#cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.types.CertificateIssuerPrivateKeyTypes).

comments.author: userappgate
comments.body:
See this example code:

```python3
from cryptography import x509

def is_signature_valid(crl: bytes, ca_cert: bytes) -> bool:
    crl_object = x509.load_pem_x509_crl(crl)

    ca_cert_object = x509.load_pem_x509_certificate(ca_cert)

    return crl_object.is_signature_valid(ca_cert_object.public_key())

mypy fails with

title: Thread-safety: data race in ImagingDefaultArena block cache (memory_get_block / memory_return_block)
security_topic: thread-safety of Pillow's block cache in multi-threaded usage
qa_summary: The developer asked if the ImagingDefaultArena data race is a security vulnerability and whether a fix exists; the maintainer answered that Pillow 11.0.0 (see issue #8238) includes threading fixes, so upgrading resolves it.

comments.author: ctkhanhly
comments.body:
### What did you do?

Used `asyncio.to_thread()` / `ThreadPoolExecutor` to offload PIL Image operations (create, load, resize, encode) to multiple threads concurrently.

### What did you expect to happen?

Thread-safe access to PIL Image allocation/deallocation, or documentation stating that multi-threaded usage requires `set_blocks_max(0)`.

### What actually happened?

`ImagingDefaultArena` in `src/libImaging/Storage.c` uses shared mutable state (`blocks_cached`, `blocks_pool`) without any synchronization. When multiple threads call `memory_get_block` / `memory_return_block` concurrently (which happens when PIL's GIL-releasing C operations run in parallel), data races can occur:

```c
// memory_get_block (line 310) — no lock
if (arena->blocks_cached > 0) {
    arena->blocks_cached -= 1;                          // ← read-modify-write, no lock
    block = arena->blocks_pool[arena->blocks_cached];   // ← concurrent read, no lock
}

// memory_return_block (line 347) — no lock
if (arena->blocks_cached < arena->blocks_max) {
    arena->blocks_pool[arena->blocks_cached] = block;   // ← concurrent write, no lock
    arena->blocks_cached += 1;                          // ← read-modify-write, no lock
} else {
    free(block.ptr);
}
```

**Race scenario** (two threads returning blocks simultaneously):
```
Thread A: reads blocks_cached = 19 (< blocks_max 20)
Thread B: reads blocks_cached = 19 (same stale value — no lock)
Thread A: writes blocks_pool[19] = block_A, increments to 20
Thread B: writes blocks_pool[19] = block_B (OVERWRITES block_A)

Result: block_A.ptr is permanently lost — malloc'd, never free'd.
```

Similarly, `memory_get_block` can hand the same cached block to two threads simultaneously (use-after-free / double-free risk).

The race window is narrow under the GIL (requires concurrent C-level execution during GIL-released operations like resize/encode), making it hard to reproduce in simple tests. Under sustained high-concurrency production workloads with longer GIL-released operations, the race triggers more frequently.

**Workaround:** `Image.core.set_blocks_max(0)` disables the cache entirely, eliminating the shared mutable state.

### What are your OS, Python and Pillow versions?

* OS: Linux x86_64
* Python: 3.12
* Pillow: 10.4.0

```python
import asyncio
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from PIL import Image

# This triggers concurrent access to ImagingDefaultArena from multiple threads.
# The race is probabilistic and more likely under sustained production load
# with longer GIL-released operations (resize, encode).
async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
    loop.set_default_executor(ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=20))

    resolutions = [(512, 512), (1024, 1024), (1536, 1536), (2048, 2048)]

    async def process(res):
        def _work():
            img = Image.new("RGB", res)
            img.load()
        await asyncio.to_thread(_work)

    for _ in range(1000):
        await asyncio.gather(*[process(resolutions[i % 4]) for i in range(20)])

asyncio.run(main())
```

**Additional context:**

PIL's C extensions release the GIL during image operations, enabling true parallelism in thread pools. However, `ImagingDefaultArena` is a process-global struct with no mutex or atomic operations protecting its state. When `asyncio.to_thread` dispatches PIL work to a `ThreadPoolExecutor`, multiple threads can call `memory_get_block` / `memory_return_block` concurrently during the GIL-released portions of operations like `Image.resize()` or `Image.save()`.

This is particularly relevant for:
- Python's increasing use of `asyncio.to_thread` for GIL-releasing C extensions
- The upcoming free-threaded CPython (PEP 703), which will remove the GIL entirely and make this race trivially triggerable

**Suggested fixes:**
1. Add a `pthread_mutex` around `blocks_cached` / `blocks_pool` access in `memory_get_block` and `memory_return_block`
2. Or use per-thread arenas (eliminates contention)
3. Or document that the block cache is not thread-safe and recommend `set_blocks_max(0)` for multi-threaded usage

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
You have said that you are using Pillow 10.4.0. Is there any particular reason you are not using the latest version of Pillow?

#8238 helped threading in Storage.c in Pillow 11.0.0, so would you be interested in testing a more recent version?

Any fix for this issue will be applied only to new Pillow releases. https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/releasenotes/index.html
> Please use the latest version of Pillow. Functionality and security fixes should not be expected to be backported to earlier versions.

comments.author: wiredfool
comments.body:
Do you have a specific test case/code path where you've got a provable issue here, or is this a theoretical issue from reading/llming the code?

1) You're testing a version from before free-threading support. Newer versions have explicit handling for this for free threaded builds. (using `PyMutex_Lock/UnLock`, which compiles to a noop for GIL builds)

2) We do release the GIL for long running operations, but the GIL releases are generally around tight loops or calls out to third party library calls (e.g. `webpAnimDecoderGetNext`). A quick scan of the code isn't showing any mallocs or similar in any of the locations where we're releasing the GIL. (in the code, anywhere where `ImagingSectionEnter/Leave` are called). 

Specifically looking at the code for resize, the GIL is dropped in the `ImagingResampleHorizontal* and ImagingResampleVertical*` methods of `Resample.c`, all of which take in `imIn` and `imOut`. (e.g. https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/main/src/libImaging/Resample.c#L543)

The other fork of the code calls `ImagingTransform`, passing in an `imOut`, and these operations only drop the GIL around the tight loops. (e.g. https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/main/src/libImaging/Geometry.c#L1010)

example.png  CRC error in chunk pHYs (computed d2dd7efc, expected 679fd252)
ERROR: example.png
```

So there is a problem with your image.

If you would like to ignore the problem, you can do so with [`LOAD_TRUNCATED_IMAGES`](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/ImageFile.html#PIL.ImageFile.LOAD_TRUNCATED_IMAGES).
```python
from PIL import Image, ImageFile
from io import BytesIO

ImageFile.LOAD_TRUNCATED_IMAGES = True

with open('example.png', 'rb') as image_file:
    Image.open(image_file)
```

My conclusion was
> I don't think our formats allow for this.
> - FpxImagePlugin initially `_accept`s an image, but may later decide [it's not FPX after all](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/55cec2a0d0ea345705b27c0e12e0ad30af89ffb3/src/PIL/FpxImagePlugin.py#L62-L66). > - ImtImagePlugin does not have a good ability to distinguish between a malformed file and a file of another type.

title: Security concerns when loading user-provided fonts: Can they contain malware?
security_topic: malicious font handling risk in Pillow ImageFont.truetype
qa_summary: The developer asked whether loading user‑provided fonts with ImageFont.truetype could be a security risk, and the maintainer answered by referencing Pillow’s OSS‑Fuzz font fuzzing and the specific fix documented in the Pillow 8.2.0 release notes (memory DoS in ImageFont).

comments.author: daeeros
comments.body:
Hello! I have a question regarding the security of using user-provided fonts in Pillow.

I'm implementing a feature where a font uploaded by a user is loaded as a byte stream and then used in `ImageFont.truetype`. The loading and usage look like this:

```python
font_22 = None

if creator_profile.quote_font_file_id is not None:
    downloaded_font = await pl.app.backend._get_file(creator_profile.quote_font_file_id)
    if downloaded_font:
        font_22 = ImageFont.truetype(BytesIO(downloaded_font.content), 22)
```

My question:
How safe is it to accept fonts as byte streams and load them through ImageFont.truetype? Is there a risk that malicious fonts could contain viruses or otherwise disrupt the application? Are there any known vulnerabilities with font handling in Pillow or best practices for validating fonts before use?

Thank you very much in advance for any guidance!

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
Hi. This is a security problem that we consider when developing Pillow.

[One](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/actions/workflows/cifuzz.yml) of our GitHub Actions uses [OSS-Fuzz](https://github.com/google/oss-fuzz) to check for security problems that may occur when [opening and using random font data](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/5bff2f3b2894ec6923c590d0c37b18177d0634bd/Tests/oss-fuzz/fuzzers.py#L31-L43).

When a problem in Pillow is found, we endeavour to fix it. You can see and example of a problem that was found and fixed in the past at https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/releasenotes/8.2.0.html#fix-memory-dos-in-imagefont

As far as what you should be doing as a user, https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/releasenotes/index.html
> Please use the latest version of Pillow. Functionality and security fixes should not be expected to be backported to earlier versions.

If you do not use our pre-built wheels, and instead compile Pillow from source, I would also suggest using the latest version of dependencies - in this case, FreeType.

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
My commit was inspired by @homm's comment that he considered it a bug [when an image changed size after it was loaded.](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/pull/8341#discussion_r1760807429)

I think `load()` is a method that many users are probably not even aware of, and so they might the behaviour unexpected if it is internally called and the mode changes.
```python
from PIL import Image
im = Image.open(...)
print(im.mode)  # L
print(im.copy().mode)  # RGB
```

When I made the mode change, none of our internal plugins had to be updated to handle it. GifImagePlugin changes modes between frames, sure, but the the core image can be reset before loading, in its own `load_prepare()`. TiffImagePlugin creates a new core image at the end of `seek()`. It doesn't look like WebP does change modes between frames.

@bigcat88 a few questions - do you disagree with my idea in theory? Do you think pillow_heif could be updated handle this new way of doing things? Is the problem simply that this change was made suddenly, and you would prefer a deprecation?

comments.author: bigcat88
comments.body:
> When I made the mode change, none of our internal plugins had to be updated to handle it.

I don't know how common it is that frames have different modes.
I know that in modern formats like AVIF or HEIF this is supported, and this can happen.
*But I do never see real world examples of this, and not custom crafted images*


> @bigcat88 a few questions - do you disagree with my idea in theory? Do you think pillow_heif could be updated handle this new way of doing things? Is the problem simply that this change was made suddenly, and you would prefer a deprecation?

I don't mind updating "pillow_heif", that's why I created issue to determine the way to do it, knowing that here everyone can always get an answer to the question of what is best


> TiffImagePlugin creates a new core image at the end of `seek()`

After receiving a hint that TiffImagePlugin does this in the seek method, in theory it should be done the same way.

Like this:

```python3
    def seek(self, frame: int):
        if not self._seek_check(frame):
            return
        self.__frame = frame
        self._init_from_heif_file(frame)  # this fills  `self._size` and `self._mode` with new frame info

        if pil_version[:3] != "10.":
            # Pillow 11.0+
            # We need to create a new core image object on second and
            # subsequent frames in the image. Image may be different size/mode.
            # https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/issues/8439
            self.im = Image.core.new(self._mode, self._size)

        _exif = getattr(self, "_exif", None)  # Pillow 9.2+ do no reload exif between frames.
        if _exif is not None and getattr(_exif, "_loaded", None):
            _exif._loaded = False  # pylint: disable=protected-access
```

It seems to work and tests passed successfully, many thanks to everyone for help.

 I think the issue can be closed?

comments.author: homm
comments.body:
I still think it's better to revert this, especially now, when we realise not only TiffImagePlugin relies on this behaviour.
https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/pull/8390/files#r1764864935

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
Reverted and deprecated?

I think the ideal behaviour when changing modes between frames is actually to set `self._im = None` at the end of seek - https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/pull/8392. I think `load()` shouldn't change the image mode, and in theory at least, `load()` doesn't have to be called after `seek()`, so if there's a core image with the wrong mode hanging around, it can be discarded.

comments.author: homm
comments.body:
> is actually to set self._im = None

This will lead to unnecessary memory allocation if all frames have the same size and mode. The previous implementation of `load_prepare` was straightforward: it prepared `self.im` with the correct mode and size, so there was no need to worry about handling `self.im` in the plugins.

> I think load() shouldn't change the image mode

I fully agree, just like with size changes, which I also tried to fix, as you might remember. But I don't quite understand how this would happen if we return to the previous `load_prepare` behavior.

> load() doesn't have to be called after seek()

Possibly. But I'm specifically talking about `load_prepare`, which I believe is the correct API for managing the `self.im` object.

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
Returning to the previous `load_prepare` behaviour wouldn't cause a problem, no. I was sort of trying to enforce the core image to either be `None` or the correct mode/size before calling `load()`, to allow for the core image to be dropped if it theoretically became unnecessary. However, once I take on board your comment about unnecessary memory allocation, that's hard to do simply. I've created #8450 to try - at the end of `seek()`, an external plugin could call `super().seek()`, and if the mode or size has changed, then `self._im` is set to `None`.

If you're not a fan of that suggestion though, then I'm happy to just revert the `load_prepare()` change.

comments.author: homm
comments.body:
> I was sort of trying to enforce the core image to either be None or the correct mode/size before calling load()

Good point. I'll take a look.

Hi. You are hitting a limit when opening images.

https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/plugins.html#PIL.PngImagePlugin.MAX_TEXT_CHUNK
> PIL.PngImagePlugin.MAX_TEXT_CHUNK = 1048576

from PIL import Image, PngImagePlugin

Image.open('001041.png')
```

comments.body:
The problematic part of the image is the ICC profile, which is just over 1mb. We are raising an error to try and prevent decompression bombs, where compressed data becomes excessively large when expanded.

Without a self-contained example, it's hard to go into further detail, but it would appear that something external to Pillow is providing a large ICC profile. I think there is an expectation that Pillow saves exactly the data that it is given. I considered splitting it into multiple iCCP chunks, but http://www.libpng.org/pub/png/spec/1.2/PNG-Chunks.html#C.iCCP doesn't say anything about concatenating.

We could raise an error when saving a large ICC profile, but I don't think you would find that helpful.

If there was a self-contained example, we could try and figure out where the ICC profile comes from, but otherwise, I don't think there is anything for us to do here.

I would never have been able to diagnose this without your help.

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
I've created #8391. That will change the error message to "Decompressed data too large for PngImagePlugin.MAX_TEXT_CHUNK".

If a user sees that, and searches our docs for "PngImagePlugin.MAX_TEXT_CHUNK", they will find https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/handbook/image-file-formats.html#png-opening

title: Is Pillow affected by WebP vulnerability?
security_topic: applicability of CVE-2023-4863 to Pillow versions
qa_summary: The developer needed to know if Pillow is vulnerable to CVE‑2023‑4863 and whether upgrading libwebp (instead of Pillow) mitigates the issue, with the answer citing Pillow 10.0.1 and newer libwebp versions as anchors.

comments.author: afk42
comments.body:
Being aware that CVE-2023-4863 was already fixed in Pillow 10.0.1 and as I'm unable to update to that version at the moment, I want to understand if Pillow really uses any of the functionality where the issue resides or if the CVE can be whitelisted since use of this vulnerable library is excluded by the functional design of Pillow.

Thank you

### What are your OS, Python and Pillow versions?

* OS: 
* Python: 
* Pillow:  < 10.0.1

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
Pillow calls WebPAnimDecoderGetNext, which calls WebPDecode, calling DecodeInto, calling VP8LDecodeHeader, calling DecodeImageStream, calling ReadHuffmanCodes, calling ReadHuffmanCode, calling VP8LBuildHuffmanTable, calling BuildHuffmanTable - so I don't see why we wouldn't be vulnerable.

You might also be interested in this distinction - the source code of Pillow itself did not really change in 10.0.1 to address this situation. 10.0.1 was released to provide new wheels to those who do not compile Pillow from source. You could use an earlier version of Pillow with a recent version of libwebp and not be vulnerable.

comments.author: afk42
comments.body:
Thank you for your answer. @radarhere 
So if I understood correctly I can just bump up the version of libwebp and maintain compatibility with <10.0.1 versions.

security_topic: applicability of CVE-2023-45853 to Pillow 9.3.0 on Windows

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
Hi. Given that "[MiniZip is not a supported part of the zlib product](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-45853)", and when compiling for Windows, Pillow merely runs "[`win32\Makefile.msc", "zlib.lib`](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/14c539e7873b816cdb4f0f7aeeeed50a094197cf/winbuild/build_prepare.py#L144)", I'm going to say no. It would seem that separate steps are required to involve minizip, which Pillow doesn't take. https://github.com/madler/zlib/issues/868#issuecomment-1783525536 states that "This is not a zlib vulnerability."

As an aside, if you are concerned about security, I would recommend upgrading from Pillow 9.3.0. We have fixed various security problems since then.

security_topic: insecure loading of truncated PNG files

comments.body:
### What did you do?
Trying to open one png file
### What did you expect to happen?
open and skip all the file checks
### What actually happened?
returning error
### What are your OS, Python and Pillow versions?

* OS:  WIN 11
* Python:  3.10.11
* Pillow: 10.0.1/10.1.0


```python
from PIL import Image
import requests
from io import BytesIO

IMG_URL = "https://i.ibb.co/QN1JyLp/IMG-20231030-100421.png"

# do things here
img.show()
```

i tried some third party tools to check the PNG file. [https://processing.compress-or-die.com/repair-process](https://processing.compress-or-die.com/repair-process)

```

```
is there a way i can skip those checks in pillow, and just open it in insecure way of something.

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
You can set `LOAD_TRUNCATED_IMAGES`.

```python
from PIL import ImageFile
ImageFile.LOAD_TRUNCATED_IMAGES = True
```

comments.author: MayankFawkes
comments.body: alright that's working, also @radarhere it would be great if you could explain a little about LOAD_TRUNCATED_IMAGES constant.

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/handbook/image-file-formats.html#png
> By default Pillow doesn’t allow loading of truncated PNG files, set [ImageFile.LOAD_TRUNCATED_IMAGES](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/ImageFile.html#PIL.ImageFile.LOAD_TRUNCATED_IMAGES) to override this.

https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/ImageFile.html#PIL.ImageFile.LOAD_TRUNCATED_IMAGES
> PIL.ImageFile.LOAD_TRUNCATED_IMAGES = False
> Whether or not to load truncated image files. User code may change this.

title: Set up GitHub release token for Travis CI
security_topic: secure storage of CI deployment token

comments.author: hugovk
comments.body:
For https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/issues/7390.
Re: https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/issues/7348#issuecomment-1763383329, https://github.com/python-pillow/pillow-wheels/pull/156#discussion_r450959499.

We need to set up a token for Travis CI to be able to upload wheels to this repo's release section.

1. Create a GitHub personal access token scoped to this repo. ⚠️ A repo admin needs to do this due to permissions.
2. Install Travis CLI:

```console
❯ sudo gem install travis --no-document
...
❯ travis --version

```
❯ travis login --github-token GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN

❯ travis setup releases -r python-pillow/Pillow 
```

5. Save the new token as `GITHUB_RELEASE_TOKEN` at https://app.travis-ci.com/github/python-pillow/pillow/settings.

The current GitHub Actions wheel build takes ~10 to ~40 minutes: https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/actions/runs/7383669755 I added manylinux and musllinux to GitHub Actions using QEMU emulation. I forgot that Travis actually does two manylinux builds (manylinux_2_17 (aka manylinux2014) and manylinux_2_28), so we're actually missing some in this experiment, but let's come back to that. I used a matrix, so each job ran for a single Python version and created 1 manylinux (by default manylinux_2_17) and 1 musllinx wheel (except PyPy which doesn't have musllinux so had a single manylinux). The 7 QEMU jobs took 2-3 hours: https://github.com/hugovk/Pillow/actions/runs/7387963337 Next, also split so each job does a single Python version and manylinux OR musllinux (except only manylinux for PyPy). The 12 QEMU jobs took 1.5-2 hours: https://github.com/hugovk/Pillow/actions/runs/7390943205 Is this an acceptable cost? We ditch Travis CI (40 minutes) and use GitHub Actions (2 hours)? Note this the human waiting time, making use of parallel builds, the actually CPU time used is much greater. --- As mentioned, I forgot manylinux_2_28 in this experiment. Do we actually need wheels for both manylinux_2_17 and manylinux_2_28? If so, this would add another 7 jobs to GHA, I expect also taking 1.5-2 hours. We'd have 19 QEMU jobs taking 1.5-2 hours + 7 native jobs taking 10-40 mins. We get max 20 parallel jobs, so it would be fully saturated meaning some have to wait to be started, and so maybe take 2.5-3 hours for the whole thing.

title: Provide a documented way to turn off EPS handling via Ghostscript
security_topic: disable EPS handling to mitigate Ghostscript RCE risk
qa_summary: The developer needed a way to disable Ghostscript/EPS handling to mitigate RCE vulnerabilities, and the answer provides the concrete solution of setting EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = False (see PR #7392 and the documented API change).

comments.author: raphaelm
comments.body:
Pillow parses EPS files through ghostscript.

Ghostscript is troubled with regular security issues of critical impact, such as remote code execution. There has been [this one](https://github.com/farisv/PIL-RCE-Ghostscript-CVE-2018-16509), two CVEs this year already, and there is another one [just coming up](https://git.ghostscript.com/?p=ghostpdl.git;a=commit;h=e59216049cac290fb437a04c4f41ea46826cfba5) with the patch not yet included in any release.

We do not need EPS handling and we can turn it off in our code using `Image.open(…, formats=["JPG", "PNG", …])`. However, we use third-party components that also use Pillow (such as `reportlab`) and we'd like to make sure they also don't accidentally open EPS files and we can't modify the code.

From what I can tell, we can accomplish this with:

```python
from PIL import Image

if "EPS" in Image.ID:
    Image.ID.remove("EPS")
```

However, that seems to be undocumented and feels like unclean monkeypatching. I think it would be worth it providing a documented API to turn off third-party backends like ghostscript globally.

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body: Hi. See what you think of #7392. It adds `EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary`, so that setting `EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = False` would result in `OSError: Unable to locate Ghostscript on paths` when trying to load an EPS image.

comments.author: raphaelm
comments.body: Wow, that was fast! Not sure if I read the code exactly, but wouldn't this trigger OSError from line 72 whenever I set it to `False` and import the module?

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
No, the `Ghostscript` function is only called when an image is loaded.
https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/a84a43528ebf8756369a3b7248312c4122ef3bc9/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py#L383-L386

With the workaround that you posted above, an EPS file won't be identified. In my suggestion, it will be identified. `Image.open` will complete successfully. It will just raise an OSError once `load()` is called on it (which many Pillow operations call internally).

comments.author: raphaelm
comments.body: Ah sorry, I've mistaken `Ghostscript` to be a class. My bad! Yes, sounds good then. (A note in the docs about it would be great to make it "official" so I can somehow expect it to continue to work in future versions.)

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
Sure. I've added a commit to the PR. You can see the preview at https://pillow--7392.org.readthedocs.build/en/7392/handbook/image-file-formats.html#eps
> To use Ghostscript, Pillow searches for the “gs” executable. On Windows, it also searches for “gswin32c” and “gswin64c”. If you would like to customise this behaviour, `EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = "gswin64"` will set the name of the executable to use. `EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = False` will prevent Ghostscript from being used altogether.

title: Automate build and release to PyPI
security_topic: process for securely uploading release artifacts to PyPI via Trusted Publishers
qa_summary: The developer asked how to securely upload release artifacts to PyPI using Trusted Publishers, and the answer pointed to a concrete CI run showing the upload step (see actions run https://github.com/radarhere/Pillow/actions/runs/7329629479/job/19960359962#step:4:1008).

comments.author: hugovk
comments.body:
Currently the [release process](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/main/RELEASING.md) has many steps, including preparing things in this repo, and then starting a build in https://github.com/python-pillow/pillow-wheels, before downloading the sdist + wheel artifacts to disk, and manually uploading them to PyPI using twine.

I'd like us to move towards more automated releases, including using the new Trusted Publishers to upload wheels directly from the CI to PyPI, which is more secure:

* https://blog.pypi.org/posts/2023-04-20-introducing-trusted-publishers/

We can do this in a phased manner, not all of these things would need to be done at once, to ensure we can still make releases with just some of them completed.

We could potentially deal with the Travis CI wheels later, and tackle GitHub Actions first as they're a bigger win and we don't know when Travis CI will go away.

Big picture:

* Prepare release
* Push a tag
* The CI builds release artifacts
* The CI uploads artifacts to PyPI

I'd suggest something along these lines:

1. Move Linux and macOS https://github.com/python-pillow/pillow-wheels to this repo https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow. We already have Windows wheels build here.
   * We'll need to add [`paths:` / `paths-ignore`](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/workflow-syntax-for-github-actions#onpushpull_requestpull_request_targetpathspaths-ignore) to workflows so we only trigger the main test workflows for "normal" code changes, and only trigger the wheel workflow for things like release and modifying its config
   * Upload wheels as GitHub artifacts in this repo instead

2. Add automation to download artifacts and upload them to PyPI via Trusted Publishing
   * This may need refactoring to move all the wheel building to the same workflow (but separate jobs), and then a final job that runs when the wheels have all been built, that builds sdist, checks and uploads them all.
   * See https://github.com/ultrajson/ultrajson/blob/main/.github/workflows/deploy.yml and https://github.com/ultrajson/ultrajson/actions/workflows/deploy.yml for examples.
   * We also have https://test.pypi.org/project/Pillow/ which we can use to verify the upload machinery is working smoothly before release. For example, we can upload for non-tagged wheel builds.

Thoughts?

comments.author: hugovk
comments.body: I've opened https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/pull/7544 to create the sdist during the release build. --- Next, I'd like us to move the Windows wheel building from `test-windows.yml` into the same `wheels.yml` workflow. So we get something like this: And the Windows wheels should be part of the same `dist.zip` artifact containing the Linux and macOS wheels, and the sdist. I think we also probably want to use a reusable workflow, similar to `wheels-linux.yml` and `wheels-macos.yml`. We don't need to build the wheels anymore in `test-windows.yml`. If there's a lot of common steps needed for testing (in `test-windows.yml`) and building wheels, a reusable workflow could be useful here. This doesn't all need to be done in one go, incremental steps are fine, as long as they're atomic changes and we're still able to make releases during any intermediate step. Any thoughts on how to approach this? cc @nulano --- After all this is done, we have all* the release files created in one place on the CI, and do the upload to PyPI! But one step at a time :) (\* All the GHA files, not Travis CI, which will still need manual upload, but they should be ready before all the automation.)

title: "close" syscall run twice on same file descriptor when loading binary LZW-compressed TIFF
security_topic: race condition causing double file descriptor close in Pillow TIFF handling
qa_summary: The developer needed to know if the double‑close race condition constitutes a security risk and which fix resolves it; the issue is addressed by PR #7199 (and later PR #8458) which modifies TiffImagePlugin to prevent the duplicate file‑pointer close.

comments.author: philip-bl
comments.body:
If I open an LZW-compressed binary TIFF file using pillow and load its data, pillow calls the "close" syscall on one of the two relevant file descriptors twice. The second call results in a "EBADF (Bad file descriptor)" error. The program doesn't crash and everything seems to work ok. But if multithreading is used and a race condition happens, this might crash the program.

In this example, the expected behaviour would be that there is only one "close" syscall on each of the two relevant file descriptors and that there is no "EBADF" error. Below, I show how to reproduce the problem.

$ cat read_tiff_file.py

import PIL.Image as Image

print("Right before the with-block", flush=True)

    print("Right after load()", flush=True)

comments.author: nurumaik
comments.body:
### Updated example that actually leads to bugs

create_tiff_file.py

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python

import numpy as np
import PIL.Image as Image

# Create really big file so it will take time to load. But even bigger file will cause libtiff to complain that we are trying to zip-bomb it
Image.fromarray(np.random.rand(5000, 30000) > 0.9) \  
    .save("example.tif", format="TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw")
```

reproduce.py
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python
from threading import Thread
import os
from collections import deque

finish = False

def load_files():
    descriptors = deque()
    while not finish:
        try:
            fd = os.open("test", os.O_RDONLY)
            descriptors.append(fd)
        except:  # in case of too many descriptors
            os.close(descriptors.pop())
    
    for d in descriptors:
        os.close(d)
    
    print("success")


t = Thread(target=load_files)

import PIL.Image as Image

print("Right before the with-block", flush=True)

with Image.open("example.tif") as mask:
    print("Right in the beginning of the with-block", flush=True)
    t.start()
    mask.load()  # replace it with time.sleep(10) and it works just fine without exceptions
    print("Right after load()", flush=True)
print("Right after the with-block", flush=True)
finish = True
t.join()
```


Steps to reproduce:

```sh
touch test
./create_tiff_file.py
./reproduce.py
```

_Note: you need to delete example.tif and test before every iteration of running this. otherwise the OS might cache the files and thus the problem won't reproduce because libtiff will load file too fast_

Expected behavior:
`load_files` outputs "success"

Actual behavior:
```
Right in the beginning of the with-block
Right after load()
Right after the with-block
Exception in thread Thread-1 (load_files):
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/usr/lib/python3.10/threading.py", line 1016, in _bootstrap_inner
    self.run()
  File "/usr/lib/python3.10/threading.py", line 953, in run
    self._target(*self._args, **self._kwargs)
  File "reproduce.py", line 17, in load_files
    os.close(d)
OSError: [Errno 9] Bad file descriptor
```

### Cause of bug

1. tiff loader creates file duplicate of file descriptor for use in external c library code
https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/5832362215f5fa661fa05ad31e6c97aab87d410a/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py#L1256

2. As comments say "[libtiff closes the file descriptor, so pass in a dup.](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/5832362215f5fa661fa05ad31e6c97aab87d410a/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py#L1254)", libtiff probably closes `fp` after decoding here
https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/5832362215f5fa661fa05ad31e6c97aab87d410a/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py#L1298

3. Pillow closes `fp` again
https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/5832362215f5fa661fa05ad31e6c97aab87d410a/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py#L1308

If another thread decides to open new file between steps 2 and 3 (like `load_files` in example), it may get file descriptor that was just closed by libtiff. Then, in step 3, pillow closes this file, making descriptor invalid

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
Because it's unclear if libtiff will close the file descriptor or not, what about this as an alternative solution? It checks if the file descriptor is open first, by trying to read 0 bytes.

I've tested it against create_tiff_file.py and reproduce.py and it works.

```diff
diff --git a/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py
index 3d4d0910a..97d184f5f 100644
--- a/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py
+++ b/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py
@@ -1305,6 +1305,9 @@ class TiffImageFile(ImageFile.ImageFile):
 
         if fp:
             try:
+                # Test if the file descriptor is still open
+                os.read(fp, 0)
+
                 os.close(fp)
             except OSError:
                 pass
```

comments.author: nurumaik
comments.body:
I reproduced the problem with this fix. Unfortunately, reproduction code doesn't work in all cases, and I don't know how to make a better version without hooking something in libtiff. I can only suggest storing file "test" on some very slow drive to ensure read is really slow

How this can still lead to a bug:
1. We call `os.dup` on `self.fd` and get descriptor, let's say 4
2. decode finishes and calls `close(4)`
3. Other thread opens another file, and os gives it the same number 4 as descriptor, since it's already freed
4. We call `os.read(4, 0)` on file descriptor and it successfully reads that other file
5. We close file that doesn't belong to us

I checked libtiff code and it should always close the descriptor after performing decode. It will stay open only if libtiff contains a bug (but this will probably lead to much more serious errors anyway)

https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/main/src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c#L723

If libtiff may not close the fd in some cases, the proper fix would be to either:
1. Somehow report back if it closed fd or not
2. Disable fd closing in libtiff

comments.author: wiredfool
comments.body:
As to why we're duping the file pointer in the firster place,  I think the original logic was:
* Libtiff always closes the pointer when read on an image is complete.
* If we have a multiple frames in an image, we're looping over calls into libtiff to decode individual frames. If libtiff closes on the first frame, we don't get subsequent frames
* Our original source for the file pointer may be one of a filename, tempfile, or open file like object. We can't necessarily re-open a file once it's been closed. 

One option was to use python/our code for all the byte shuffling at the file level. IIRC there was a pretty decent performance and complexity improvement for cases when we did have a file pointer to be able to send that into libtiff and let it manage all of that. 


(edit: yeah, that's definitely my comment style)

### What did you do?

We are using PIL for reading PPM images of 1280x1024 or 1920x1080 pixels in RGB 24 bits with maxval of 255 in the header.

### What did you expect to happen?

We expect the PPM to open correctly.

### What actually happened?

The opening of PPM images failed due to a maxval error "Channel value too large for this mode"

### What are your OS, Python and Pillow versions?

* Python: 3.9

When I first try to load my PPM, PIL return the channel value too large error with the value of 20458 with a maxval of 255. Then I searched in my PPM this value and there is no data higher than 255.
After investigated the issue, I saw that the concatenation of the half_block and the next block block give this:
-> end of previus block: ... 204 ]
-> half_block + block:    [20458 ...
-> expected:                   [204 58 ...

```python
if half_token:

By
```python
if half_token:
    block = half_token + b' ' + block  # stitch half_token to new block
    half_token = False
```

title: Accessing the key generator in an initializer silently changes the hash digest class for the entire application
security_topic: unexpected hash algorithm downgrade due to early key_generator access
qa_summary: The developer needed to know that accessing Rails.key_generator before setting config.active_support.key_generator_hash_digest_class can downgrade the hash algorithm to insecure SHA1, and that this was fixed in PR #56746 which now raises a RuntimeError to prevent the misconfiguration.

comments.author: ankane
comments.body:
### Steps to reproduce

Create a new Rails application and add `config/initializers/repro.rb` with:

```ruby
Rails.application.key_generator
```

And run:

```sh
rails runner "p Rails.application.key_generator.instance_variable_get(:@key_generator).instance_variable_get(:@hash_digest_class)"
```

### Expected behavior

`OpenSSL::Digest::SHA256`, which is the output without the initializer.

### Actual behavior

`OpenSSL::Digest::SHA1`

### System configuration

**Rails version**: 8.1.2

**Ruby version**: 3.4.8

### Additional notes

turbo-rails was [affected by this](https://github.com/hotwired/turbo-rails/blob/v8.0.21/UPGRADING.md#key-digest-changes-in-111) and made a change to initialization to workaround it.

A few ideas to address this would be:

- apply `config.active_support.key_generator_hash_digest_class` earlier in initialization
- warn or raise if `Rails.application.key_generator` is already cached when applying `config.active_support.key_generator_hash_digest_class`
- include the hash digest as part of the cache key in `Rails.application.key_generator`

comments.author: 6temes
comments.body:
I've opened a PR to address this: #56746

The fix raises a `RuntimeError` when `key_generator` is accessed before the `key_generator_hash_digest_class` configuration has been applied. This turns the silent misconfiguration into an immediate, actionable error.

Apps that don't configure `key_generator_hash_digest_class` (pre-7.0 defaults) are unaffected.

title: `ActiveRecord::Rollback` is silenced in nested transactions - including ApplicationRecord callbacks
security_topic: silencing of rollback errors in nested transactions leading to potential data inconsistency
qa_summary: The developer needed to know that raising ActiveRecord::Rollback in a nested transaction is intentionally swallowed by Rails (as documented in the Rails transaction docs), see https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveRecord/ConnectionAdapters/DatabaseStatements.html#method-i-transaction

comments.author: ipvalverde
comments.body:
### Steps to reproduce

<!-- (Guidelines for creating a bug report are [available
here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#creating-a-bug-report)) -->

<!-- Paste your executable test case created from one of the scripts found [here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#create-an-executable-test-case) below: -->
[Full script
](https://gist.github.com/ipvalverde/e442ccaf22657b2457ce50981c11a305)

```ruby
    user = User.create!(name: "john")

    assert_equal true, user.active
    assert_equal true, user.email.active

    User.transaction do
      user.active = false

      Email.transaction do
        email = user.email
        email.active = false
        email.save

        raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
      end
    end

    user.reload

    # Both are committed to the database even though an ActiveRecord::Rollback was raised
    assert_equal true, user.active, "Expect that the whole transaction fails and the user is not saved"
    assert_equal true, user.email.active, "Expect that the email is not updated"
```

### Expected behavior

This is related to the issue reported in [this PR](https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/44518). The error should bubble up and not be silenced by Rails.

Raising an error should always have an effect, swallowing it is error-prone and can easily throw people off.
Based on [this GitHub search](https://github.com/search?q=%2Fraise%5B%5C%28%5Cs%5Cn%5D*ActiveRecord%3A%3ARollback%2F+-org%3Ashop+language%3ARuby+-org%3AShopify+-path%3Aspec%2F+-path%3A_test.rb&type=code), it looks like people seem to be raising `ActiveRecord::Rollback` errors.

if the idea is that developers should not be manually raising `ActiveRecord::Rollback`, then the documentation should be clear about it (even better if people are blocked from raising it).

### Actual behavior

Raising the error in nested transaction is a no-op. This means that ApplicationRecord callbacks will also silence `ActiveRecord::Rollback` errors. Example (also include in the [full test](https://gist.github.com/ipvalverde/e442ccaf22657b2457ce50981c11a305)):

```ruby
# definition
class User < ActiveRecord::Base
  after_create :create_email_for_user

  private

  def create_email_for_user
    email = build_email(email_address: "#{name}@example.com")

    unless email.save
      errors.add(:base, email.errors.full_messages.first || "Email creation failed")
      raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
    end
  end
end

# usage
user = User.new(name: "john")
saved = User.transaction do
  # This will attempt to create an email with `john@example.com` which already exists
  # and raise an ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid error in `create_email_for_user`
  user.save
end

user.reload

# user is successfully saved, this fails:
refute user.persisted?, "User should not be persisted since create_email_for_user raised an ActiveRecord::Rollback error"
```


### System configuration

**Rails version**:  Latest from main

**Ruby version**: `3.4.4`

comments.author: eglitobias
comments.body:
This is expected behavior and well documented, not a bug:
https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveRecord/ConnectionAdapters/DatabaseStatements.html#method-i-transaction

Nested transactions in Rails are joinable by default. That means the inner transaction does not start a new database transaction, so raising `ActiveRecord::Rollback` there does not issue a SQL `ROLLBACK`. The exception is intentionally swallowed, and the outer transaction can still commit.

At the SQL level, most databases don’t support true nested `BEGIN/COMMIT`. There is only one transaction per connection. To roll back part of a transaction, SQL uses SAVEPOINTS, not nested `BEGIN`s:
```
BEGIN;
  INSERT INTO posts ...;          -- first
  SAVEPOINT sp1;
    INSERT INTO posts ...;        -- second
    ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1;    -- undo only inner work
COMMIT;
```
Rails maps this explicitly via ^requires_new: true`:
```
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  Post.create!(title: "first")
  ActiveRecord::Base.transaction(requires_new: true) do
    Post.create!(title: "second")
    raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
  end
end
```

Without `requires_new`, there is no SQL boundary to roll back so the behavior is correct by design.

Changing this would be a significant backward-compatibility change, so it’s likely outside the scope of a bugfix. As already discovered, this is being discussed in more depth in https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/44518, which seems like the appropriate place for exploring a broader proposal or deprecation path.

comments.author: ipvalverde
comments.body:
Thanks for taking a look into this @eglitobias . I was aware of it being documented, but I was expecting this decision could be re-evaluated.

I cannot see a scenario where a developer would expect that raising a `ActiveRecord::Rollback` would **not** rollback. I think this is misleading and very likely a source of bugs and corrupt data. I understand changing it at this stage would be complex since this would be a breaking change.


From some conversation with @matthewd and @rafaelfranca , it looks like the recommendation would be to not manually raise `ActiveRecord::Rollback` if you have an application that is too complex with many layers of nested transactions.

For this particular issue, what about just reporting when these rollbacks are silenced and the transactions is committed? This could, at least, give insight that something fishy might've happened running the application.

[Example of changes](https://github.com/rails/rails/compare/main...ipvalverde:instrument-silenced-ar-rollbacks)

comments.body:
Just a thought but here instead of trying to keep track of all the rollback errors, we just emit a notification when swallowing them:
https://github.com/rails/rails/compare/main...ipvalverde:instrument-silenced-ar-rollbacks#diff-88e231c48eb5559ac3be58a024b019e86f7c74d388f5d49fac3f4e47bf851cc6R435

That way the behavior is the same but we can at least be aware of such a case should it occur and observe it.

> 
> That way the behavior is the same but we can at least be aware of such a case should it occur and observe it.

That's a good point. This will be less resource intensive and make it simpler, the only thing thought, is that it will not be too assertive. One pattern that I see in code is something like this (simplified here for clarity, usually happens in several layers of classes):


```ruby
def delete_user
  User.transaction do # <-- top-level transaction
    user = User.find(1)
  
    User.transaction do
      # ...
      destroy_addresses(user)
      # ...
    end

    user.destroy

    # The rollback from the nested transaction is silenced, but the parent transaction is still rolledback:
    raise ActiveRecord::Rollback if user.errors.any?    
  end
  # ...
end

def destroy_addresses(user)
  unless AddressService.destroy_user_addresses(user)
    user.errors.add(:base, "Failed to destroy addresses") unless user.addresses.destroy_all
    raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
  end
end
```

I'll add an alternative implementation and get some feedback to see which one would make more sense in Rails. For my particular use case, being more assertive (ie. making sure a `rollback` was raised as part of a transaction that was indeed committed) would be more helpful, otherwise it would generate too much noise.

comments.author: ipvalverde
comments.body:
## Proposed mitigations

Given changing the existing behavior of silencing rollbacks in nested transaction would be a breaking change, and given @zzak suggestion above, I would like to propose just "bringing awareness" to the issue. I understand this is documented, but we still have the fact that a rollback error should rollback.

### 1) Instrument when rollback is silenced **and transaction is committed** [Preferred IMHO]

This approach will capture all silenced rollbacks in nested transactions, and, if the `RealTransaction` is committed, it will send an `ActiveSupport::Notification`.

[Implementation](https://github.com/rails/rails/compare/main...ipvalverde:instrument-silenced-ar-rollbacks)

Code example:

```ruby
ActiveSupport::Notifications.subscribe("transaction.active_record.silenced_rollback_errors") do |event|
  rollback_errors = event.payload[:errors]

  # rollback_errors will have an array with error silenced in the nested transaction(s)
end

def trigger_notification_with_silecend_rollback
  User.transaction do
    user = User.lock.find(1)
    User.transaction do
      user.addresses.destroy_all
      raise ActiveRecord::Rollback # < -- silenced rollback
    end
  
    user.destroy
  end # <-- when transaction commits, transaction.active_record.silenced_rollback_errors will be emitted
end

def do_not_trigger_notification
  User.transaction do
    user = User.lock.find(1)

    operation_result = User.transaction do
      user.addresses.destroy_all
      raise ActiveRecord::Rollback # <-- silenced rollback
    end
  
    # Propagate silenced rollback and perform a real rollback ✅
    # This will NOT emit transaction.active_record.silenced_rollback_errors
    raise ActiveRecord::Rollback if operation_result.nil?

    user.destroy
  end
end
```

### 2) Instrument when rollback is silenced, even if the real transaction is also rolled back

This approach is simpler as it will always send an `ActiveSupport::Notification` whenever a rollback is silenced in a nested transaction. This can lead to false positives though, since the real transaction might also be rolled back.

[Implementation](https://github.com/rails/rails/compare/main...ipvalverde:rails:instrument-possible-silenced-ar-rollbacks)

Code example:

```ruby
ActiveSupport::Notifications.subscribe("silenced_rollback.active_record") do |event|
  rollback_error = event.payload[:error]

  # rollback_error will have the error raised in the nested transaction below
end

def trigger_notification_with_silecend_rollback
  User.transaction do
    user = User.lock.find(1)

    operation_result = User.transaction do
      user.addresses.destroy_all
      raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
    end # <-- The rescue for the transaction will immediately emit the 'silenced_rollback.active_record' notification

    # Even if the actual transaction is rolled back, the notification will be sent
    raise ActiveRecord::Rollback if operation_result.nil?

    user.destroy
  end
end
```

title: Deadlocked transactions are still seen as "usable" for MySQL (trilogy / mysql2)
security_topic: transaction state misreporting after deadlock leading to unintended writes
qa_summary: The issue asks if deadlocked MySQL transactions incorrectly remain marked as usable, allowing writes outside a transaction, and the answer points to a concrete fix in PR #44127 that restores the invalidated transaction state.

comments.author: ipvalverde
comments.body:
### Steps to reproduce

<!-- (Guidelines for creating a bug report are [available
here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#creating-a-bug-report)) -->

<!-- Paste your executable test case created from one of the scripts found [here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#create-an-executable-test-case) below: -->

[Full reproduction script gist](https://gist.github.com/ipvalverde/2d2f6b91d593e09b89a86a7c61a3ca5b). Important bit:

```ruby
Account.transaction do
  Account.create!(name: "Account in top-level transaction", balance: 50)

  begin
    puts "1) Is transaction open? #{Account.connection.transaction_open?}"

    # consider the logic in here will raise a deadlock:
    Account.lock.find(1).update!(balance: 10)
    Account.lock.find(2).update!(balance: 20)

  rescue ActiveRecord::Deadlocked => e
    puts "2) Is transaction open? #{Account.connection.transaction_open?}"

    # Everything up to this point is DISCARDED from the Database perspective.
    # No account being created, no accounts being updated.
    
  end

  # This will write directly to the database - no valid transactions in here.
  Account.create!(name: "Last account in top-level transaction", balance: 999)

  # this will be a no-op since there's no transaction open
  raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
end
```

### Expected behavior

Any database write operations (or maybe also read?) that happens in a code that is intended to run within a transaction should fail if there's no transaction open. Currently it misleads you, where you might think there is a transaction but there isn't.

This works as expected in postgres, but it looks like it's because postgres, when attempting to create an account after the deadlock will raise an error:

```
ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid: PG::InFailedSqlTransaction: ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block
```

### Actual behavior

After the transaction is deadlocked it gets killed, if that error is swallowed, any code that runs within a transaction block will write directly to the database!


### System configuration

**Rails version**: 8.1.1

**Ruby version**: 3.4.4

comments.author: ipvalverde
comments.body:
I did a bit more digging.

It looks like [this fix](https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/44127) changed how the transaction state works, now an `invaldiated` transaction that is rolled back has its state also going from `invalidated -> rolledback`, which means it will still look like a healthy transaction even though it is not.

I'll propose a PR to fix that transaction state issue and preserve the `invalidated` state without fully invalidating the connection.

title: SSL certificate verification fails on macOS (OpenSSL 3.6 + Ruby 3.4) due to CRL check
security_topic: SSL verification failure due to CRL check on macOS with OpenSSL 3.6
qa_summary: The developer needed to know how to fix SSL certificate verification failures caused by OpenSSL 3.6 CRL checking on macOS, and the answer references ruby/openssl issue #949 (and PR #950) recommending adding the openssl gem or rebuilding Ruby with a compatible OpenSSL version.

comments.author: fitterfly-jainam-parikh
comments.body:
When running any HTTPS requests (e.g., through Net::HTTP, ActiveStorage::Service::S3Service, or AWS SDK) on macOS with Ruby 3.4.x and OpenSSL 3.6, SSL handshakes fail with the error:

```bash
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError:
  SSL_connect returned=1 errno=0 peeraddr=1xx.1xx.6x.1xx:443 state=error:
  certificate verify failed (unable to get certificate CRL)
```

This occurs on a clean macOS (M2) setup using Homebrew OpenSSL@3 and rbenv.

### Steps to reproduce

1. On macOS (Apple Silicon):
```bash
brew install openssl@3 ca-certificates rbenv ruby-build
RUBY_CONFIGURE_OPTS="--with-openssl-dir=$(brew --prefix openssl@3)" rbenv install 3.4.1
rbenv global 3.4.1
```

2. Run inside IRB:
```bash
require 'net/http'
Net::HTTP.get(URI('https://aws.amazon.com'))
```

3. Observe the error:
```bash
SSL_connect ... certificate verify failed (unable to get certificate CRL)
```

### Expected behavior
Ruby (and by extension, Rails apps using Net::HTTP or ActiveStorage) should complete HTTPS requests successfully without manual CRL configuration.

### Actual behavior
The SSL handshake fails because OpenSSL’s default verification flags include V_FLAG_CRL_CHECK and V_FLAG_CRL_CHECK_ALL.
macOS’s OpenSSL build does not provide a CRL bundle, so verification fails even though the certificate chain is valid.

### Workarounds
Disabling CRL checking resolves the issue:
```bash
# config/initializers/ssl_fix.rb
require 'openssl'
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext::DEFAULT_PARAMS[:verify_mode] = OpenSSL::SSL::VERIFY_PEER
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext::DEFAULT_PARAMS[:verify_flags] &=
  ~(OpenSSL::X509::V_FLAG_CRL_CHECK_ALL | OpenSSL::X509::V_FLAG_CRL_CHECK)
```

### System configuration

**Rails version**: 8.0.2

**Ruby version**: 3.4.1

title: Migrations that alter SQLite table structure can cause data loss
security_topic: proper handling of SQLite foreign key enforcement during migrations to prevent data loss
qa_summary: The developer needed to know the correct sequence for disabling and re‑enabling SQLite foreign key enforcement during migrations to prevent data loss, as documented in the SQLite PRAGMA foreign_keys and foreign_key_check specifications (see SQLite docs and the related Rails commit).

comments.author: skipkayhil
comments.body:
[A mere add_foreign_key can wipe out your whole Rails+SQLite production table](https://kyrylo.org/software/2025/09/27/a-mere-add-foreign-key-can-wipe-out-your-whole-rails-sqlite-production-table.html)

We likely should be disabling and re-enabling the `foreign_keys` PRAGMA before/after the transaction to change the table per the [sqlite docs](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_altertable.html#otheralter).

Edit: actually it looks like we already do that since https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/45881b0a64b4039e3b0d27e2c4d959dc2d744b9d

Edit2: Ah, this is complex. We currently do

```
transaction do
  disable_referential_integrity do
```

but it should be

```
disable_pragma_foreign_keys do
  transaction do
    enable_defer_foreign_keys do
```

because `PRAGMA foreign_keys`

> is a no-op within a transaction; foreign key constraint enforcement may only be enabled or disabled when there is no pending [BEGIN](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html) or [SAVEPOINT](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_savepoint.html).

per [doc](https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html#pragma_foreign_keys), and "`PRAGMA foreign_keys` before `TRANSACTION`" is the order recommended in the first sqlite doc link above. However, `PRAGMA defer_foreign_keys` is [set _per transaction_](https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html#pragma_defer_foreign_keys) so it has to be inside the transaction block.

comments.author: ruyrocha
comments.body:
The fix is ready for reviews. It disables foreign key enforcement before the table recreation process, and re-enables it afterwards. Since `PRAGMA foreign_keys` cannot be modified inside a transaction in SQLite, the operations are sequenced as:

1. Disable foreign keys (outside transaction)
2. Perform table recreation (inside transaction for atomicity)
3. Re-enable foreign keys
4. Validate schema integrity with `PRAGMA foreign_key_check`

title: ActiveRecord::Middleware::DatabaseSelector sets cookies on asset requests
security_topic: asset requests setting cookies unexpectedly
qa_summary: The developer asked whether asset requests should set a session cookie, and the maintainer replied that it’s a bug in Propshaft, pointing to the Propshaft railtie file at commit e49a9de659ff27462015e54dd832e86e762a6ddc as evidence.

comments.author: EmilioCristalli
comments.body:
Not sure if this is a bug, but noticed that when using the automatic DB switching ([docs](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/active_record_multiple_databases.html#activating-automatic-role-switching)), with the default resolver `ActiveRecord::Middleware::DatabaseSelector::Resolver` and context `ActiveRecord::Middleware::DatabaseSelector::Resolver::Session`, it seems like requests for assets are getting a cookie sent back in the response.

Noticed this while investigating issues with system tests not rendering flash messages correctly, and it looks like it was happening because of race conditions between redirect requests and asset requests, causing it to override the cookie and remove the flash message. This might be a different issue on our side (that we are not properly waiting for asset requests to finish before submitting a form or something like that), but it made me wonder if it's correct for asset requests to respond with a cookie.

I don't know too much about the session and cookie management, but from what I could debug, it seems like this is happening because the `ActiveRecord::Middleware::DatabaseSelector::Resolver::Session` middleware reads `request.session[:last_write]`, so it's like it makes it load the session, and maybe this makes `ActionDispatch::Session::CookieStore` send the cookie back in the response?

### Steps to reproduce
Created [this repo](https://github.com/EmilioCristalli/test_db_selector) to reproduce the issue. Has a few commits with the steps to create the app, but it's a normal Rails app with scaffold for one model (Post). 

The last commit in main has the automatic db switching enabled, but moving one commit back (to `9232d6768d`) should disable it to see the difference.

Can open the root page (which loads posts#index) and observe any asset requests (like http://localhost:3000/assets/application-bfcdf840.js) in the developer tools to see the `Set-Cookie` header in the response.

### Expected behavior
The asset requests shouldn't have a `set-cookie` header in the response.

(not 100% sure this is the expected behavior, but it looks like it's what happens when automatic DB switching is not enabled)

### Actual behavior
Asset requests have a `set-cookie` header in the response.

### System configuration

**Rails version**: 8.0.2.1
**Ruby version**: 3.4.5

comments.author: byroot
comments.body:
This IMO is a bug in propshaft. It's mounted inside the Rails routes: https://github.com/rails/propshaft/blob/e49a9de659ff27462015e54dd832e86e762a6ddc/lib/propshaft/railtie.rb#L48-L50

So it's invoked after all rack middlewares.

Instead, it should probably be early in the rack middleware chain, likely right after `ActionDispatch::Static`.

Now the good news is that this is a development only setup (should be fixed regardless).

title: Handle links and other safe content inside translations
security_topic: safe interpolation of HTML in i18n translations to prevent XSS
qa_summary: The developer needed a secure method to interpolate HTML‑safe strings into I18n translations without introducing XSS, and the answer provides a concrete implementation in a Gist (https://gist.github.com/henrik/f6619f298de3b6f59dfba589fa5476d7).

comments.author: runephilosof-abtion
comments.body: Currently, if I want to put a link into a translation, I have to do ```erb <%= t(".text", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)).html_safe %> ``` or ```erb <%= t(".text_html", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)) %> ``` However, the `text_html` translation should not have to know whether the `insert` contains html or not. ~Also, the `insert` translation cannot have unescaped html content, because it is used as content inside another `_html` translation.~ The rails i18n guide does not mention how to do this nicely. The best would be if rails-i18n could handle it automatically by being aware of SafeBuffer. ```yml text: some <> text with an %{insert} text_html: some <> text with an %{insert} insert: a link, properly escaping <> ``` ```erb <%= t(".text", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)) %> ``` Rails-i18n should handle safe joining the above example. `link_to` returns a `html_safe` string, so this should output ```html some <> text with an a link, properly escaping <> ```

comments.body: Related issue in https://github.com/svenfuchs/rails-i18n/issues/1147, which was closed with a suggestion of implementing it in Rails.

If you really need this grade of freedom for the `insert`, the second option seems totally fine to me. You might consider translations to be untrusted user input, except `_html` ones, which would be more expensive to maintain. 3. Rails already has the concept of SafeBuffer, so why throw that information away when translating.

title: Authentication generator missing rate limiting on PasswordsController despite ActionMailer being available
security_topic: missing rate limiting on password reset endpoint
qa_summary: The missing rate‑limiting protection is addressed by commit e87af0f3235ca555f7864de9bb44da1d464d012d, which will be included in the upcoming Rails 8.1 release.

comments.author: sebasfourn
comments.body:
# Authentication generator missing rate limiting on PasswordsController

## Description

The Rails 8 authentication generator is missing rate limiting on the `PasswordsController` despite ActionMailer being available. This leaves the password reset endpoint vulnerable to abuse.

## Steps to reproduce

```bash
# Create a new Rails application
rails new test_app
cd test_app

# Verify ActionMailer is available
rails runner "puts defined?(ActionMailer::Railtie)"
# Output: "constant"

# Generate authentication
rails generate authentication

# Check the generated PasswordsController
cat app/controllers/passwords_controller.rb
```

## Expected behavior

The generated `PasswordsController` should include rate limiting on the `create` action when ActionMailer is available:

```ruby
rate_limit to: 10, within: 3.minutes, only: :create, with: -> { redirect_to new_password_path, alert: "Try again later." }
```

This protection is essential to prevent abuse of the password reset email functionality.

## Actual behavior

The generated `PasswordsController` is missing the rate limiting line, despite ActionMailer being available. The controller includes the `create` action that sends password reset emails, but lacks the rate limiting protection that should be conditionally included when `ActionMailer::Railtie` is defined.

This leaves the password reset endpoint vulnerable to abuse for email spam attacks.

## System configuration
- **Rails version**: 8.0.0
- **Ruby version**: 3.2.0

## Additional context

The authentication generator template appears to have an ERB conditional that should include rate limiting when ActionMailer is available:

```erb
<%- if defined?(ActionMailer::Railtie) -%>
rate_limit to: 10, within: 3.minutes, only: :create, with: -> { redirect_to new_password_path, alert: "Try again later." }
<%- end -%>
```

However, this conditional is not evaluating correctly during template generation, resulting in missing rate limiting protection.

title: ActiveRecord call `.lease_connection` inside `.transaction` cause connection leak
security_topic: connection leak causing resource exhaustion in ActiveRecord transactions
qa_summary: The developer needed to know how to prevent the ActiveRecord connection leak (a potential availability/security risk) when using lease_connection inside a transaction, and the answer cites the Rails API docs and PR #51192, recommending calling release_connection or using with_connection(prevent_permanent_checkout: true).

comments.author: tevvi
comments.body:
### Steps to reproduce
1. rails c
2. run code:
```ruby
puts "Before: #{ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.active_connection?}"
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  ActiveRecord::Base.lease_connection
end
puts "After: #{ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.active_connection?}"
```
### Expected behavior
```
Before:
After: 
```

### Actual behavior
```
Before:
After: #<ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::Mysql2Adapter>
```

#### Explanation
When .lease_connection called in .transaction, connection is not released when exiting from .with_connection. So connection is leaked(or stuck) to current thread

#### Why it is a problem
Our application send mixed db queries with http requests, which much slower than db queries so. And we faced with connection limit on mysql server side. So we have to release(return back to process pool) all obtained db connections before start execute http requests

#### When we faced with it
1. Our legacy have dirty call db queries(.connection.execute) inside transaction, but nested in several methods. So refactor(to forward connection from .transaction yield) is complicated
2. When we added after_commit_everywhere 1.6.0 to application(rails 7.2.2.1 only) to use Sidekiq.transactional_push!. And following code cause connection leak:
```ruby
class MyWorker
  include Sidekiq::Worker
  sidekiq_options queue: :default

  def perform; end
end

puts "Before: #{ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.active_connection?}"
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  MyWorker.perform_async
end
puts "After: #{ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.active_connection?}"
```

Connection leak because next trace:
https://github.com/sidekiq/sidekiq/blob/v6.5.12/lib/sidekiq/transaction_aware_client.rb#L16
https://github.com/Envek/after_commit_everywhere/blob/v1.6.0/lib/after_commit_everywhere.rb#L100
https://github.com/Envek/after_commit_everywhere/blob/v1.6.0/lib/after_commit_everywhere.rb#L111
https://github.com/Envek/after_commit_everywhere/blob/v1.6.0/lib/after_commit_everywhere.rb#L144
https://github.com/Envek/after_commit_everywhere/blob/v1.6.0/lib/after_commit_everywhere.rb#L172

### System configuration
rails 7.2.2.1 with ruby 3.3.2
rails 8.0.2 with ruby 3.4.4

comments.author: skipkayhil
comments.body:
Isn't this by design? The API docs say

> The connection will remain leased for the entire duration of the request or job, or until [release_connection](https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveRecord/ConnectionHandling.html#method-i-release_connection) is called.

So if you want the connection returned to the pool you must use `release_connection` after `lease_connection`

comments.author: tevvi
comments.body:
@skipkayhil So how i can easily receive connection without this behaviour in complicated, nested code? 
For example:
```ruby
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  do_call
end

def do_call
  # ActiveRecord::Base.connection or something else that will release connection after #transaction block
end
```

comments.author: skipkayhil
comments.body:
```ruby
# call `release_connection` when you're done with a connection
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  do_call
end
ActiveRecore::Base.release_connection

# or only checkout connections where you need them (nesting with_connection always gives you the same connection)
def do_call
  Base.with_connection do |c|
  end
end
```

comments.author: tevvi
comments.body:
@skipkayhil So next step to rewrite all code(application and gems) which use ActiveRecore::Base.lease_connection. I think it is a complicated solution

Easier solution is return back previous logic. Add method sticky_connection with new behaviour(The connection will remain leased for the entire duration of the request or job, or until release_connection is called.) and rewrite lease_connection to release connection after with_connection block

comments.author: skipkayhil
comments.body:
> Add method sticky_connection with new behaviour(The connection will remain leased for the entire duration of the request or job, or until release_connection is called.)

This is how `ActiveRecord::Base.connection` has always worked (1 connection per request/job). `with_connection`/`release_connection` _is_ the new behavior that allows you to not have a single connection checked out for a whole request/job.

comments.author: byroot
comments.body:
What @skipkayhil said, this was done by design to not break code that had expectations about the connection being sticky: https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/51192

You can manually call `release_connection` after, or wrap the whole thing in `.with_connection(prevent_permanent_checkout: true)`.
