comments.author: zzak
comments.body:
I don't think this has anything special to do with your associations, but modifying the `key` directly like this is not supported.

The key is a secure token designed to be unique and generated automatically:
https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/ce359806416550c3b1b790c116aee5f0f9a182d4/activestorage/app/models/active_storage/blob.rb#L22

See also: https://edgeapi.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveStorage/Blob.html#method-i-key

> The key is the secure-token format from Rails in lower case. So it’ll look like: xtapjjcjiudrlk3tmwyjgpuobabd. This key is not intended to be revealed directly to the user. Always refer to blobs using the [signed_id](https://edgeapi.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveStorage/Blob.html#method-i-signed_id) or a verified form of the key.

And: https://edgeapi.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveStorage/Blob.html

> Blobs are intended to be immutable in as-so-far as their reference to a specific file goes. You’re allowed to update a blob’s metadata on a subsequent pass, but you should not update the key or change the uploaded file. If you need to create a derivative or otherwise change the blob, simply create a new blob and purge the old one.

Does this match your understanding or am I missing something?

comments.author: ysteo
comments.body:
If I were to change the code to edit the blob's `filename` instead of the blob's `key`, I'll still end up with the same bug though.

For example:

```ruby
class User < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_one_attached :profile
  belongs_to :post
  after_save :override_blob_filename

  def override_blob_filename
    profile.blob.filename = "#{id}_#{(Time.now.to_f * 1000).to_i}"
  end
end
```

The original intent of modifying the `key` was because I would like to have my files in the remote storage (i.e. Amazon S3) to be easily findable and also contains the information of the `user.id`. And I'm quite not sure if there are any other ways of achieving that intent.

https://discuss.rubyonrails.org/t/active-storage-provide-filename-for-use-where-file-is-actually-stored/86081/2

comments.author: rafaelfranca
comments.body:
@Mth0158 that code will still trigger the issue. It is wrong. You can't load the Rails frameworks without the load hooks.

Change it to:

```ruby
module ActiveStorageValidations
  class Railtie < ::Rails::Railtie
    initializer 'active_storage_validations.extend_active_storage_blob' do
      ActiveSupport.on_load(:active_storage_blob) do
        include(ActiveStorageValidations::ASVBlobMetadatable)
      end
    end
  end
end
```

comments.author: djpremier
comments.body:
Hi,

As a workaround for version 7.2 (while a new release is not made), it is possible to make the adjustment below:

```rb
# config/environments/production.rb

Rails.application.configure do
  ...
  # Store uploaded files on the local file system (see config/storage.yml for options).
  config.active_storage.service = ENV.fetch("STORAGE_PROVIDER", :azure)
  ...
end
```

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile

RUN RAILS_ENV=production SECRET_KEY_BASE_DUMMY=1 STORAGE_PROVIDER=local bundle exec rails assets:clean && \
    RAILS_ENV=production SECRET_KEY_BASE_DUMMY=1 STORAGE_PROVIDER=local bundle exec rails assets:precompile
```

This way, assets compile will run using local storage, but will maintain the desired service in other cases.

* Note: Remember of replace `:azure` with the service you're already using.

security_topic: transitive-dependency vulnerability remediation

comments.author: Kishan-Talaviya-TBS
comments.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

**Issue Description**

Hello Stripe team 👋,

We are currently using the Stripe Node SDK and noticed that it pulls in a vulnerable version of the qs package as a transitive dependency.

The qs versions < 6.14.1 are affected by CVE-2025-15284 / GHSA-6rw7-vpxm-498p, where the arrayLimit option can be bypassed using bracket notation (a[]=x), allowing unbounded array creation and leading to potential Denial of Service via memory exhaustion.

**Affected Dependency Chain**
stripe → qs@^6.11.0

This version range resolves to a vulnerable qs release.

**Impact**

Even when applications configure arrayLimit in qs.parse(), the limit is ignored for bracket notation (a[]=value), which makes it possible for an attacker to submit a single crafted request that consumes excessive memory.

This issue is particularly impactful for applications parsing user-controlled query strings or request bodies.

### Describe the solution you'd like

**Suggested Fix**

Upgrade the qs dependency to the patched version:

qs >= 6.14.1

This version includes the upstream fix that enforces arrayLimit consistently for both indexed and bracket notation, resolving CVE-2025-15284.

**References**

CVE-2025-15284
GHSA-6rw7-vpxm-498p
[References link](https://github.com/ljharb/qs/security/advisories/GHSA-6rw7-vpxm-498p)

### Describe alternatives you've considered

_No response_

First off, I would strongly recommend using the PaymentMethod API instead as we rebuilt our ACH Debit integration entirely. Please carefully read https://stripe.com/docs/payments/ach-debit and related docs which go over how to do this in details. It also encourages you to collect bank account details **client-side** securely instead of having access to those server-side which is dangerous and increases your security burden (and PCI compliance burden if you do the same for cards).

Ultimately though the code you have works just fine, it's just old and discouraged. There are no types for this, both because it's deprecated and because we discourage passing raw bank account details server-side. If you want to move forward with that approach, you will have to explicitly suppress the type errors on that code.

I'm going to close this out as this is more an integration support question and not really a bug with the library. If you have follow up questions, please work with our support team directly: https://support.stripe.com/contact

title: PaymentIntentCreateParams.PaymentMethodData does not support 'card' type
security_topic: PCI compliance rationale for API type definitions
qa_summary: The developer asked if using a token with payment_method_data type='card' is safe and why the TypeScript interface lacks the 'card' type, and the maintainer explained that raw card details require higher PCI compliance, referencing Stripe’s security guide, and confirmed that casting to any is the supported workaround.

comments.author: willbt
comments.body:
Hello, 

I used the payment_method attribute in the paymentIntents.create function and received this error: 

`A token may not be passed in as a PaymentMethod. Instead, use payment_method_data with type=card and card[token]=tok_xxxx"`


So I tried to use the payment_method_data and set the type as 'card' as below: 
payment_method_data: { type: 'card', card: { token: 'tok_xxxxx' } },

However, with TypeScript this doesn't work as the interface  PaymentIntentCreateParams.PaymentMethodData does not support the 'card' type.  

I solved by casting to any before passing to .paymentIntents.create and it works. 



```
const stripeRequest = {
      amount: request.amount,
      currency: request.currency_code,
      application_fee_amount: 0,
      payment_method_types: ['card'],
      confirm: true,
      capture_method: 'manual',
      payment_method_data: { type: 'card', card: { token: 'tok_xxxx' } },
    };

    const res = await this._stripe.paymentIntents.create(stripeRequest as any);
```

comments.author: remi-stripe
comments.body: @willbt Thanks for the report. We avoid typing the `card` hash because it'd also contain types for passing raw card details server-side which requires a higher level of [PCI compliance](https://stripe.com/docs/security/guide#validating-pci-compliance). Passing a Token id (tok_123) like you do is definitely supported but it's seen more as a temporary migration path than a canonical integration path as you should be confirming the PaymentIntent client-side instead of server-side on creation. We don't have plans to add types for that scenario but casting as any should solve the issue as you found!

comments.body:
Hi,

My client side code sends a request to the server to validate a basket. The server checks all the pricing is correct then creates a PaymentIntent object on the server side using a POST fetch. The response from that fetch is the full Stripe.PaymentIntent type (for example, including the `metadata` field in the response JSON). Returning this response back to the client will expose too much info, so I'm using the reducer function below to strip out the fields that are not available for publishable key.

```
import { PaymentIntent } from '@stripe/stripe-js'
import Stripe from 'stripe'

// pi parameter should be of Stripe.PaymentIntent type - the server side PaymentIntent type definition
// But Stripe.PaymentIntent is incompatible with @stripe/stripe-js version of PaymentIntent.
// The below code results in Typescript error.

function reduceStripePIToPublishableKeyPermissions(pi: Stripe.PaymentIntent): PaymentIntent {
    return {
        id: pi.id,
        amount: pi.amount,
        client_secret: pi.client_secret,
        currency: pi.currency,
        description: pi.description,
        last_payment_error: pi.last_payment_error,
        next_action: pi.next_action,
        payment_method: pi.payment_method,
        payment_method_types: pi.payment_method_types,
        receipt_email: pi.receipt_email,
        setup_future_usage: pi.setup_future_usage,
        shipping: pi.shipping,
        status: pi.status,
        object: pi.object,
        canceled_at: pi.canceled_at,
        cancellation_reason: pi.cancellation_reason,
        capture_method: pi.capture_method,
        confirmation_method: pi.confirmation_method,
        created: pi.created,
        livemode: pi.livemode
    }
}
```

Hope this clears it up.

comments.author: remi-stripe
comments.body: @imdavidmin Thanks for the extra details. Just to make sure I understand, the issue here is unrelated to stripe-node and its types and is instead related to Stripe.js, our client-side library, and its own types? And you get an error because you are doing your own logic to truncate/redact the JSON yourself server-side, unrelated to stripe-node?

comments.author: imdavidmin
remi-stripe
comments.body:
@imdavidmin From what I can tell, the problem is that server-side the `customer` property on `PaymentMethod` can be a `string` **or** a `Customer` object. This is due to the [Expand feature](https://stripe.com/docs/expand) which can be used server-side (and not client-side).

So when you retrieve the `PaymentIntent`, the `last_payment_error` can have the `PaymentMethod` object in it, and that could technically have the whole `Customer` object in `customer` because the types are identical to the top-level `PaymentMethod` object which it describes. This is reflected by the types in `stripe-node` for that reason [here](https://github.com/stripe/stripe-node/blob/master/types/2020-08-27/PaymentIntents.d.ts#L273)

Client-side though, the `customer` property can never be anything else than a `string` on `PaymentMethod` since it can't be expanded for security reasons. This means that inside `last_payment_error`, the type definition points to a `PaymentMethod` too but that one only supports `string` as defined [here](https://github.com/stripe/stripe-js/blob/master/types/api/PaymentMethods.d.ts#L30)

This does mean that, since you're the one turning a server-side PaymentIntent into a client-side PaymentIntent, you'll need to force the type for that specific part of the JSON (and possibly others) explicitly. You could also ignore `last_payment_error` in the returned property since it could have sensitive information such as the entire `Charge` object.

comments.author: imdavidmin
comments.body:
Thanks @remi-stripe 

I had a further read and seems like for most operations on the front-end, the client only needs the client secret, and not other attributes in a PaymentIntent. I'm trying to use the PaymentIntent object as a single source of truth so that the displayed amount, currency etc on the UI matches what the PI will charge. 

In this case, I guess Stripe's preferred way is for me to pass from the server the client secret only, and then the client makes additional queries to Stripe's server as needed? There is no built in redaction function on the stripe-node library, I assume?

Correct, there's no built-in redaction in stripe-node and it's not something we would add for now unfortunately. You could retrieve the PaymentIntent server-side with the publishable key I guess though it'd be the same as doing it client-side after passing the client_secret back.

I do understand wanting to pass more than just `client_secret`, like amount/currency, but I'd recommend doing this as your own object instead between your server-side code and client-side code.

I'm going to close as we've resolved the confusion. Don't hesitate to ask for help from developers on our Discord server: https://stripe.com/go/developer-chat

comments.author: yilmazbingo
remi-stripe
comments.body:
@yilmazbingo This is by design on our end. Sending raw card details server-side changes your PCI compliance requirements and are harmful to the vast majority of developers and businesses out there. We strongly discourage doing this and instead recommend that you collect card details securely client-side via [Elements](https://stripe.com/docs/stripe-js#elements) instead.

Ultimately though, this works if you are already meeting the higher [PCI compliance requirements](https://stripe.com/docs/security/guide#validating-pci-compliance) and you can pass card details, it will just be untyped to avoid mistaken adoption by developers.

title: Consider retrying on 429 Too Many Requests?
security_topic: automatic retry on rate limit (429) errors
qa_summary: The developer asked whether the SDK should automatically retry on 429 Too Many Requests (a rate‑limit security control), and the maintainer answered that it does not retry to avoid hiding underlying problems, citing Stripe’s rate‑limit documentation (https://stripe.com/docs/rate-limits).

comments.author: jli
comments.body:
I expected that setting `maxNetworkRetries` would result in retries when rate limited (429 Too Many Requests errors), but in testing, I noticed this isn't the case. Would the team consider adding 429 as a condition that gets retried automatically (e.g. [here, in _shouldRetry](https://github.com/stripe/stripe-node/blob/v8.131.1/lib/StripeResource.js#L251))?

I think the typical "right" thing to do when rate limited is automatic retries with exponential backoff, which is why it would be nice to have it be part of the built-in retry mechanism (though having a higher max delay than 2s might also be nice in this particular use case as well).

Thanks!

comments.author: paulasjes-stripe
comments.body:
The reason we don't automatically retry on 429 errors is that getting that error usually means there's something up with your application. It's actually quite difficult to reach Stripe's rate limit with normal traffic, so getting that error usually means you need to review your application to make sure you aren't making unnecessary requests.

Getting rate limited shouldn't be solved by automatically retrying within the SDK, as that will obfuscate the actual underlying problem.

comments.author: jli
comments.body:
Thanks @paulasjes-stripe, that makes sense!

FWIW, what prompted this is that my team gets alerted for errors in our staging environment which uses the Stripe test environment, which I know has lower rate limits[1]. (The error occasionally gets triggered during server startup, when many processes spin up at the same time and make a Stripe API call as part of initialization.)

I guess I'll find some other workaround for our staging environment. Thanks!


[1] per the Stripe error message: `Testmode request rate limit exceeded, the rate limits in testmode are lower than livemode. You can learn more about rate limits here https://stripe.com/docs/rate-limits.`

comments.author: remi-stripe
comments.body:
@jli The way we approach rate limits is that we expect the vast majority of integrations to never hit this, even at scale. In Test mode the rate limits are 25 requests per second which is extremely high overall for a test suite. If we were retrying the requests automatically for you, you might not even notice that your test suite is making that many requests to our API per second (which is a pretty high load for our servers and yours).

In this world, we would expect no test integrations to go over a few of rps other than random peaks. Otherwise you should actively look into adding mocks to your tests and not hit the API directly in test suites!

comments.author: D47A
comments.body:
_Environment used for validation_: Python 3.12 virtualenv at `.venv` with `urllib3==2.6.2` (latest on PyPI) plus optional `h2==4.3.0`.

## Findings

### 1. Unlimited decompression can exhaust client memory (High)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/response.py:619`-`src/urllib3/response.py:1110`
- **Impact:** When `Accept-Encoding` is enabled (default), `HTTPResponse.read()` always fully inflates compressed bodies without any upper bound on the decoded size. A malicious peer can send a very small gzip/brotli/zstd payload that expands to gigabytes, leading to client-side memory exhaustion or process termination, independent of the advertised `Content-Length`.
- **Details:** `_decode()` forces `max_length=-1` when `flush_decoder` is true (line 637) and directly feeds all incoming bytes to the decoder (line 641) while `read()` keeps appending to `_decoded_buffer` until the requested amount is satisfied or EOF (line 1097 onward). There is no limit tied to `Content-Length`, streaming hint, or caller-provided cap, so any compressed response is eagerly expanded into RAM.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import gzip, http.server, socketserver, threading, urllib3

  payload = gzip.compress(b"A" * (50 * 1024 * 1024))  # 50 MB after inflate

  class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_GET(self):
          self.send_response(200)
          self.send_header("Content-Encoding", "gzip")
          self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(payload)))
          self.end_headers()
          self.wfile.write(payload)
      def log_message(self, *args):
          pass

  server = socketserver.TCPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
  threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

  http = urllib3.PoolManager()
  resp = http.request("GET", f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_address[1]}/")
  print(len(resp.data))  # prints 52428800, showing the inflated size held in memory

  server.shutdown()
  ```
  Increasing the payload size proportionally increases instantaneous memory usage in the urllib3 client process.
- **Recommendation:** Introduce configurable limits for the decoded body size (e.g., cap based on `Content-Length`, a new `max_decoded_bytes` parameter, or stop inflating once a threshold is hit) and allow streaming decoders to hand off chunks directly to the caller without buffering everything in `_decoded_buffer`.

### 2. `Retry-After` header induces unbounded client sleep (Medium)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/util/retry.py:308-339`
- **Impact:** When `Retry.respect_retry_after_header` (True by default) is set, urllib3 trusts any `Retry-After` header and performs `time.sleep(retry_after)` with the parsed value. A malicious origin or intermediary can respond with `Retry-After: 31536000` to block the caller’s worker thread for a year, bypassing request-level timeouts and causing denial of service across thread pools.
- **Details:** `sleep_for_retry()` parses either a delta seconds or HTTP-date (lines 308-323) and, if present, unconditionally calls `time.sleep(retry_after)` (line 338) before reattempting the request. There is no upper bound, no linkage to the configured timeout, and no way to abort the sleep other than thread interruption.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import http.server, socketserver, threading, time
  import urllib3

  class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_GET(self):
          self.send_response(503)
          self.send_header("Retry-After", "5")  # attacker controls this value
          self.end_headers()
      def log_message(self, *args):
          pass

  server = socketserver.TCPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
  threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

  retries = urllib3.util.retry.Retry(total=1, respect_retry_after_header=True)
  http = urllib3.PoolManager()
  start = time.time()
  try:
      http.request("GET", f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_address[1]}/", retries=retries)
  except urllib3.exceptions.MaxRetryError:
      pass
  print(round(time.time() - start, 2))  # ~5.0 seconds, equal to Retry-After header

  server.shutdown()
  ```
  Raising the header to hours or days will stall the thread for the same duration.
- **Recommendation:** Cap `Retry-After` sleeps to a configurable maximum (defaulting to a few seconds) or tie the sleep to the original request timeout; allow users to opt out or enforce asynchronous cancellation.

### 3. HTTP/2 responses are always fully buffered despite `preload_content=False` (Medium)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:226-266` and `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:324-347`
- **Impact:** The experimental HTTP/2 backend accumulates the entire response body in a `bytearray` (line 230) and materializes it into `HTTP2Response.data` regardless of the caller’s `preload_content` flag. There is no streaming API, so any large HTTP/2 download forces full buffering, opening the door to memory exhaustion when a remote server (or CDN) sends multi-GB responses. Dependent services expecting streaming semantics (e.g., `stream=True` in requests) silently lose back-pressure when HTTP/2 is enabled.
- **Details:** `HTTP2Connection.getresponse()` reads until `StreamEnded`, appending each `DataReceived` chunk to `data` (lines 248-255). The resulting bytes are stored in `_data` inside `HTTP2Response` (line 331), and methods such as `.stream()` are not implemented. The passed `preload_content` flag from `HTTPSConnectionPool.urlopen()` is ignored entirely for HTTP/2 connections.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import urllib3, urllib3.http2

  urllib3.http2.inject_into_urllib3()
  http = urllib3.PoolManager(headers={"accept-encoding": "identity"})
  resp = http.request(
      "GET",
      "https://nghttp2.org/httpbin/stream-bytes/10240",
      preload_content=False,
  )
  print(resp.version_string, len(resp.data))  # -> HTTP/2 10240
  urllib3.http2.extract_from_urllib3()
  ```
  Despite `preload_content=False`, the full payload is buffered in `resp.data`. Increasing the endpoint size quickly spikes RAM.
- **Recommendation:** Honor `preload_content=False` by exposing a streaming HTTP/2 response object (e.g., forward `DataReceived` frames to an iterator) or block HTTP/2 upgrades unless the caller explicitly opts in to buffering. At a minimum, document the limitation and provide safeguards (max buffered bytes) to prevent accidental memory exhaustion.

### 4. Redirect draining eagerly decompresses attacker-controlled bodies (High)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:500`-`src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:503` and `src/urllib3/response.py:793`-`src/urllib3/response.py:801`
- **Impact:** When a response triggers a redirect, `PoolManager` always calls `response.drain_conn()` before following the `Location`. `drain_conn()` simply invokes `HTTPResponse.read()` with default arguments, which eagerly inflates any `Content-Encoding` on the response body. An attacker can reply with `302 Found`, a tiny compressed payload that expands to hundreds of megabytes, and a benign `Location`. The client must fully decompress the unused body before the redirect is honored, leading to CPU and memory exhaustion without the application ever touching the response object.
- **Details:** The redirect logic at `poolmanager.py:500-503` calls `response.drain_conn()` unconditionally. `drain_conn()` in turn calls `self.read()` (response.py:799-800), which performs the same unlimited decompression described in Finding 1. Because redirects are handled internally, even a single GET to an attacker-controlled URL can force the client to inflate arbitrary amounts of data just to reach the next hop.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import gzip, http.server, socketserver, threading, time, urllib3

  payload = gzip.compress(b"A" * (200 * 1024 * 1024))  # ~200 MB once inflated

  class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_GET(self):
          if self.path == "/next":
              self.send_response(200); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(b"ok")
              return
          self.send_response(302)
          self.send_header("Location", "/next")
          self.send_header("Content-Encoding", "gzip")
          self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(payload)))
          self.end_headers()
          self.wfile.write(payload)
      def log_message(self, *args): pass

  srv = socketserver.TCPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
  threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

  http = urllib3.PoolManager()
  start = time.time()
  resp = http.request("GET", f"http://127.0.0.1:{srv.server_address[1]}/")
  print(resp.status, resp.data, "elapsed", round(time.time() - start, 2), "s")
  srv.shutdown()
  ```
  Even though the redirect target is only “ok”, the client spends noticeable time decompressing the 200 MB payload. Scaling the compressed bomb quickly leads to out-of-memory conditions.
- **Recommendation:** Avoid decompressing or even reading redirect bodies entirely—most clients ignore them. At minimum, cap the number of bytes that `drain_conn()` will pull (both raw and decoded) or skip draining compressed redirect bodies by closing the socket instead of decompressing attacker data.

### 5. HTTP proxy redirects always drop `Authorization`/`Cookie` headers (Medium)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:602`-`src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:616` and `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:477`-`src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:487`
- **Impact:** When using a plain HTTP proxy (no CONNECT), urllib3 mis-identifies every redirect as “cross-host” because `ProxyManager.connection_from_host()` builds pools keyed on the proxy host (line 614). Consequently `conn.is_same_host(redirect_location)` always returns `False`, so the redirect logic strips every header listed in `Retry.remove_headers_on_redirect`—including `Authorization`, `Cookie`, and any user-provided entries—even if the redirect stays on the exact same origin. Authenticated HTTP workflows behind proxies therefore lose credentials or session cookies after the first redirect and often fall into infinite login loops.
- **Details:** For HTTP destinations, `connection_from_host()` ignores the target host and instead returns a pool for `self.proxy.host` (`poolmanager.py:614-616`). Later, `PoolManager.urlopen()` removes “unsafe” headers whenever `not conn.is_same_host(redirect_location)` (`poolmanager.py:477-487`). Because `conn.host` is the proxy, not the origin, this condition is always true and every redirect is treated as cross-origin.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import urllib3
  proxy = urllib3.ProxyManager("http://proxy.local:8080")
  conn = proxy.connection_from_host("example.com", 80, "http")
  print("pool host:", conn.host)  # -> proxy.local
  print("same host redirect?",
        conn.is_same_host("http://example.com/secure"))  # -> False
  ```
  The above means cookies/Authorization headers will be stripped before following even a relative redirect to `/secure`. Users behind mandatory HTTP proxies cannot stay authenticated on any site that issues redirects (OAuth, SSO, login flows).
- **Recommendation:** Track the original destination host separately from the proxy host when evaluating `is_same_host` for redirects, or short-circuit the removal logic when a forwarding proxy is in use so headers are only stripped when the *destination* host truly changes.

### 6. Enabling HTTP/2 globally makes proxy usage fail outright (Low)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:94`-`src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:103` and `src/urllib3/http2/__init__.py:30`-`src/urllib3/http2/__init__.py:42`
- **Impact:** Calling `urllib3.http2.inject_into_urllib3()` replaces every `HTTPSConnection` with `HTTP2Connection`, which explicitly raises `NotImplementedError` whenever `proxy` or `proxy_config` is supplied. Any deployment that uses proxies (corporate networks, tests that rely on mitmproxy, etc.) immediately loses outbound HTTPS support once HTTP/2 is injected, effectively taking the client offline.
- **Details:** `HTTP2Connection.__init__` rejects all proxy kwargs (line 94) and the injector rewires `HTTPSConnectionPool.ConnectionCls` globally to `HTTP2Connection` (http2/__init__.py lines 30-36). Proxied requests therefore crash before any network traffic is attempted.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import urllib3, urllib3.http2

  urllib3.http2.inject_into_urllib3()
  proxy = urllib3.ProxyManager("http://127.0.0.1:3128/")
  try:
      proxy.request("GET", "https://example.com/", timeout=urllib3.util.Timeout(1))
  except Exception as exc:
      print(type(exc).__name__, exc)
  finally:
      urllib3.http2.extract_from_urllib3()
  # -> NotImplementedError: Proxies aren't supported with HTTP/2
  ```
- **Recommendation:** Either keep HTTP/1.1 as a fallback ALPN option when proxies are present or block the injection entirely when proxy settings are detected so that enabling HTTP/2 cannot silently break every proxied request.

## Summary

| #   | Title                                                         | Location                                                                        | Severity |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| 1   | Unlimited decompression grows unbounded client memory         | `src/urllib3/response.py:619-1110`                                              | High     |
| 2   | `Retry-After` header can stall threads indefinitely           | `src/urllib3/util/retry.py:308-339`                                             | Medium   |
| 3   | HTTP/2 responses ignore streaming hints and buffer entirely   | `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:226-347`                                       | Medium   |
| 4   | Redirect draining decompresses attacker-controlled bodies     | `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:500-503`, `src/urllib3/response.py:793-801`         | High     |
| 5   | HTTP proxies treat every redirect as cross-host and drop auth | `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:477-487`, `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:602-616`      | Medium   |
| 6   | Global HTTP/2 injection disables all proxied HTTPS traffic    | `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:94-103`, `src/urllib3/http2/__init__.py:30-42` | Low      |

comments.author: illia-v
comments.body:
Hi @D47A,

Thanks for the report! However, we'd appreciate if you reported potential security vulnerabilities privately using our security contact mentioned in [our Security Policy](https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/security/policy).

> 1. Unlimited decompression can exhaust client memory

We are aware of the issue, but we do not consider it a vulnerability.
urllib3's users are advised to use [the streaming API](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/advanced-usage.html#streaming-and-i-o)  when dealing with responses of large or unknown length including responses from untrusted sources.

FYI, we applied a security hardening to the streaming API in the recent 2.6.0 release, check GHSA-2xpw-w6gg-jr37.

While unlimited decompression by the non-streaming API is not a security issue due to the described reasons, we consider adding parameters for configuring the maximum allowed response size as a new feature.


> 2. `Retry-After` header induces unbounded client sleep

Duplicate of #3743, fixed in 2.6.3


> 3. HTTP/2 responses are always fully buffered despite `preload_content=False`

It is fine to report HTTP/2 issues publicly because it is an experimental and uncomplete functionality.
#3300 exists for adding support for streaming HTTP/2 responses.


> 4. Redirect draining eagerly decompresses attacker-controlled bodies

This is a valid security issue, fixed in 2.6.3, see GHSA-38jv-5279-wg99


> 5. HTTP proxy redirects always drop `Authorization`/`Cookie` headers

I am not inclined to accept this as a security issue since the confidential information is not passed to third parties, but the issue does sound like a bug.


> 6. Enabling HTTP/2 globally makes proxy usage fail outright

#3299 exists for adding support for proxies with HTTP/2.

human_note: Confirmed security vulnerability with advisory and fix (redirect draining + attacker-controlled decompression).

comments.author: nuclearpidgeon
comments.body:
For practicality purposes for anyone else hitting this error: a decent downgrade-avoiding workaround if you can control the SSL context passed into urllib3 is to just disable the `VERIFY_X509_STRICT` verification flag that is now set by default (courtesy @vstinner on https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/112389#issuecomment-2024625491 ):

```
>>> import ssl

>>> ctx = ssl.create_default_context()
>>> ctx.verify_flags & ssl.VERIFY_X509_STRICT
<VerifyFlags.VERIFY_X509_STRICT: 32>
>>> ctx.verify_flags & ssl.VERIFY_X509_PARTIAL_CHAIN
<VerifyFlags.VERIFY_X509_PARTIAL_CHAIN: 524288>

>>> ctx.verify_flags &= ~(ssl.VERIFY_X509_STRICT | ssl.VERIFY_X509_PARTIAL_CHAIN)
>>> ctx.verify_flags & ssl.VERIFY_X509_STRICT
<VerifyFlags.VERIFY_DEFAULT: 0>
>>> ctx.verify_flags & ssl.VERIFY_X509_PARTIAL_CHAIN
<VerifyFlags.VERIFY_DEFAULT: 0>
```

from here you can pass this `ctx` into a urllib3 PoolManager via:
```py
pool = urllib3.PoolManager(ssl_context=ctx)
```

As per the other linked issues, python/cpython/pull/112389 introduced the change causing the AKI validation behaviour by tightening the flags used in OpenSSL - it seems it got merged in to Python v3.13.0a5, so presumably it affects all 3.13 versions of Python.

human_note: Security-relevant (TLS certificate validation / X.509 verification behavior), with a mitigation tied to Python 3.13 verification changes.

comments.author: 8fuhst
comments.body:
### Context

What are you trying to do?

I‘d like to set up an mTLS connection between a client and a server. The client has the private key for their certificate in a TPM/HSM, and thus cannot pass a keyfile via path into urllib.request(), as a TPM/HSM typically only ever takes data it then signs internally and returns the signature, but never directly exposes its private keys.

How do you expect to do it?

Optimal solution would be to allow passing a key handle for a given TPM (e.g. /dev/tpmrm0) instead of a keyfile into urllib.request()

Is it something you currently cannot do?

This is currently not supported to my knowledge

Is this related to an existing issue/problem?

Not as far as i know

### Alternatives

Can you achieve the same result doing it in an alternative way?

The only apparent workaround seems to be to not use urllib, or generate a highly custom SSLContext in which you use e.g. OpenSSL managed keys or the tpm2-pkcs11 interface, all of which requires extensive setup, and even that might end up requiring using a lower-level library like Python http.

Is the alternative considerable?

Not really, required effort is very large.

### Duplicate

Has the feature been requested before?
If so, please provide a link to the issue.

I was unable to find anything using the search function.

### Contribution

Would you be willing to submit a PR?
_(Help can be provided if you need assistance submitting a PR)_

Sure, if I can get some pointers in the right direction (e.g. to where the certificateVerify response signature for a mTLS handshake is generated)

comments.author: tsturzl
pquentin
comments.body:
The `ssl` module in Python *is* OpenSSL-specific, which is unfortunate for several reasons. [PEP 748](https://peps.python.org/pep-0748/) is trying to fix that and does mention TPM/HSM, but this effort appears to have stalled.

We wanted to deprecate pyOpenSSL support for 2.0, but [reverted course](https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/pull/3127) as it's the only way to support in-memory certificates. If supporting KEYTYPE/CERTTYPE is possible (and maintainable) through `pyOpenSSL`, we could accept pull requests here.

comments.author: sigmavirus24
comments.body:
https://github.com/pyca/pyopenssl/blob/62a0f5041e6a7e8c0f01b6421b4e95c6daca5f99/src/OpenSSL/crypto.py#L2343-L2351

pyOpenSSL does not support this today from what I can tell.

comments.author: tsturzl
comments.body:
> https://github.com/pyca/pyopenssl/blob/62a0f5041e6a7e8c0f01b6421b4e95c6daca5f99/src/OpenSSL/crypto.py#L2343-L2351
> 
> pyOpenSSL does not support this today from what I can tell.

I'm not sure those are the right methods the PyOpenSSLContext wrapper object in this project seems to be using the `OpenSSL.SSL.Context` class and loading the certs and key into that SSL Context. Still, I don't think PyOpenSSL gives explicit support for this, because from what I can tell from digging through the C code is that OpenSSL lets you load a provider and basically use that provider to retrieve a key and/or cert. So the challenge would be getting PyOpenSSL to support this, and that may or may not require a change to PyOpenSSLContext. It all depends on what changes PyOpenSSL might allow in terms of contributions.

From what I can tell PyOpenSSLContext doesn't currently support loading keys from in-memory buffers, though PyOpenSSL does. So to me the logical path here would likely be:

1. Allow PyOpenSSLContext to set the private key and certificate objects that PyOpenSSL provides back from those functions referenced in the qutoed link, this allows the developer to directly interact with PyOpenSSL to load the cert (`X509`) and private key (`PKey`) object themselves however they see fit. This would also then give direct support for loading in-memory keys/certs. Alternatively you could just create a getter on the PyOpenSSLContext wrapper object to get `self._ctx` and then they can act on it directly. Technically it's accessible as is, but `_ctx` implies that it's a protected field.

2. Either there needs to be an addition to pyOpenSSL to implement loading a provider and using the provider to load the corresponding `PKey` and `X509` objects, this doesn't seem too hard. It all depends on whether or not pyOpenSSL will allow this. It would also be entirely possible to spin this off into a third-party extension to pyOpenSSL. Either way this interface would simply just allow you to load a provider and load the private key and cert from that provider into the corresponding `PKey` and `X509` pyOpenSSL types.


The first point I think is desirable either way for flexibility sake and adding the formal ability to load in memory cert/keys, and that's basically where the changes to urllib3 would end in this case. If we can load `PKey` and `X509` pyOpenSSL objects into the PyOpenSSLContext in some way then the rest of the work would be to add the ability to load these objects from the provider in PyOpenSSL or some third party PyOpenSSL extension.

I can probably start by creating a PyOpenSSL extension, and then proposing that to the pyca team as a PR. Once that's done it should be possible to load TPM/HSM/SmartCard private keys and certs either through their direct providers or through a PKCS#11 provider.

I can make the urllib3 changes too, unless someone else can make those quick changes.

comments.author: sigmavirus24
comments.body: PyOpenSSL's `SSL.Context` has a way to use a `PKey` or better yet a `cryptography` PrivateKey. As far as an extension goes, we're not going to support any extension, it would need to land in pyOpenSSL upstream.

comments.author: tsturzl
comments.body:
In this case urllib3 wouldn't need to support an extension, the extension would just be to provide the missing FFI integrations with OpenSSL. Ultimate you'd just be loading a key and cert into the existing SSL context. The point of an extension would mostly just be to add support before an upstream patch to pyopenssl can be fully decided upon. For me it'll just be a convenient test bed. I have most of it hashed out, can probably test it this weekend, and I can reach out to pyopenssl maintainers and see what it might take to get this in. It'll probably be best to focus on PyOpenSSL since that's what these providers are integrating with and that's what this SSL Context is expecting as input.

Have a good weekend!

comments.author: tsturzl
comments.body:
Unfortunately, I hit a dead end. I ended up having to add some FFI bindings into OpenSSL. Turns out all the pyopenssl stuff actually lives in pyca/cryptography. I got the bindings working locally, and even integrated into pyopenssl, however the pyca team does not want to expose the provider API from OpenSSL that makes this possible. They didn't give a solid explanation, but just said they feel like it's not well designed, and ultimately are going to deprecate openssl c-bindings, which really makes it seem like they have no plan to expand pyopenssl to support any of the new openssl v3 APIs.

The only option will be to use the old engines interface, which OpenSSL v3 has deprecated, but pyca has bindings for. However, I know that certain engines don't work correctly in OpenSSL v3. For example the tpm2-pkcs11 project will not work with a pkcs11 OpenSSL engine.

So as far as things go in python, there's not a lot of good options other than wrapping OpenSSL yourself. I might work with the pyca team to implement some kind of pkcs11 support into the cryptography package, since pkcs11 is probably the best way to integrate with the most options, but that will take time.

You can keep this ticket open, but I don't think this is going to happen for a while, and furthermore I don't actually think it's a urllib3 related feature. The feature is just lacking anywhere in the python ecosystem as far as TLS support with hsm/tpm secured keys goes.

comments.author: pquentin
comments.body: Thanks @tsturzl! This makes sense. Thanks a lot for keeping us updated. Closing this for now, but happy to reopen if there's something urllib3 can do.

It also relative with https://github.com/openssl/openssl/issues/12566

The underscore is available to domain name, but not available to host name

So, if you need to pass the host name verification then you can disable it on ssl context

example follows

```
import ssl
from urllib3 import PoolManager

context = ssl.create_default_context()
context.check_hostname = False

with PoolManager(ssl_context=context) as pool:
  pool.request('GET','https://cs_sample_feed.s3.amazonaws.com/')
```

Disabling `check_hostname` isn't a good workaround here. While you can't rely on OpenSSL to verify the non-conforming hostname, you can use `assert_hostname` instead, which will use our own hostname checking implementation:

```python3
import urllib3

with urllib3.PoolManager(assert_hostname="cs_sample_feed.s3.amazonaws.com") as http:
    resp = http.request("GET", "https://cs_sample_feed.s3.amazonaws.com/")
    print(resp)
```

And next time you choose a bucket name, try to avoid underscores!

comments.author: sigmavirus24
comments.body: To be fair, openssl also enforces a limit on a DNS name in the list of SANs when generating a CSR. That limit is the defined max length of a common name but it does not apply in the specifications to SANs. So openssl applying validations that are invalid isn't strictly new or surprising.

comments.author: mmulich
comments.body:
@pquentin Thank you for the workaround!

And for anyone else that might come across this from the `requests` API perspective. Here is a quick and dirty solution that incorporates this workaround.

```py
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter as BaseHTTPAdapter
from requests.sessions import Session as BaseSession
from urllib3.util import parse_url


class HTTPSAdapter(BaseHTTPAdapter):
    def send(self, request, stream=False, timeout=None, verify=True, cert=None, proxies=None):
        _, _, host, _, _, _, _ = parse_url(request.url)
        # Re-initialize the PoolManager with the hostname assertion.
        # https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/issues/3465#issuecomment-2324655893
        self.init_poolmanager(
             self._pool_connections,
             self._pool_maxsize,
             block=self._pool_block,
             assert_hostname=host,
         )
        return super().send(request, stream=stream, timeout=timeout, verify=verify, cert=cert, proxies=proxies)


class Session(BaseSession):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        # Override the base adapter to use our adapter
        self.mount('https://', HTTPSAdapter())
```

comments.author: sethmlarson
comments.body:
urllib3 v2.0 uses whatever the system (or OpenSSL's) configured cipher suites are by default. My guess is that your OpenSSL is configured to use non-weak ciphers, so when the handshake happens there is no overlap between the client and server. The work-around is to either configure the exact ciphersuite you need in urllib3 or to configure your OpenSSL to allow a weaker ciphersuite (not recommended, as it would impact all applications).

Going to close this as I believe this is the issue you're facing, if there's additional information we can reopen this issue.

comments.author: sigmavirus24
comments.body: urllib3 allows you to post file-like objects. Those may not be rewindable and thus we can't retry them. When users pass those, it's often to avoid storing everything in memory and so we also cannot cache that data to resend it.

title: Deprecate schemeless URLs?
security_topic: deprecation of schemeless URLs
qa_summary: The developer asked whether schemeless URLs should be deprecated/removed to avoid parsing ambiguities (a potential security risk), and the answer provides a concrete fork branch that removes support for schemeless URLs (https://github.com/JohnJamesUtley/urllib3/tree/remove_schemeless_urls).

comments.author: kenballus
comments.body:
### Context

Schemeless URLs can cause a lot of parsing confusion because they aren't standardized in the RFC. Examples like the following are especially weird, and could cause problems when interoperability with other parsers matters:
```
"evil.com://good.com"
```

Here are some popular URL parsers' interpretations:
urllib3:
```
Scheme:   (nil)
Userinfo: (nil)
Host:     evil.com
Port:     (nil)
Path:     //good.com
Query:    (nil)
Fragment: (nil)
```

cpython urllib:
```
Scheme:   evil.com
Userinfo: (nil)
Host:     good.com
Port:     (nil)
Path:     (nil)
Query:    (nil)
Fragment: (nil)
```

furl:
```
Scheme:   evil.com
Userinfo: (nil)
Host:     good.com
Port:     (nil)
Path:     (nil)
Query:    (nil)
Fragment: (nil)
```

hyperlink:
```
Scheme:   evil.com
Userinfo: (nil)
Host:     good.com
Port:     (nil)
Path:     /
Query:    (nil)
Fragment: (nil)
```

rfc3986:
```
Scheme:   evil.com
Userinfo: (nil)
Host:     good.com
Port:     (nil)
Path:     (nil)
Query:    (nil)
Fragment: (nil)
```

yarl:
```
Scheme:   evil.com
Userinfo: (nil)
Host:     good.com
Port:     (nil)
Path:     /
Query:    (nil)
Fragment: (nil)
```

As you can see, we're the outlier here.

In my opinion, this is something worth fixing, but I imagine that schemeless URLs are in pretty widespread use with urllib3. Thus, we might consider adding a DeprecationWarning that encourages people to explicitly state their schemes.

comments.author: sethmlarson
comments.body:
Totally agree that this is something worth fixing, thank you for doing all this research and opening this. My hope is that schemeless URLs aren't as widespread as we think and that we've been supporting this mostly for backwards compatibility and not because a large swath of the ecosystem relies on it.

I think adding a `DeprecationWarning` as you mentioned that links to this issue (we can edit the issue body to provide actionable feedback for users) and says that a removal will occur in a future version. We can then get that released in 1.26.x and 2.x to start warning users and gathering feedback if necessary.

comments.body: In my experience these often occur in the Location header and require resolution per the specifications. I don't remember how urllib3 does redirect handling but this may be required to support that

title: `util.parse_url` allows invalid characters in reg-names
security_topic: percent-encoding vs rejection of invalid characters in URL parsing
qa_summary: Developer asked whether invalid characters in URL reg-names should be percent‑encoded or cause a parse failure; the maintainer referenced the WHATWG URL spec (e.g., https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#forbidden-host-code-point) indicating they should reject such characters.

comments.author: kenballus
comments.body:
### `util.parse_url` allows invalid characters in reg-names.

RFC3986 defines reg-name as follows:
`reg-name = *( unreserved / pct-encoded / sub-delims )`
`unreserved = ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" / "." / "_" / "~"`
`sub-delims = "!" / "$" / "&" / "'" / "(" / ")" / "*" / "+" / "," / ";" / "="`
`pct-encoded = "%" HEXDIG HEXDIG`

Currently, `urllib3.util.parse_url` accepts reg-names containing characters outside those enumerated above.
The incorrectly accepted ASCII characters are `[\x00-\x20]`, `"`, `<`, `>`, `^`, `` ` ``, `{`, `|`, `}`, and `\x7f`.

### Environment
```python3
>>> print("OS", platform.platform())
OS Linux-6.0.7-arch1-1-x86_64-with-glibc2.36
>>> print("Python", platform.python_version())
urllib3 2.0.0.dev0
>>> print("urllib3", urllib3.__version__)
Python 3.10.8
```

### Steps to Reproduce

```python3
>>> import urllib3
>>> urllib3.util.parse_url("http://|") # Whatever happens, "|" should not end up in a reg-name.
Url(scheme='http', auth=None, host='|', port=None, path=None, query=None, fragment=None)
>>> # But it does!
```

comments.author: kenballus
comments.body:
WHATWG also disallows many of these characters. Quoting the WHATWG spec:

"If input contains a [forbidden host code point](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#forbidden-host-code-point), [validation error](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#validation-error), return failure."
"A forbidden host code point is U+0000 NULL, U+0009 TAB, U+000A LF, U+000D CR, U+0020 SPACE, U+0023 (#), U+002F (/), U+003A (:), U+003C (<), U+003E (>), U+003F (?), U+0040 (@), U+005B ([), U+005C (\), U+005D (]), U+005E (^), or U+007C (|)."
(If you see any of these characters, the parse should fail)

"If input contains a [code point](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#code-point) that is not a [URL code point](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#url-code-points) and not U+0025 (%), [validation error](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#validation-error)."
"The URL code points are [ASCII alphanumeric](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#ascii-alphanumeric), U+0021 (!), U+0024 ($), U+0026 (&), U+0027 ('), U+0028 LEFT PARENTHESIS, U+0029 RIGHT PARENTHESIS, U+002A (*), U+002B (+), U+002C (,), U+002D (-), U+002E (.), U+002F (/), U+003A (:), U+003B (;), U+003D (=), U+003F (?), U+0040 (@), U+005F (_), U+007E (~), and [code points](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#code-point) in the range U+00A0 to U+10FFFD, inclusive, excluding [surrogates](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#surrogate) and [noncharacters](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#noncharacter)."
(If you see any characters other than these characters, they will later be percent-encoded.)

comments.author: kenballus
comments.body:
> 3986 isn't the end of the line. WHAT WG supports Unicode ignoring 3987

The docs say "This parser is RFC 3986 and RFC 6874 compliant," so I would assume that RFC compliance trumps WHATWG compliance. Is that a safe assumption to make?

I'm not sure what Unicode has to do with this; this is about incorrectly accepted ASCII characters. The PR currently breaks Unicode, but that's pretty easily fixable, I just need to know which Unicode URL spec to comply with (RFC3987 or WHATWG).

comments.author: sethmlarson
comments.body: @kenballus Yeah that's a safe assumption, we implement RFC 3986 instead of WHATWG. Why have you closed your PR btw?

comments.author: kenballus
comments.body:
I closed the PR because I made it from the main branch of my fork and it had an extraneous fix built in. Working on making a series of PRs, each from separate branches, that fix a few different things.

Currently traveling for Thanksgiving, but will submit in the next few days.

comments.author: kenballus
comments.body: If someone tries to encode a URL containing an invalid character (e.g. `'\x00'`) in a reg-name, should we automatically percent-encode it, or should we reject the parse?

comments.author: sethmlarson
comments.body: Sorry for taking so long to get to this. I'm going to make a call that we continue doing what we're doing and percent-encode everything that's outside the valid ranges for each component. Can discuss more but I think it's better to make a call rather than delay indefinitely.

title: Investigate HTTPConnection.auto_open
security_topic: purpose and deprecation of urllib3 auto_open property related to CPython host/port mutation bug
qa_summary: The developer needed to know the security purpose of urllib3’s auto_open flag—added to work around a CPython bug that could cause proxy‑bypass and socket‑reuse issues—and the answer cites the CPython bug BPO 7776 and the fixing commits/PRs (e.g., urllib3 #385, commit 4fb351cd27cc5ce7b55ed961eee695743c95f9c6) as concrete evidence.

comments.author: sethmlarson
comments.body:
urllib3 makes multiple mentions to a property on `http.client.HTTPConnection` called `auto_open`. The property isn't used much in the current stdlib `http.client` module, but has some implications for urllib3: mainly that connections may not be re-used based on this value?

In `urllib3.connection.py`:

```python
# Calls self._set_hostport(), so self.host is
# self._tunnel_host below.
self._tunnel()  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
# Mark this connection as not reusable
self.auto_open = 0
```

In `urllib3.connectionpool.py`:

```python
conn.close()
if getattr(conn, "auto_open", 1) == 0:
    # This is a proxied connection that has been mutated by
    # http.client._tunnel() and cannot be reused (since it would
    # attempt to bypass the proxy)
    conn = None
```

I suspect that `http.client.HTTPConnection._tunnel()` in the past may have rewritten `.host` and `.port` properties or something like this and this was our method of "guarding" against that? Currently `host` and `port` properties on a connection point to the first origin (read: proxy) on a requests' journey to the destination origin.

- What is the intent of this property and it's values?
- Has that intent changed since the original code in urllib3 using the value was written (git blame!)?
- Can we remove our use/dependence on this value?
- Should we write some tests for this value? (We currently have none!!! :scream:)
- Can any of these fixes land in 1.26.x?

comments.author: pquentin
comments.body:
Your suspicion is correct!

> * What is the intent of this property and it's values?

#369  added `auto_open` to work around a bug in CPython where host and port were mutated to the target origin, which broke socket reuse. It can be unset, or set to 0.
 
> * Has that intent changed since the original code in urllib3 using the value was written (git blame!)?

Yes. This CPython bug was then fixed as part of [BPO 7776](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/52024) by https://github.com/python/cpython/commit/9da047b3a5d1a5421ee829aab1e9bc57427826c9 which went to Python 3.4.1 and was [backported to Python 2.7.7](https://github.com/python/cpython/commit/36f28f7ae830197330b7d30f7b40e727d30d5d25).

That change caused a regression in urllib3 that was fixed in https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/pull/385 and https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/commit/4fb351cd27cc5ce7b55ed961eee695743c95f9c6. I found this difficult to follow given the two changes, so here is the full diff:

```diff
diff --git a/urllib3/connection.py b/urllib3/connection.py
index 45bef659..5feb3322 100644
--- a/urllib3/connection.py
+++ b/urllib3/connection.py
@@ -168,21 +168,25 @@ class VerifiedHTTPSConnection(HTTPSConnection):
         resolved_cert_reqs = resolve_cert_reqs(self.cert_reqs)
         resolved_ssl_version = resolve_ssl_version(self.ssl_version)
 
-        # the _tunnel_host attribute was added in python 2.6.3 (via
-        # http://hg.python.org/cpython/rev/0f57b30a152f) so pythons 2.6(0-2) do
-        # not have them.
+        hostname = self.host
         if getattr(self, '_tunnel_host', None):
+            # _tunnel_host was added in Python 2.6.3
+            # (See: http://hg.python.org/cpython/rev/0f57b30a152f)
+
             self.sock = sock
             # Calls self._set_hostport(), so self.host is
             # self._tunnel_host below.
             self._tunnel()
 
+            # Override the host with the one we're requesting data from.
+            hostname = self._tunnel_host
+
         # Wrap socket using verification with the root certs in
         # trusted_root_certs
         self.sock = ssl_wrap_socket(sock, self.key_file, self.cert_file,
                                     cert_reqs=resolved_cert_reqs,
                                     ca_certs=self.ca_certs,
-                                    server_hostname=self.host,
+                                    server_hostname=hostname,
                                     ssl_version=resolved_ssl_version)
 
         if resolved_cert_reqs != ssl.CERT_NONE:
@@ -191,7 +195,7 @@ class VerifiedHTTPSConnection(HTTPSConnection):
                                    self.assert_fingerprint)
             elif self.assert_hostname is not False:
                 match_hostname(self.sock.getpeercert(),
-                               self.assert_hostname or self.host)
+                               self.assert_hostname or hostname)
 
 
 if ssl:
```

We used to rely on the mutation because we wanted to know the hostname of the target origin, which is why we needed that fix.


> * Can we remove our use/dependence on this value?

Yes, given we don't support any CPython version with the bug anymore. Pull request incoming.
 
> * Should we write some tests for this value? (We currently have none!!! :scream:)

Actually, we do have a test: #363 added test_connect_reconn. I confirmed that it does cover the `if getattr(conn, "auto_open", 1) == 0` condition. Thankfully, we'll be able to remove `auto_open` but keep the test.
 
> * Can any of these fixes land in 1.26.x?

No, given [we currently support Python < 2.7.9 in 1.26.x](https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/blob/34d7348bb96eca390c2115aeeee31d1147830844/src/urllib3/util/ssl_.py#L129-L179).
